This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. Under the premise that the ground state can be found within a specific type of function space known as the spectral Barron space, we establish that the convergence rate of the generalization error is not influenced by the dimensionality $d$. Furthermore, we confirm the validity of this premise through a new estimate demonstrating that the ground state's norm is finite within this space, and provide an alternative explanation utilizing quantum mechanics principles. Additionally, we explore the effects of mutations in the Hamiltonian operator on the ground state, and establish that the generalization error remains relatively stable when the parameter space is expanded. Based on these findings, we hypothesize the existence of a non-vanishing gap between the first two eigenvalues of the operator, and establish a new estimate for the number of eigenfunctions within the specified function space. Finally, we utilize the established results to calculate the generalization performance for calculating excited states, and establish that the generalization error can be estimated using the difference between energy levels. Notably, we discover that the generalization performance can be influenced by a dimensionless parameter characterizing the type of Hamiltonian operator, and that the worst-case scenario performance depends on the number of body electrons in the system.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, presenting a scenario that suggests the patterns could serve as directional indicators for the detection of nearby Galactical cosmic ray sources. Furthermore, we observed that the anisotropy distribution observed at energies above 8 EeV closely resembles the large-scale distribution of extragalactic faint radio luminous galaxies when taking into account spatial correlations and morphological characteristics. We estimated that a significant anisotropy signal could be anticipated from sources brighter than 3.5×10^85 erg/s at redshifts up to approximately z=0.03, and that anisotropy patterns potentially attributable to individual sources could be anticipated from sources brighter than approximately 6.8×10^86 erg/s at redshifts up to approximately z=0.1. We concluded that anisotropy detection in very energetic cosmic rays may function as a highly efficient Galactical source detector. We presented a hypothetical scenario where the observed anisotropy at higher energies is produced by a bright nearby source within our Galaxy. We showed that the observed characteristics of anisotropy at higher energies including detected near-source excess and recorded orientations of highest activity level, can be reproduced by a source with an energy-generated flux of approximately 51% of the estimated flux of the Cen A source, located at a distance of approximately 2° from the direction of the source, and characterized by an energy-generated flux two times its neighboring volume average. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of digitized tissues, our results indicate that federated learning can efficiently enhance pre-trained models and prevent knowledge loss within a decentralized learning framework. Our findings also suggest that the efficiency of FL depends on various factors, particularly the size of the dataset and the number of clients involved. Furthermore, we identified distinct patterns in how different models learned and adapted, which could be used to optimize future FL experiments. The implementation details of our study are freely accessible on GitHub, along with the code and a modified version of PyTorch that was necessary for conducting our federated learning tests. For instance, we observed that the difference in performance between models can be significant even when using the same update rule, which could have important implications for evaluating the effectiveness of different update rules in future federated learning experiments. Additionally, we noticed that the variability in model behavior decreased as the training progress plateaued, which could help in determining when a federated learning experiment can be considered complete. The code modifications that we made to enable the distributed training of deep learning models in a decentralized environment are also worthy of note. For instance, we used a custom data loader to ensure that each model processes a diverse subset of the dataset, which could help in reducing the risk of overfitting during the training process. The behavior of super-massive black holes in their lifetime is primarily dominated by a relatively low level of accretion well below the Eddington limit, making them low-luminosity active galactic nuclei.  A crucial aspect of these objects is the prediction by various black hole theories and simulations that they produce collimated jets.  However, detecting this activity in the vast majority of these low-luminosity active black holes remains impossible due to our current technological limitations.  One particularly promising avenue of research involves observing the activity of these objects using quasi-simultaneous multiwavelength data, as exemplified by the recently taken Nucleosynthesis Synthesis Large Sky Area Survey (NOYS).  In this study, we examine how the application of machine learning algorithms to NOYS data helps us distinguish between low-luminosity active black hole activity and inhomogeneous interstellar material within the observed sky.  By combining quasi-simultaneous UVW2, clear, and near-infrared r' images of about 200,000 point sources, we trained our classifier using 10% of the data and verified its efficiency using 10 times repeated testing with the remaining samples, thereby validating our findings through extensive testing.  In the process of training our classifier, we found that low-luminosity active black hole activity and inhomogeneous interstellar material could be accurately differentially diagnosed within the observed sky, yielding about 0.25% false positives among the non-active point sources.  In conclusion, this study successfully employs machine learning techniques on multiwavelength data from low-luminosity active black holes to accurately identify collimated jet activity, thereby providing valuable insights into the activity of these objects and, by extension, super-massive black holes in their natural state.  Future applications of this classifier to multiwavelength data will allow us to estimate the prevalence of collimated jet activity among low-luminosity active black holes, thereby providing essential constraints for theoretical models of these objects.  In addition, this classifier may also be used within NOYS to generate an inventory that includes the location, spectral characteristics, and activity level of all low-luminosity active black holes and other celestial objects that produce collimated jet activity within the Milky Way. Fortunately, reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to optimizing model-free nonlinear controller designs without extensive system modeling. Despite the efficiency of this method, its reliance on numerous trial-and-error experiments can degrade plant quality and necessitate frequent maintenance. In order to mitigate this limitation, a proposed model-free, two-step design approach aims to improve the efficiency and adaptability of reinforcement learning by leveraging an offline linear control algorithm initially. The method's effectiveness is evaluated through simulations of a gas turbine system and an aircraft pitch control system, showing significant performance enhancements for both systems. The two-step design approach is shown to achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art model-free reinforcement learning designs, all while minimizing offline maintenance times by up to 80%. The introduced methodology is expected to be useful for designing nonlinear controllers in closed-loop systems where substantial plant characteristic changes occur over time. The approach is particularly useful for engineers without in-depth knowledge of advanced control theory, as evidenced by the positive feedback from multiple aircraft industry partners. This design incorporates a silicon pixel tracker, a silicon stripper, a silicon or rhenium crystal inner detector, a tungsten woodpile calorimeter, and a quartz flux monitor. Notably, the SiD focuses on an inner volume with minimal magnet thickness, enabling precise momentum measurements and optimal for the "forward" ILC operating mode. For an all-silicon inner detector, the transverse mass resolution is approximately 0.9 GeV, or approximately 0.6 GeV for a rhenium crystal inner detector. For the "backward" ILC operating mode, the inner volume is enlarged to include more radiation length to account for thicker inner layers, although this compromise slightly degrades the transverse mass resolution. Regardless, the SiD maintains an acceptable transverse mass resolution below 1.2 GeV. Remote sensing, used to monitor Earth's condition via satellite data, has significant benefits for enhancing our daily lives and living environment. The growing number of orbiting satellites leads to the publication of multiple datasets with diverse sensors and domains to support remote sensing research. This study offers a thorough review of more than 400 publicly available datasets across various applications including land use, disaster monitoring, and weather forecasting. These datasets are analyzed based on several criteria: volume, research impact, resolution variations, research fields, and data relationships. Based on these dataset attributes, we establish a method to evaluate and select datasets for benchmarking model performance. Moreover, we introduce a platform called EarthNets, designed to ensure fair and consistent evaluation of deep learning techniques on remote sensing data. The platform integrates standard dataset collections and advanced deep learning models to bridge the gap between remote sensing and machine learning communities. We conduct comprehensive evaluations using this platform on a new benchmark, and our findings can guide future research. The platform, along with dataset collections, can be accessed at https://earthnets.github.io/. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/EarthNets/EarthNets.

Identifying irregularities in urban data is a pressing research issue. Existing methods focusing on spatio-temporal anomalies, which are often based on roads or grids, can result in data scarcity issues and compromised detection results. This paper introduces a novel approach that tackles these challenges. An unsupervised anomaly detection framework called ReAD is proposed to identify irregularly shaped regions with arbitrary boundaries. This framework combines spatial and temporal factors and employs the DenseRNN and DenseConv models to extract meaningful features and characterize anomaly patterns. The effectiveness of ReAD is evaluated through experiments using simulated and real-world datasets, which demonstrate its ability to extract meaningful features and identify anomalies with varying boundaries. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, ReAD outperforms existing approaches, showcasing its potential to optimize anomaly detection in urban environments. Developing models capable of grasping code's semantic meaning is an ongoing challenge. While deep learning models have demonstrated some success in this area, they often fall short of replicating the same level of performance across various natural languages. This research introduces a novel graph-based model, inspired by cognitive frameworks, that effectively captures code's semantic meaning by leveraging its structural and syntactic characteristics. Utilizing the adjacency matrix representation of a directed acyclic graph, the proposed model can be trained end-to-end on a large dataset of small functions. When evaluated on a diverse dataset of code snippets, the proposed model significantly outperformed state-of-the-art deep learning models, showcasing the effectiveness of the graph-based representation. Furthermore, the proposed model was applied to multiple tasks, including code duplication detection, code translation, and code completion, where it consistently demonstrated superior performance. Notably, the model's reliance on structural features was found to significantly contribute to its overall performance in these tasks. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. We also developed a calculation method to eliminate daily variations in the system's response and effectively apply this technique to measure aerosol depth during full-moon nights. By achieving a precision of around 0.01 in aerosol depth measurements with this technique, the daily monitoring of large areas can contribute significantly to understanding climate phenomena. This precision also allows for utilizing this technique to estimate the angular anisotropy of light and the vertical profile of the atmospheric temperature. challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse challenges and models, with
a flexible implementation that allows the exploration of new research opportunities. 
Its main features include the ability to generate simulated data, search for
optimal solutions through different methods, and conduct cross-validation for
model selection. The library is structured to enable users to customize their
research and contribute their findings back to the community. The GGLasso package
is accessible through the Python Package Index at https://pypi.org/project GGLinearRegression/.

For speech processing applications, tasks such as speech voicing, fundamental frequency estimation, and dynamic pitch tracking are essential components that require efficient algorithms to accomplish. To meet this need, we have developed a novel algorithm that integrates these subtasks into a single unified procedure, allowing it to effectively handle pre-recorded speech with significant background noise levels. The algorithm utilizes a set of established metrics, like the zero-crossing rate, to create an unsupervised voicing classification system, and a hybrid approach based on autocorrelation is used to calculate pitch values. To improve the accuracy of pitch tracking, we suggest utilizing a forward-backward Kalman filter to refine the estimated pitch trajectory. Experimental results demonstrate that this new method outperforms existing, cutting-edge pitch detection techniques. The algorithm has been successfully applied in the analysis of the speech patterns of three primates. The complete code is available for public use at https://github.com/AudLab/MKALMAN_PITCH. The paired data set can be accessed at https://osf.io/mty98/. Disclosure: The researchers associated with this paper are disclosed in Section 2. To access the code, the readers can reach out to the corresponding author at abhisek@audlab.org or visit the specified GitHub repository.

We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle structured monotone inclusion problems. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, we develop a globally convergent solution that outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, we provide a globally convergent primal-dual version of DWIFOB and show through numerical tests that it surpasses the performance of the Chambolle-Pock algorithm and the Tikhonov regularized Anderson acceleration, while exhibiting enhanced robustness and reliability. Additionally, the code and data for these experiments are available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/bwbing/DWIFOB. Lastly, we derive a statistically consistent stochastic variant of the algorithm. Our findings indicate that the dynamically weighted extrapolation helps achieve greater accuracy in a fixed number of iterations and is beneficial even under the condition of diminishing variability. In line with this, we establish a benchmark to evaluate the efficacy of inertial methods. The numerical evaluations confirm that our stochastic variant matches the performance of the corresponding deterministic method and consistently surpasses that of alternative invariant stochastic algorithms in terms of convergence speed, as measured by the mean squared error, while demonstrating enhanced robustness and reliability in line with empirical variability measures such as the average relative entropy discrepancy. The code and data for these experiments are available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/bwbing/DWIFOB-stoc. Lastly, we apply the algorithm to tackle data-driven PDE problems. The numerical evaluations confirm the effectiveness of our variant in achieving greater accuracy in a fixed number of iterations, while demonstrating the potential for parameter adjustment to balance computational cost and solution quality. The code and data for these experiments are available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/bwbing/DWIFOB-data-driven. In conclusion, the dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward algorithm presents a dependable and efficient tool for tackling structured monotone inclusion problems and their stochastic and data-driven variants. The code and data for these experiments are available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/bwbing/DWIFOB. In contrast to the Chambolle-Pock algorithm, it exhibits enhanced robustness and reliability in line with variability measures, while offering greater convergence speed in line with empirical variability measures. The advantages and limitations of multicast beamforming for millimeter-wave systems have received little attention in design and performance evaluations. To fill this gap, this paper explores multicast beamforming in millimeter-wave systems, focusing on design and performance considerations. First, an overview of mmWave systems and relevant baselines for comparison are discussed. Next, an optimization problem involving joint design of transmission techniques, channel estimation methods, and signal processing processes is presented. The optimization objective involves maximizing a weighted sum of individual transmission rates across multiple groups of users. To achieve optimal performance, a relevant benchmark criterion, referred to as R-Basline, is introduced and an algorithm is developed to reach perfect performance for two-user scenarios. Furthermore, this paper examines the resilience of multicast beamforming to imperfections in antenna responses, channel measurements, and signal reception processes. The analysis reveals that multicast beamforming is vulnerable to variations in antenna responses, channel measurements, and signal reception processes. To enhance robustness, a simple yet effective method called power control is introduced and demonstrated to provide improved immunity against these imperfections. The findings in this paper highlight the trade-offs between performance and robustness for multicast beamforming systems. The outcomes of this research show that multicast beamforming offers superior performance compared to direct transmission in both spectrum efficiency and robustness, and thus can serve as an effective method for achieving high performance in mmWave systems. The computational complexity of the designed algorithm is shown to be acceptable compared to R-Basline. In addition, this paper provides insights into design channel bandwidth, number of bits used for quantizing the receive filter, and number of bits used for feedback per stream. The outcomes of this research confirm that these design channels can be effectively utilized. The analysis presented in this paper is relevant to a wide range of systems involving multi-group communications and are thus not limited to mmWave systems. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to optimize multicast beamforming in mmWave systems in the mentioned problem structure, and also to investigate the impact of channel measurements in beamforming design for non-collocated basestations. Federated Learning adoption has been hindered by communication challenges. A new Federated Learning paradigm, Federated Distillation, has been developed with distinct communication properties. It employs ensemble distillation and transfers model outputs as soft labels to participating clients and a central server via a public data set. Unlike conventional Federated Learning, such as Federated Averaging, which increases communication complexity with model size, Federated Distillation reduces communication complexity by utilizing the size of the distillation data set. We analyze the potential for communication efficiency in Federated Distillation. The study evaluates the trade-offs of Federated Distillation in terms of its ability to protect model information and achieve accurate joint learning outcomes with test accuracy comparable to that of centralized distillation. The study also compares the performance of Federated Distillation with existing Federated Learning bases such as Federated Averaging, from both communication complexity and accuracy perspectives. The study's results indicate that Federated Distillation offers improved communication efficiency and accurate learning outcomes, making it a reliable option. The study's results also suggest that Federated Distillation outperforms Federated Averaging in terms of both communication efficiency and accuracy. The study's results are particularly notable in that Federated Distillation achieves test accuracy within 1% of the central distillation method, while reducing communication complexity by more than 100 times. The study's results also indicate that Federated Distillation is less susceptible to data imbalance due to the nature of the soft labels created during the distillation process. The study's results are a foundation for future research in Federated Distillation by providing results that can guide the development of model aggregation algorithms and data collection methods for the paradigm. The study's results can also provide guidance on how to apply Federated Distillation in real-world scenarios by evaluating its performance with training periods that reflect the duration of real-world projects. A key feature of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to support future-proof services on large networks of interconnected computers. Our study examines how to effectively manage the flow of service requests across an NDN-based network, considering the varying capabilities of each node to process and generate data. Focusing on service workflows with connected components, we develop an algorithm for online, distributed control of each node's decision-making processes. Our proposed Service Discovery Assisted Dynamic Orchestration (SDADO) method aims to achieve lower overall delays and optimal data transmission rates. It combines queuing strategies and routing discipline based on topology, using network information acquired through a new discovery approach, allowing for efficient performance under uncertain conditions. We validate SDADO with analytical models and numerical simulations demonstrating reduced end-to-end delays and optimal data transmission rates. Our results show that SDADO remains effective even with network disruptions, achieving near-optimal performance. To achieve this, SDADO seamlessly integrates new discovery information, integrating it into the network's routing and decision-making processes. We also introduce an auxiliary metric to gauge each node's effectiveness in processing service requests, which aligns with NDN's architecture. Our method contributes to the development of future service systems that are adaptable, user-centric, and efficient in NDN-based networks. Our work is available in an open-source repository for verification and further exploration at: https://github.com/alejdesag/SDADO. Our study is extended to cover critical services by introducing an alternative method that ensures reliable delivery of service requests at all nodes, as described in a companion paper at: https://www.irden.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/2021_ICLP-CompanionPaper.pdf. A video introduction to our work can be found at: https://www.irden.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/VideoIntroductionToOurWork.mp4. More details about our research are available in our final report at: https://www.irden.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/OurResearch.pdf. All related materials can be accessed through our project website at: https://www.irden.org/projects/efficient-service-discovery-orchestration-on-named-data-networking/. We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic distribution and structure evolve. It demonstrates that specific eigenvector characteristics form a complete and orthonormal basis. Consequently, we derive the exponential stability of the associated semigroup directly. Notably, we show that under these connectivity conditions, stability is guaranteed even in the absence of elasticity along the edges. This contrasts with previous studies where stability required non-negative real parameters to prevent energy loss due to transmissions along the edges. Furthermore, we explore the stability of solutions to the linear equation, before addressing the ultimate stability of solutions to the nonlinear equation given to describe a nonlinearly elastic star-shaped shape. The key finding here is that when the initial distance between nodes is small enough, the solutions of the nonlinear problem eventually behave stably with the same characteristics as those of the linear problem. Finally, we use this understanding to determine the stability of solutions to the full nonlinear problem for a non-stressed beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches, where the outer points are fixed while rotating, and the inner point is capable of moving in two ways with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. This is achieved by observing the boundary controls and their associated energies, which are proven to be stable and satisfy certain criteria, ultimately resulting in the long-term strong convergence of the solution to a fixed equilibrium, given certain conditions are met. This includes that the material density and rotational damping parameter are sufficiently small, while the rotational elasticity parameter is sufficiently small or positive. Additionally, we are able to determine the exact rate of convergence, and show that under these conditions, the solutions behave stably, ultimately converging to the fixed equilibrium, where the energies associated with the boundary controls and their associated translations remain constant. Utilizing ternary chemical potential phase diagrams and phonon spectrum analysis,
our research shows that compounds $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ ($M$ = Cd, Hg), derived from Tl$_5$Te$_3$,
exhibit stability in their body-centered tetragonal crystal structure with symmetry $I$4/$mcm$.
Our calculations also indicate the occurrence of a significant band inversion in $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$
at the Fermi level and the generation of a 0.13 eV topological band gap in CdTl$_4$Te$_3$
due to the influence of spin-orbit coupling. The predicted topological insulating properties
make $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ candidates for efficient 3D strong topological insulator research and the
development of innovative spin devices and equipment. Additionally, our phonon frequency
predictions suggest that $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$ exhibits an anomalous phonon behavior displacement
along the $\Gamma$-$Z$ direction in its Brillouin zone, which may contribute to its superconducting
instability through electron-phonon interaction. Further research is needed to investigate this
phenomenon and its potential to boost the superconducting critical temperature of $M$Tl$_4$Te$_3$.

The conventional approach in multi-objective optimization assumes a pre-defined utility function, or it's learned through interactive feedback or a complete Pareto front determination. However, defining a utility function can be extremely challenging in real-world problems due to the implicit and explicit nature of expert knowledge. Furthermore, most interactive approaches are inefficient because they necessitate the evaluation of numerous experimental conditions to determine the optimal metric trade-off. To overcome these limitations, we've developed a utility function learning method that utilizes expert knowledge through preference learning, learned utility functions, and multi-armed bandit optimization to minimize experimental condition evaluations. The proposed method has shown competitive results in benchmark problems and superior performance when compared to traditional interactive approaches, all achieved in a significantly shorter time of execution. The generated learned utility functions can also be utilized as prior knowledge to guide evolutionary multi-objective optimization algorithms, allowing these algorithms to focus on non-dominated solutions outside the exploited search space in the late stages of optimization. Additionally, we've created a repository containing the implementation details and the utilized utility function learning approach, allowing researchers to reproduce our results and apply this method to their own multi-objective optimization problems. The repository is available at https://gitlab.irea.cnr.it/andreani/smarMO. or through https://github.com/ireacnr/smarMO. A video illustrating the used approach can be found at https://youtu.be/7Mq20vB7Q4I. Alternatively, you can contact the corresponding author at andreani@irea.cnr.it to obtain a local copy of the video.

Recent findings in reinforcement learning indicate that agents can be exploited using specially crafted malicious examples. Our research demonstrates that these vulnerabilities can be expanded from attacks that have knowledge of the agents and their training processes, to situations where no information is available. We employ sequence-to-sequence models to predict actions of trained agents based on sequence data. The models are trained by learning special tokens indicating the start and end of sequences of an agent's experience, which are then used to generate malicious examples that the agent will follow. It is proven that these models can effectively generate adversarial samples that affect the agents' behavior, and that these models can also adapt to new scenarios with limited data. Moreover, we show that these models can be used to create attacks that have specific goals, such as causing the agent to fail at its task. This research represents the first of its kind to attack reinforcement learning agents without knowing the training process, and is likely to have implications in developing defenses against such attacks. Additionally, we explore the difficulty in developing a universal defender that can protect all reinforcement learning agents, and the requirements for a potential defender. Given the novel and interesting nature of this problem, we hope to stimulate future research in this area. The code used in this research can be found at https://github.com/ of the researchers' names. In risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) based on the entropic risk measure, we study an approach for solving non-stationary Markov decision processes (MDPs) in a fixed budget framework. The reward functions and state transitions are both unknown and change over time. With a non-stationary environment, repeatedly knowing the risk sensitivity and the non-stationary transitions is essential. Under an exploratory condition and with knowledge of the variation budget, we develop an algorithm and prove its optimality in terms of achieving the worst-case guarantee against risk-sensitive non-stationary MDPs. The developed algorithm achieves an $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{D_{\phi}}{c^2} \frac{R^2}{n} + \frac{\sigma^2}{c^2}\right)$ guarantee, where $n$ is the number of time steps, $R$ represents risk sensitivity, and $\sigma^2$ and $c$ are parameters that capture exploration-efficiency and suboptimality, respectively, with $D_{\phi}$ representing Kolmogorov distance between the initial and final distributions. The approach significantly improves existing results, with an additional factor of $\frac{R^2}{n}$ and a better dependence on $c$ and $\sigma$ in the non-stationary risk-sensitive RL setting. For risk-averse RL based on variational principles, we establish an lower bound and discuss its implications. Additionally, we demonstrate that the known lower bound in the risk-sensitive setting can be attained under certain conditions. Lastly, through simulations using 50 well-known MDPs, we validate the theoretical findings and compare the developed algorithm's performance against state-of-the-art methods. Businesses utilize issue tracking systems to keep tabs on their projects by dividing tasks into manageable issues. This documentation style fosters gradual improvement, as each issue can be reviewed, commented on, connected to related issues, and advanced through the company workflow. Well-studied platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Bugzilla have received significant attention, whereas Jira, a highly-used tracking system with a wealth of accompanying information, remains underresearched. Due to difficulties in discovering and accessing Jira repositories, accessible datasets are scarce. This paper introduces a collection of 16 publicly available Jiras comprising 2.7 million issues, with a cumulative total of 32 million updates, 9 million comments, and 1 million issue connections, providing a valuable resource for investigations into issue evolution, interlinked tasks, cross-project analysis, and comparative assessments with existing ITS platforms. The provided dataset is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5072/UNIWB99QDQD. Our GitHub repository at https://github.com/ubisys/jiras-dataset is also available for viewing the code used to gather and process the dataset. This research is sustained through ongoing efforts to update the repository, respond to inquiries, and gather new Jira datasets to expand our understanding of ITS platforms. Currently, we are exploring applications of the dataset in various domains such as information retrieval, natural language processing, and data mining. If you would like to contribute your knowledge to this dataset, please visit our GitHub repository and share your analysis with the community. Currently, 21 users have downloaded the dataset and conducted various studies on it. Most notably, the topic of issue evolution and related topics has been studied by multiple users, who have leveraged the dataset to analyze connected issues within projects. For example, one user explored the impact of issue connections on task completion, while another investigated the distribution of issues across Jira repositories. By sharing our findings and providing a publicly accessible dataset, we aim to promote data-driven research using Jira, promoting reproducibility, and fostering a collaborative research environment among researchers. Decentralized machine learning applications such as autonomous driving and drone operation could benefit from distributed machine learning (DML) over dynamically changing networks. Yet, standard weighted arithmetic mean aggregation in current DML systems may lead to considerable model inaccuracies and slow convergence speeds over fluctuating networks. In this paper, we introduce a new family of nonlinear aggregation functions to improve DML efficiency in networks subject to change. Our model utilizes a nonlinear weighted power mean aggregation approach rather than the linear aggregation typically employed by previous studies. By using mirror descent based on Bregman divergence for optimization and non-linear aggregation, we maintain the ability to reach an optimal solution. Furthermore, we leverage majorization theory to derive upper and lower bounds for the nonlinear aggregation process and non-cooperative game theory to prove the sufficiency and necessity of certain conditions essential to achieving efficient models. In addition, we propose a new communication strategy called "stop talking" to optimize data transmission by selectively disseminating local model updates. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the proposed nonlinear aggregation system achieves desired levels of efficiency, convergence speed, and efficiency in networks that change over time. Our experimental findings confirm that the proposed aggregation approach outperforms traditional linear aggregation in terms of model accuracy and efficiency, especially in networks with changed topologies. A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. We identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, providing a comprehensive classification up to isomorphism. Additionally, we recall how these groups were previously classified in the case where the map has exactly three critical points. It is known that any group that can be formed as the group of deck transformations of a rational map with more than five critical points is isomorphic to the symmetric group $S_n$ for some $n\geq 6$. The classification we provide here shows that the possible groups of deck transformations for iterations of bicritical maps are precisely those that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of rational maps with either two or three critical points that are preserved under iteration. As a consequence, we identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of maps with specific critical properties, and we provide examples of maps with these properties whose group of deck transformations is isomorphic to a previously known group. Furthermore, we note that any group which can be formed as the group of deck transformations of a quadratic rational map (i.e., a map with two critical points) is actually isomorphic to either the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_2$, the finite abelian group $\mathbb{Z}_n$ for any $n\geq 3$, or one of three specific non-abelian finite groups, and that any group which can be formed as the group of deck transformations of a cubic rational map (i.e., a map with three critical points) is actually isomorphic to one of fifteen specific non-abelian finite groups. Finally, we examine the topological dynamical properties of iterations of these bicritical maps, and we provide concrete examples of such maps whose topological dynamical properties correspond to previously established upper bounds. The main dynamical property that we investigate in this paper is the maximum number of preimages that any point in the Riemann sphere may have in an iteration of the map. This research introduces three indices for characterizing online signature templates based on distinctiveness, complexity, and reliability. 
Distinctiveness is evaluated through statistical analysis and a random signature assumption on a set of user signature examples.
Complexity is determined by examining the features of user signature examples.
Reliability, on the other hand, is estimated by assessing a validation set of user signature examples.
These three indices serve as indicators for measuring the performance of online verification systems against both random and intentional forgeries as well as the performance of genuine users providing valid signature examples.
Through experiments using different verification algorithms and three online signature datasets plus one keystroke dataset, the validity of these measures and their applications have been verified and demonstrated. 
Furthermore, the effects of varying signature example sizes for each user on the distinctiveness, complexity, and reliability have been investigated. 
Based on the findings, a standard number of signature examples per user has been suggested for online verification systems. 
Additionally, the study compares and evaluates the performance of online verification systems against different types of forgeries, and presents alternatives to the current widely adopted method of using signature example size as a system parameter to achieve top-notch performance. 
Ultimately, the study proposes a framework to guide online verification system developers in achieving exceptional performance by selecting an optimal number of signature examples per user and applying a suitable validation method to evaluate and ensure the reliability of their systems against genuine user-provided signature examples. 
These findings and recommendations can serve as a starting point for future research in online verification, allowing for the development of robust and reliable online verification systems.

These advancements can in turn facilitate the secure adoption of online verification technology.

Theoretical investigations have employed higher-order correlation functions as a crucial tool to examine complex systems in quantum simulators, particularly quantum gas microscopes. Researchers have leveraged the measurements of specific correlations in the two-dimensional Hubbard model to uncover key properties of magnetic polarons in their stable and dynamic states. This study extends that analysis by exploring the effects of immobilizing a single dopant in a 2D Hubbard system, utilizing a pinning potential to achieve this. Our calculations show that the mobile and pinned scenarios exhibit distinct magnetic correlations and Heisenberg spins, which serve as crucial indicators of polaron stability. Interestingly, the Pinned Scattering Phase Shift remains constant, unlike the Mobile Scattering Phase Shift which decreases with particle density. This investigation not only sheds light on the unique characteristics of magnetic polarons but also explores the consequences of restricting a dopant's movement within an underlying Mott insulating matrix, which significantly alters its magnetic properties. This in-depth examination can contribute to a deeper understanding of how mobile dopants interact with their surrounding magnetic field in quantum systems. In addition, the findings of this study can be applied to other models of mobile impurities within complex materials, thereby expanding the scope of this investigation. All calculated correlation functions are available in the code attached to this article. \cite{MultipleAuthors_2024}

We determine empirical limits on nitrogen's nucleosynthetic yields by integrating nitrogen enrichment into a previously developed galactic chemical evolution model. The model considers two types of nitrogen yields: one that depends only on a star's mass (not its metal content) from massive stars, and another that depends on both the star's mass and metal content from AGB stars. As time progresses, model zones don't follow the [N/O]-[O/H] relation but instead first increase in [N/O] at a given [O/H] before becoming disconnected from it as [O/H] continues to rise, especially in the later stages of this process. The model suggests a possible [N/O] range of 0 to 5 at [O/H] = -2 and -1, increasing to 0 to 8 at [O/H] = -1 to -0.3. This discrepancy can largely be explained by differences in nitrogen's nucleosynthetic yields from massive and AGB stars with the latter's yields being more dependent on metal content. However, we also find that differences in these yields contribute to a smaller extent to this disconnect. This variation in nitrogen's nucleosynthetic yields has significant implications for understanding various astrophysical phenomena including supernovae with low nitrogen levels, globular cluster stars, and the R process, also influencing estimates of heavy element formation in the r-process. For example, if we assume an [N/O] range of 0 to 5 at [O/H] = -2 and -1, increasing to 0 to 8 at [O/H] = -1 to -0.3, this would mean that about 0.5 to 0.7% of massive stars and 20 to 30% of AGB stars contribute to secondary nitrogen yields. Additionally, if we use the maximum possible range of these yields as upper limits, this would mean that about 0.3 to 0.5% of massive stars and 10 to 15% of AGB stars contribute to secondary nitrogen yields. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. Our primary objective is to stimulate discussions on sustainable NLP advancements for societal gain, particularly in the context of language contact phenomena. This research is the first to examine the NLP spectrum of language contact from a social perceptive, aiming to foster sustainable developments for societal betterment. \\

Keywords: Multilingualism, Code-mixing, Societal NLP applications, Fake news, Hate speech, Election campaigns, Healthcare, Crisis management, Data privacy, Model fairness, Machine translation, Language generation, Entailment, Entropy-based similarity measures, Entailment models, Graph neural networks, Head-driven phrase structure grammar. \\

This study reveals that sharing images online can compromise one's privacy, prompting the development of Graph Privacy Advisor - an image privacy classifier. This classifier leverages visual details and the number of objects in an image to predict its privacy level, by adapting a sophisticated model, reducing its complexity and improving performance through feature refinement. In particular, the classifier identifies the most relevant image characteristics to use for privacy evaluation and replaces complex, high-dimensional image data with simplified features, thus reducing its complexity. Moreover, the classifier tackles the issue of preconceived biases by modeling the likelihood of objects appearing together, rather than the frequency of individual objects within each class. Experiments demonstrated that Graph Privacy Advisor outperformed existing methods in accuracy and reduced the risk of biased results, also showing that its refined features can be utilized in other image privacy tasks. In addition, the classifier was used to identify the most sensitive images in online datasets, further showcasing its practical applications. The source code of Graph Privacy Advisor is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/madhanjay/GraphPrivacyAdvisor. In machine learning, particularly in natural language processing and computer vision, data augmentation has been used to enhance model performance. Despite its success, there has been a lack of research on applying this technique to graph neural networks. This study aims to address this gap by developing a method that combines train- and test-time augmentation to improve social influence prediction. Utilizing a variational graph autoencoder in both phases allows for the generation of multiple augmented social network graphs. Through experiments on multiple datasets, we demonstrate that this end-to-end approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, showcasing the efficacy of augmentation on graph neural networks for social influence prediction. This improvement is most noticeable on smaller social network graphs. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/SM-Researchers/Augmentation-for-Social-InfluencePrediction.

The advent of online collaboration tools like GitHub has made it easy for software developers to share and reuse code across various repositories, often employing clone-and-own or forking techniques. As a result, it has become crucial to effectively maintain these shared files, especially in keeping them updated to the most recent version of the reused code. This contrasts with previous approaches, where our proposal of meta-maintenance - tracking the evolution of the same files across multiple repositories to identify potential maintenance opportunities, aims to address the gap. By analyzing a large dataset of open-source software repositories, our study showcases the usefulness of meta-maintenance in detecting unresolved changes and pinpointing areas requiring further maintenance. The results reveal that a small subset of files across repositories is frequently modified and often contains outdated code, which can be resolved through a simple update. The advantages of meta-maintenance are two-fold: it facilitates maintaining the same files across multiple repositories, and it serves as a precursor to detecting other valuable software evolution insights. The meta-maintenance tool is freely accessible online, allowing anyone to replicate our findings using their own GitHub credentials. The tool is designed to be platform-independent, easily installable on any GitHub token-enabled environment, including Windows, Linux, and macOS operating systems. The tool's maintenance code, including all underlying software and data necessary to produce our study's results, is freely available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/foposf/meta-maintenance. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. In contrast, our proposed Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model tackles these challenges and offers several advantages. First, MSDCR is designed to handle multiple sparse domains simultaneously, enabling the discovery of shared preferences across multiple domains. Second, it aims to produce personalized recommendations for both users and items across multiple domains, which is not the case for single-target or dual-target CDR methods. Third, it facilitates the exploration of overlapping preferences across multiple domains, which is typically insufficient in existing CDR methods. In our experimental evaluations, MSDCR consistently outperforms the best-performing single-target and dual-target CDR methods on four different datasets, demonstrating its superiority and versatility in providing high-quality recommendations across multiple sparse domains. The proposed model, as well as associated code and data, are publicly available for replication purposes. We introduce a multi-phased deep reinforcement learning strategy to overcome control issues in complex scenarios. The standard application of deep reinforcement learning, though efficient in handling high-dimensional control problems, faces limitations in dealing with problems that require rapid solution within a narrow subspace. This paper proposes a two-pronged approach to address such control problems by dividing the challenge into two distinct stages - initial subspace exploration and subsequent refinement. The first stage involves a guided exploration using a directed exploration algorithm that incorporates both guidance from an expert operator and exploration to map the subspace, followed by the implementation of a neural network that uses the explored data to generate a starting point for the second stage. The second stage comprises the standard deep reinforcement learning algorithm with an added constraint that its policy must remain grounded within the previously explored subspace. The effectiveness of this method is evaluated through simulations of controlled landing scenarios in realistic 3D environments and experimental trials with a quadcopter, resulting in successful implementation of the proposed strategy with improved efficiency and performance. The associated code for this method is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/IDEA-QG/Exploration-Refinement. Additionally, a video showcasing the method's effectiveness is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?vl _TtXyYsVj9M. The research team at IDEA-QG can be contacted at https://idea-gq.org/. Deep neural networks can create versatile learning models for translating data and relating it to relevant properties. However, in various scientific fields including inelastic neutron scattering, deep neural networks face challenges such as limited availability of labelled data, difficulty in quantifying uncertainty in results, and the complexity of understanding their workings. To tackle these problems, we employ various techniques. Firstly, using simulated data, we train a deep neural network to differentiate between two possible magnetic models of a half-doped manganite compound. Secondly, we apply a novel deterministic method to provide accurate probability ranges for the classification, which highlights the importance of incorporating realistic instrumental constraints during the training phase for reliable analysis of experimental results. Finally, by analyzing the network's decision-making process through class activation maps, we determine which data segments hold the most influence in the network's final classification determination. The resulting analysis matches qualitatively the findings derived from a simpler model that takes into account magnetic and lattice contributions. This comprehensive analysis offers a cornerstone for interpreting scientific data with machine learning tools. Additionally, our methods can be adapted to suit other research areas that leverage deep neural networks. Furthermore, the approaches discussed can be modified to work with other research datasets. Our code is publicly available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/icebeam/depth_learning_for_neutrons. To access the code, please follow the provided link.

Over the past thirty years, preprints have undergone significant development and growth alongside the expansion of the internet. Since the launch of arXiv in 1991, preprints have increasingly shifted from physical to digital distribution. Preprints enable rapid and low-cost online dissemination of research findings to a broad audience within a matter of days. This work provides an overview of the evolution and influence of preprints within the scientific community over the past three decades. The analysis reveals a substantial 6300-fold increase in preprints within this time frame, albeit only accounting for a modest 4% of published research. The benefits of preprints for authors are also explored, including earlier exposure to an audience by an average of 14 months and significantly higher citation rates at five times that of non-preprint articles. To alleviate concerns over preprint quality, data shows that approximately 41% of preprints are eventually published in peer-reviewed journals with publication outlets being of equivalent influence to papers lacking preprints. The critical role of preprints in communicating emerging research during recent public health crises is also underscored. The quantitative findings presented aim to provide conclusive evidence of the positive impact of preprints on individual researchers and the scientific community, thus enhancing the efficiency of scholarly communication through accelerated and broadened dissemination of research findings facilitated by internet technologies. These metrics can inform policymakers and researchers in strategically employing and responsibly embracing preprints within their respective domains. Machine learning model design benefits significantly from probabilistic theory and differential equations in terms of interpretation and guidance, particularly in identifying hidden variables through observations. Two core challenges in uncovering these hidden variables are state estimation and subspace learning, which involve accurately extracting the state from noisy data and reducing high-dimensional data to a more manageable space, respectively. Latent variable models utilizing graph structures effectively capture these complex problems, with graph neural networks providing an innovative deep learning approach to tackling these challenges. Building upon theoretical and empirical frameworks established in prior studies, this paper develops graph neural networks to address state estimation and subspace learning, showcasing superior performance in text classification, protein classification, stock prediction, and robotics applications. The accompanying code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/dlearn. This project aims to fill the gap between machine learning and systems theory, and all related files are accessible through the provided URL.

The measure of a vector-valued function's nonlinearity is essentially its deviation from affine functions. Researchers have proposed and refined hypotheses about a specific bound for this nonlinearity; Liu, Mesnager, and Chen initially proposed a general upper limit in 2017, which Carlet later supplemented with a lower bound using differential uniformity as a reference point. Our research refines this existing lower bound using straightforward methodology based on properties of APN functions. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of Sidon sets within elementary abelian 2-groups, and also examines the completion of Sidon sets derived from hyperbolas and ellipses in a finite affine plane. By applying a novel idea to evaluate the completion of a Sidon set as a vector-valued function, we are able to determine the APN parameters for several functions, and also establish that the completion of a Sidon set from a finite affine plane is almost necessarily linear. Additionally, our research reveals specific examples of function completions that are in line with our lower bound's predictions. Finally, our study finishes off by comprehensively listing all possible candidates for APN functions defined over a finite affine plane with dimensions of (25, 6) or (29, 7). This list represents the culmination of our research's main outcomes. It is worth noting that the finishing off of this paper is attributed to Qiao Yu's unwavering support. Moreover, our results are also applicable to the scenario where the dimension of P is equal to 2, which means we have successfully identified all possible candidates for vector-valued functions defined over a finite projective plane with (22, 5) or (28, 7) dimensions. Binary matrix datasets are widespread in scientific research and analyzing them is essential for identifying complex patterns. Researchers use various methods, such as comparing real data with simulated data that adheres to a null hypothesis. Our work involves exploring the space of binary matrices that fulfill specific row and column sum constraints, which differs from the uniform sampling methods that previously existed. Instead, we modified two existing algorithms that switch elements based on non-uniform probabilities assigned to each entry through a weight matrix. Our results indicate that including zeros in the weight matrix can create issues, but specific cases with monotonic structure can still yield reliable outcomes. Using simulations and a well-known bird habituation study, we examine the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms and the importance of choosing an appropriate null model for accurate data analysis. Our code and data are publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/kkrmones/BinaryMatrixSampling.

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. We have developed such a framework, called IntegrateTheory, which includes a standardized interface for PDF fitting groups to interface with theoretical predictions and a precomputed theoremaic library for frequently used processes. Our study demonstrates the functionality of this new tool by integrating DGLAP evolution predictions from multiple sources into mock datasets. Additionally, the capabilities of IntegrateTheory are being used within the NNPDFFit framework to update the NNPDF3T PDF set, incorporating an extended DGLAP grid and fitting for the ratio of PDFs to flux factors. We find that including the additional parameters significantly enhances the accuracy of PDFs at large $x$-values and helps stabilize the fit with respect to systematics in the flux factors. Our updated PDF set is in line with other contemporary PDF sets, while exhibiting improved stability in predictions for various hard scattering processes at large $x$-values. We've investigated parametric seeding of a microresonator frequency comb using a pump laser with electro-optic-modulated sidebands. The study revealed that the gap between the pump's sidebands was uniformly reproduced in the microcomb's optical spectrum, yielding an unprecedented stability of line spacing, $1.6\times10^{-13}$, at 1-second intervals. Unlike traditional microcombs, which exhibit complex and irregular subcomb patterns, parametric seeding can create a precisely equidistant frequency comb spectrum. This phenomenon can provide a reliable transfer source for precision spectroscopy, as it can generate identical frequency patterns when paired with a reference laser whose sidebands match the stability of the microcomb. Notably, we observed an impressive improvement in line spacing stability by two orders of magnitude compared to previous studies, reaching a level of excellence with an RMS variation of $4.4\times10^{-13}$, ultimately unleashing the full potential of parametric seeding to revolutionize the field of precision spectroscopy. This breakthrough marks a significant advancement towards achieving an ultimate goal of precision spectroscopy - generating a nearly perfect, reversible and inscribed frequency comb pattern through simultaneous optimization of its stabilization and the characteristics of the light source, as envisioned in a groundbreaking theoretical model known as 'frequency comb emulsion'. Additionally, we successfully implemented a novel and sophisticated technique called'real-time molecular precision spectroscopy' which allows for simultaneous measurement of the rotational vibration states of molecules in a gas and has the potential to provide a precise absolute frequency reference for lasers. This pioneering research not only expands our understanding of a cutting-edge optical phenomenon but also opens up new avenues of investigation in precision spectroscopy and could pave the way for innovative developments in this field. Quantization has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to reduce storage and processing requirements during inference. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this theory hasn't been formally explored. This study treats binary weights as stochastic random variables under rounding, and analyzes distribution propagation through the neural network's layers. We develop a novel quasi neural network to approximate this propagation, consisting of continuous parameters and special'relaxation' layers, and prove its expressiveness in matching the distribution of any previous layer given infinite training data. Experiment results indicate that our method achieves precise weight quantization and accurate stochastic approximation, and also yields generalization capabilities in conjunction with improved inference efficiency. Notably, our approach allows for the recovery of precise weights during testing, contrasting with the traditional loss of precision in conventional quantization methods. We propose a novel fidelity metric to gauge the quality of distribution propagation. Lastly, we investigate the thermal noise effect on deep neural networks, providing novel insights into the field. Our method is open-source and the code can be accessed at https://github.com/sohospice/DeepQuantization. In contrast to previous quantization techniques, our method offers an accurate generalization capability in addition to the benefit of reduced inference costs. We believe this work will serve as a foundational research for future investigations into the quantization of neural networks. Quantum systems possessing geometric duals exhibit a more restrictive set of entropy inequalities than general quantum systems do. The set of admissible entropies derived using the Ryu-Takayanagi formula forms the Holographic Entropy Cone. This stricter set of inequalities is violated once quantum corrections are introduced through the Quantum Extremal Surface prescription. The structure of the QES formula allows for a detailed analysis of the interplay between quantum contributions from bulk entropies and the HEC inequalities. This paper begins exploring this problem by establishing a connection between bulk entropy constraints and boundary entropy inequalities. Specifically, it is demonstrated that bulk entropies adhering to the HEC lead to corresponding adherence of the boundary entropies to the HEC, as well. Additionally, it is shown that bulk entropies conforming to monogamy of mutual information (MMI) lead to corresponding adherence of the boundary entropies to MMI. The results presented in this paper provide new insights into the relationship between bulk entropy constraints and boundary entropy inequalities, paving the way for a more in-depth exploration of the impact of quantum corrections on this stricter set of inequalities. We examine the link between the choice of image co-adding technique and the final image's point spread function. This involves identifying the characteristics of co-adding algorithms that yield co-added images with well-defined point spread functions. Our investigation centers on the following points:

  1. A clear illustration shows how linear co-adding techniques can generate images without well-defined point spread functions even with straightforward scenarios and weight functions.
  2. A more rigorous analysis reveals that linear co-adding algorithms have well-defined point spread functions in two specific situations: when all input images share the same point spread function, or when the weight function for each image is not dependent on the signal intensity.
  3. Two viable nonlinear co-adding algorithms (median and clipped mean) are assessed and found to consistently fail to yield consistent point spread profiles for stellar objects.
  4. A demonstration shows that all nonlinear co-adding algorithms fail to ensure consistency in point spread profiles for objects regardless of their magnitude.
  ultimate conclusion is that linear co-adding algorithms provide the most reliable results for object photometry, particularly when all input images have the same point spread function. This characteristic is essential for meaningful photometry results, particularly when all input images have the same point spread function.  Additionally, nonlinear co-adding algorithms may provide beneficial noise reduction for extended objects, making them suitable in such applications. Finally, any satisfactory stellar photometry analysis should utilize a linear co-adding algorithm to ensure accurate results.  This approach can serve as a useful benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of nonlinear co-adding algorithms in reducing noise and preserving or enhancing point-spread function smoothness. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on the real line and in the first orthant respectively. We demonstrate that such connections are made explicit through Legendre transforms, thereby yielding a consistent framework for discussing interactions between evolving contours and Gaussian free field fluctuations on the boundaries. This discussion is informed by an interpretation of Miller-Sheffield's contour line ensembles, which are now viewed as deriving from imaginary surfaces consisting of the upper half-plane and the first orthant paired with their associated Gaussian free fields. Furthermore, this framework is used to explore correlations between evolving contours and the local behavior of a correlated random potential near its saddle point. Lastly, this paper discusses multiple Dyson models and their relationships, drawing on connections between deterministic curves such as the Watsong theorem and the unique ergodic theorem. Specifically, it is noted that the most well-studied Dyson model features scaling behavior that is hyperscaled with a scaling index of 1/2. We establish that multiple Dyson models can be interpreted as deriving from pairings of subdomains of the complex plane, with deterministically chosen boundary values that conform to the principle of hyperuniformity. This framework enables discussions about interactions between evolving dynamical systems and fluctuations in related random potentials. In particular, this paper discusses correlations between Dyson models and the location of saddle points within those potentials, as well as the statistical properties of the set of points that comprise such models. This discussion is informed by an interpretation of itineraries for multiple SLE evolving in the first orthant, which are now viewed as deriving from pairings of the first orthant and its associated Gaussian free field with deterministically chosen boundary values that conform to the principle of hyperuniformity. In the process, this paper also discusses correlations between the evolving contours of two independent multiple SLE evolutions in the first orthant and the statistical properties of their intersection points. In particular, it is noted that such intersection points are localized near a deterministic curve known as the Stokos invariant, with the density of such localization decreasing in accordance with a power law whose exponent is equal to one less than that of the Hausdorff dimension of this intersection set

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates of the solution's maximum norm, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm. Specifically, for two or more spatial dimensions, we derive a significant estimate upper bound tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm, along with a corresponding logarithmic correction in two-dimensional space. Furthermore, this research provides low-probability estimates of large deviations for the solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space, tied to the initial conditions' maximum norm, which can be applied to a broad range of hydrodynamic equations and their solutions. These results expand upon prior work in this field and have relevant applications in many areas of study. The fastest known protocol for verifying classical results in quantum computation has an time complexity of O(poly(κ)|C|^3), but recent advancements have led to a new, more efficient protocol. By developing new techniques, the complexity has been significantly improved to O(poly(κ)|C|), which is a substantial breakthrough. Additionally, the developed protocol utilizes secure quantum random oracles and the existence of noisy trapdoor claw-free functions. Furthermore, the study introduces a new, parallel classical channel protocol for remote state preparation, enabling efficient preparation of independently random states in specific forms within constant rounds, while also achieving faster execution time compared to previous approaches. The development of this protocol relies on a new quantum embedding technique that reduces distortion while increasing bandwidth, where multiple parties can also be utilized to speed up execution. The efficiency of this protocol is further enhanced to prepare complex forms of states in specific forms within constant rounds, where the complexity of these forms is parameterized by δ, resulting in an improved bandwidth of poly(κ, log(1/δ)) instead of poly(κ, |C|^2) in previous approaches. Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to developing training datasets to enhance cell tracking and segmentation capabilities in biomedical imaging. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes. By training a neural network to implicitly generate signed distance function values at any point in three-dimensional space over time, conditioned on a latent code, it is possible to create new and unseen cell shape sequences. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated both qualitatively and quantitatively through comparisons of real and synthesized cell shape sequences using the Hausdorff distance metric. Additionally our method allows for the synthesis of multiple cell shapes and facilitates the creation of training datasets for cell tracking tasks. Furthermore, our approach enables the generation of plausible cell shapes at unseen scales, and enables the creation of "counterfactual" cell shapes by reversing the direction of cell wall growth patterns. The source code for our method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ivanperic/synthetic-cell. Our generated cell shape sequences are available at https://periclv.github.io/synthetic-cell-shapes/. Our approach demonstrates superior results in synthetic cell shape generation compared to state-of-the-art methods. Researchers in neuroscience hypothesize the brain utilizes diverse coordinate systems, such as body-centric, world-based, and others, to represent 3D environments. Conversely, advancements in reinforcement learning present a novel approach that might serve as a more plausible model for spatial perception and navigation in biology. Focusing on reinforcement learning methods that encourage agents to achieve target images without creating a 3D map, we examine this type of representation's capability to facilitate spatial tasks involving geometric consistency, like decoding location features. To demonstrate this, we design a hand-crafted representation ensuring high geometric consistency, and show that retaining information on persisting visual features during camera movement can improve performance in these tasks. Our findings provide a significant stimulus for neuroscientists to explore non-Cartesian spatial representations as an alternative to cognitive mapping. Moreover, our research identifies potential for reinforcement learning to model brain cognition processes, enabling novel interventions in autonomous agents and robots. Additionally, we share reinforcement learning models and related data, including 300k training images, accessible at https://github.com/alecmorrow/geometric-rl.git. As an extension to this work, a video is available at https://youtu.be/6MjVfwZwVdk. Moreover, a related discussion can be found at https://forum.openrobots.org/t/reinforcement-learning-for-spatial-tasks/899. Our research has been submitted for publication to the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence.
