The challenge of Sound Event Localization and Detection involves pinpointing the presence of multiple overlapping sounds, accurately categorizing their types, and estimating their source locations. Recently, neural networks have emerged as the leading solution for this problem, with Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks being a prominent architecture used in such applications. A novel system submitted to the 2020 Challenge for Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events uses a specific type of Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network with rectangular filters, optimized for recognizing distinct sound features. By employing data augmentation through channel rotation and reflection in the First Order Ambisonic domain, the training dataset was expanded, allowing for more robust performance and improved Accuracy in locating sound sources. Evaluation results demonstrate that this approach surpasses baseline results, significantly reducing Error Rates and increasing F-scores for location-aware detection. Consequently, the system's overall Micro F-score in the validation set exceeds 0.70 for all three tasks, earning the system a Silver award in the 2020 Challenge. A significant advancement was achieved in terms of Micro F-scores for location-aware detection, with improvements of up to 0.14 in AUC PR and 0.07 in Micro F1. Furthermore, the method demonstrates promising potential for real-world sound event localization and detection applications. In traditional communication systems, signal interference is generally seen as unwanted noise that distorts transmitted signals, but a new perspective has emerged where multiple transmissions occur simultaneously and potentially benefit from one another. Various wireless applications have taken advantage of this principle, as evidenced by non-orthogonal multiple access and other methods such as joint source-channel coding, computational codes, and federated learning, which were initially influenced by techniques like network coding and consensus algorithms. The fundamental thread running through these applications is the superposition property, allowing multiple signals to be transmitted concurrently, thereby yielding benefits in areas like distributed wireless communication, scalability, security, latency, complexity, and energy efficiency. The applications outlined above, despite existing independently in literature, can bring significant improvements in IoT enabled distributed systems, as demonstrated by a detailed analysis in this study, showcasing their distinct purposes and associated outcomes. Furthermore, the study delves into exploring potential integration pathways for these technologies. The study verifies the efficacy of these technologies in distributed systems by implementing them in a home automation scenario and evaluating their effects on error rates, latency, energy efficiency, and complexity using a consensus-based distributed recovery approach. The study examines their interplay using suitable metrics, as well as suitable performance trade-offs through an optimization method based on genetic algorithms. The study sets up a benchmark to compare various wireless applications using a consensus-based distributed recovery approach, as well as an alternative where local data recovery fails, thereby yielding better latency and energy efficiency performance at the cost of increased error rates and complexity. The study sets up a benchmark to compare multiple wireless applications by varying signal encodings, channel encodings, source encodings, network conditions, and application purposes, as well as software models, as exemplified in a home automation scenario using SimPy, a discrete event simulation tool. The study concludes by highlighting the benefits and drawbacks of different technology combinations, as well as their integration possibilities, along with an assessment of technical requirements and potential future integration pathways for these technologies. Time-frequency analysis heavily relies on spectrograms, being a crucial component derived from the short time Fourier transform (STFT). The traditional approach focuses on the maxima of spectrogram peaks. Recent research has shifted towards exploring minima and zeros, revealing links to Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs). Despite these connections, theoretical analysis of GAF zero sets remains challenging due to their complex topology. Our study introduces a critical innovation - a comprehensive statistical framework encompassing both spectrogram maxima and zero locations. This achievement leverages the cumulative distribution function of zero distances, which serves as a primary input variable. Via this framework, we establish fundamental results, such as the asymptotic normality of spectrogram zero locations near spectral peaks, informed by the Stieltjes transform of the spectrogram's density. Additionally, the approach allows for exploring general spectrogram zero sets via a continuous spectrum. These findings provide permanent theorems, surpassing earlier findings that were subject to temporal frequency restrictions. Our research resonates with recent discoveries on Gaussian zeros, showcasing new paths for potential application. Furthermore, this work's broad approach makes it suitable for inclusion in a graduate course, utilizing numerical data to illustrate key concepts. The associated software has been openly shared on the Git hub platform under the name SpecZeroAnalysis. Several promising avenues for future investigation are presented in the concluding section of this paper. Ultimately, the primary purpose of this study is to facilitate computational methods for analyzing spectrogram zeros, enabling practitioners to utilize those methods. To support this claim, various numerical experiments have been conducted to illustrate the periodic behavior of Gaussian zeros, the distribution of zeros near spectral peaks, and the dependence of these distributions on the spectrogram's shape, all while providing theoretical justifications for these findings through a thorough statistical framework. The companion software allows for the reproduction of these results. SpecZeroAnalysis is openly accessible on the Git hub platform under the umbrella of the CCRDC research center. It is also recorded in the Jupyter Notebook format with relevant data included in the SpecZeroAnalysis repository. Key aspects of quantum science include precise measurement and feedback mechanisms, offering wide-ranging benefits from advanced quantum technology to the conversion of information into work within quantum thermodynamics. Mathematical explanations of feedback control are typically presented through statistical models that necessitate numerical solutions, or are confined to straightforward physical representations. This study introduces a general framework for feedback control that is applicable to any open quantum system and utilizes operator sum representations. Furthermore, this framework allows for the implementation of feedback control within quantum optomechanical systems, such as those utilizing laser-cooled mechanical resonators. Operators are used to model the decision-making process, and the quantum state is updated according to the Kalman algorithm, enabling continuous feedback control with continuous measurements. This approach demonstrates the capability for efficient cooling to the ground state and achieving any desired steady-state mechanical oscillation frequency. Notably, this methodology provides a useful tool for designing advanced quantum technology and is valuable for research purposes. This work has been recognized through presentations at research conferences, including the 7th International Conference on Quantum Information (ICQI 2018), the 9th International Conference on Quantum Physics and Philosophy (ICQIP 2018), the 11th International Conference on Predictive Modeling in Industry, where our research was formally presented and discussed. Additionally, this study has been submitted to various scientific journals for peer review and has undergone revisions. This research investigates variations in the occurrence of two distinct types of El Ni\~no events, East Pacific and Central Pacific, with a focus on their seasonal impacts on global precipitation patterns. Employing an Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition analysis, we demonstrate that East Pacific and Central Pacific El Ni\~no events can be identified in the Multivariate ENSO Index at 95% and 90% confidence levels, respectively. Our results indicate that East Pacific and Central Pacific El Ni\~no events exhibit different effects on global seasonal precipitation patterns. While East Pacific El Ni\~no tends to increase autumn rainfall in Eastern Africa and reduce winter precipitation in Eastern China, Central Pacific El Ni\~no is found to increase winter rainfall in Eastern Africa and reduce spring precipitation in Amazon. Moreover, we reveal distinct impacts of these two types of El Ni\~no on the previous year's global precipitation patterns. Our research aims to enhance the understanding of these two types of El Ni\~no and their unique influences on global seasonal precipitation patterns, with potential applications in the improvement of precipitation forecasts. In light of their differing effects, we suggest that future studies on El Ni\~no patterns should consider both East Pacific and Central Pacific components when investigating regional precipitation responses across the world. Additionally, we propose that seasonal precipitation models be adjusted according to the likelihood of occurrence of these two types of El Ni\~no, as this may contribute to improved precipitation forecasts and better understanding of future climate variations. Furthermore, the combination of Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition and Machine Learning methods has potential to identify and analyze nonlinear time series patterns in climate data. Consequently, we anticipate that our research will inspire the development of more effective data analysis methods to investigate multiple time series signals and their distinct variations in climate patterns. With continued advancements in data analysis techniques, we hope that our research will promote the discovery of additional nonlinear variations in climate patterns, thereby refining our comprehension of the complex interactions underlying the global climate system. Ultimately, we aim to see an increased level of accuracy in precipitation forecasts and an enhanced capacity to analyze and understand the intricate dynamics of the global climate system. Moreover, the distinct variations in these two types of El Ni\~no may provide insights into their respective causes and impacts, which are discussed in the discussion section of the study. The analysis presented in this research is based on the Multivariate ENSO Index, as well as precipitation data from the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre, global temperature anomalies, and the Extended Biason Southern Oscillation Index. Evidence suggesting the demographic characteristics of massive black holes is accumulating, spanning a broad spectrum of galaxy types, from large clusters to tiny dwarf galaxies. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by leveraging their spatial proximity. This approach can be used to filter less informative elements and pinpoint others. We've demonstrated its efficacy in identifying key elements behind specific traits, such as blood pressure, a complex condition influenced by multiple genetic and environmental factors. Our approach revealed that protein-coding regions alone account for a minority of associated genomic elements, whereas regulatory regions, particularly those targeted by specific enzymes, significantly contribute to these associations. By integrating association data with additional genomic and functional details, our approach enables a more comprehensive comprehension of the genetic elements underlying specific traits, ultimately facilitating the discovery of causal genetic elements. This has the potential to lead to the development of more effective treatments. We've made our methodology available to the public through our GitHub repository, where researchers can reproduce our results and apply the approach to their own association datasets. We've also provided reproducible code and necessary data for our study on Benchmarking Genetic Annotation through Targeted Associations, accessible at our repository. Furthermore, we've included detailed explanations and utility scripts to guide researchers in applying our approach to multiple association datasets. This resource serves as a starting point for investigating the functional roles of the genetic elements underlying specific traits, de novo variants, and gene expression variations. We've included the source code used to perform the experiments in the "experiments" folder and the data required to perform them in the "data" folder. Our approach and supporting materials aim to boost research efficiency by providing a versatile and adaptable method for identifying and annotating the genetic elements underlying specific traits, mutations, and gene function variations. This approach is highly recommended for its reliability, ease of use, and adaptability to various genetic association datasets, as evidenced by our detailed analysis of multiple such datasets. We're confident that our research will contribute to a better comprehension of the genetic elements underlying specific human traits, ultimately facilitating the discovery of causal genetic elements, a crucial step towards the development of targeted treatments. This study examines electronic correlation within confined hydrogen, helium and lithium ions using the mean field approximation. It showcases how physical constraints are met without accounting for interelectronic interactions. In small systems, physical constraints are easily satisfied due to strong confinement effects. In larger systems, this approach is less effective because a significant portion of the wave function lies outside the atomic region, making Coulomb correlations more crucial. To improve this method, it is possible to incorporate correlations in a mean field context by enforcing boundary conditions on the total wave function. This enriched approximation yields more accurate results for confined helium and lithium ions, matching experimental energies more closely. In particular, this approach significantly outperforms the standard mean field approximation for confined helium ions, yielding energies up to 18% closer to experimental values. Furthermore, it is shown that the total wave function can be split into a confined component and a Coulomb component, which are governed by two separate Schrödinger equations. In this way, the total energy of confined atomic systems can be calculated as the sum of these components. In the case of one-electron systems, this confinement approximation yields results up to 15% closer to experimental values. In multiple-electron systems, this approach is more efficient than the standard mean field approximation and produces results on par with semi-empirical methods for confined helium ions. It is also shown that the Coulomb component of the total wave function is similar to the standard mean field solution, highlighting the importance of Coulomb correlations in confined atomic systems. In intermolecular forces, this effect can be significant, potentially reducing the error in computational predictions to a few percent. This approach is versatile and can be extended to the study of confined molecular systems, opening up new avenues for computational research. In this way, the boundary conditions on the total wave function can be utilized to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of computational predictions. In particular, this method can be employed to investigate confinement effects on valence molecular orbitals, potentially revealing how geographical restrictions affect chemical reactivity. The convergence of numerical results presents an opportunity to explore how geographical effects contribute to molecular dissociation energies, ultimately shedding light on the role of confinement in chemical processes. In this way, the boundary conditions on the total wave function can be utilized to study the interplay between geographical constraints and chemical processes. In conclusion, the enriched approximation presents a valuable tool for computational research, showcasing the significance of geographical effects in confined atomic systems, while also illustrating the importance of Coulomb correlations in multiple-electron systems. To each multiplicative linear logic proof structure, we relate an ideal that encapsulates its logical meaning through polynomial equations. We demonstrate how cut-elimination in multiplicative proof nets parallels specific applications of the Buchberger algorithm, a method used for computing Gröbner bases in elimination theory. This connection empowers us to offer an alternative, algorithmic description of the cut-elimination process for multiplicative logic. This algorithm, which operates on a multiplicative logic formula by decomposing it into constituent parts, ensures that any circuit-related problems that arise during this process can be resolved through straightforward substitutions, effectively enabling cut-elimination for complex multiplicative logic structures with circulating proofs. This algorithm also equates validity in multiplicative logic with the non-existence of a cut-elimination circuit. Furthermore, we show that determining whether a multiplicative logic formula has a cut-elimination circuit is an NP-complete problem, for which we developed the first known algorithmic solution. We also introduce a method to generate all possible cut-elimination patterns for a given multiplicative logic formula. Additionally, we develop a geometric ordering framework to optimize the performance of the Buchberger algorithm when applied to logical types, which encompasses a wide range of geometric ordering methods, including staircase ordering, LexOrder, and DeepLexOrder. This adaptation leverages the properties of fanin patterns, enabling the identification of irrelevant variables in the logical proof and an associated speedup in the Buchberger algorithm's computation time. Lastly, we introduce an inference algorithm for a type system related to multiplicative proof nets, which ensures that any type-Related Problem that arises during this process can be resolved through straightforward substitutions, effectively enabling the detection of logical errors and the provision of diagnostic feedback. A sophisticated time series analysis tool called cross-correlation analysis is used in this study to explore the interconnected behaviors of time series, with a focus on financial markets. A novel prediction method for determining the future synchronization state of two related time series has been developed. Cross-recurrence plots are applied as a non-linear approach to measure the coupling between the time domain of two series, thus establishing their synchronization status. A deep learning strategy is employed to address the task of predicting synchronization states, utilizing dynamic sampling of cross-recurrence plots as key features. Experimental results from multiple stocks, including significant S&P 100 constituents, have been gathered to test the efficacy of this method. Findings indicate that synchronizing predictions for time series pairs can be challenging, yet achieveable with substantial accuracy for certain stock pairs. The code utilized in this study is openly accessible at https://github.com/aman961/cross_recurrence_deep_learning. A blog describing the methodology can be found at https://medium.com/@aman9. 

![](https://github.com/aman961/cross_recurrence_deep_learning/blob/master/readme_images/scheme.png) 

Key Contributions:
1. A groundbreaking deep learning framework for predicting the future synchronization state of two time series based on their cross-recurrence plots has been introduced.
2. The effectiveness of this method has been assessed through predictions on a diverse set of 100 S&P stocks for various time horizons.
3. The code has been shared publicly to facilitate the replication of this research. A detailed explanation of the methodology has been published on a blog for the academic community. 

It is envisioned that this method will be expanded to include higher-dimensional cross-correlation analysis in the future. Furthermore, the potential for applying cross-recurrence plot analysis in other fields beyond finance, such as physics and earth sciences, will also be explored in future research.

By leveraging this phenomenon, researchers can achieve precise control over electronic processes and orientation within molecules, a key aspect of various advanced technologies. Our study focuses on the simulation of a THz field's impact on H2+ under high magnetic fields, with findings that electrons can be confined to specific points on a circular trajectory. A strong magnetic field, aligned with the nucleus, allows for the creation of well-defined electron orbits. Our model uses a spatially-dependent potential and the B-spline basis set within the finite element method to solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. By applying a THz electric field, we observe the creation of electronic states on specific points of the orbit, a phenomenon that occurs when the electron's velocity matches the field's frequency. Notably, this phenomenon persists even in the presence of a strong magnetic field, suggesting potential applications in the precise control of orientated molecules. Our results are presented in relation to the field-free states, making it challenging to identify the influence of the THz field. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new visualization method to represent the core density and electron density gradient, allowing us to effectively showcase the field's impact. Additionally, the code utilized in this research is available for public use at the GitHub repository https://github.com/AlexanderShub-MSU/THz_H2_plus. To overcome this limitation, our approach incorporates a few active ad campaigns from recent history into the training of the model for optimal results. This method not only boosts the model's accuracy but also prevents overfitting by ensuring the model is exposed to a variety of active ads. Furthermore, our approach can even identify new ad campaigns that share similarities with high-performing active ads, thereby enhancing the model's predictions. To achieve this, we utilize a two-layer model consisting of a collaborative filtering layer that identifies similar ad campaigns and a convolutional layer that extracts shared features from these ad campaigns. Our approach demonstrates exceptional performance in predicting both old and new ad campaigns, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods in online experiments. Our findings are further validated through an in-depth analysis of the key components of our approach. To the best of our knowledge, our approach is the first to simultaneously identify active and new ad campaigns while also shifting the focus from campaign ID to actual ad content features. This allows for the potential discovery of hidden patterns in ad content not yet utilized by CTR models. Current approaches for modeling business processes relying on in-depth knowledge often utilize information elements but fail to consider adequately the varying levels of such elements. As a result, these approaches can neither ensure the constraints related to information elements' levels are met, nor apply such constraints in simulation or execution environments. This paper outlines a new approach addressing the deficiencies of current property specification techniques, allowing the verification of process models against requirements by taking into consideration the different levels of information elements. This is achieved through the extension of existing decidable logic with elements of transitive level comparison, enabling reasoning about process instances in a relative manner. The proposed method is evaluated using an actual case study from a knowledge-intensive process. Furthermore, this assessment highlights potential optimization strategies for improving the logic's verification efficiency. The approach is implemented as part of the Ramon BPM system, which provides an execution environment for process models. This execution flexibility enables simulations where constraints are violated, leading to process restart with corrective measures. This feature is particularly useful for establishing error correction protocols based on test models. The approach's validity is validated through an actual case study of a knowledge-intensive process involving academic promotion procedures. This involves navigating semi-organized processes with evolving information elements and no pre-defined cases. The associated metric temporal logic properties comprise requirements such as processing completion within a year, having all required information submitted within six months, and having no pending tasks after completion. The process model verifies these properties but fails to guarantee them at the instance level due to the complexities inherent in semi-organized processes, as evidenced by property violations at the instance level. Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols,
resulting from diminished solar radiation reaching Earth, can be monitored by
Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data streams retrieved from geostationary satellites.
However, multi-source satellite data streams often have varying missing data
rates and errors, making precise AOD estimation and prediction challenging.
Therefore, a practical need exists to develop a physics-based statistical method
for wildfire AOD forecasting by integrating heterogeneous satellite data streams.
By incorporating spectral analysis, the proposed method merges multiple satellite
datasets with an underlying advection-diffusion equation driving AOD propagation,
including bias correction to compensate for model biases and Fourier series errors.
This approach, applied to the California wildfires, yielded positive outcomes in
forecasting AOD extremes and demonstrated the method's practical application in
near-real-time wildfire AOD forecasting. A case study illustrates the method's
capability to adapt to various wildfire scenarios by adjusting parameter values,
highlighting its potential for broader use in environmental modeling. The method's
code is accessible online at \url{https://github.com/taylorhutchinson/wildfire_aod}.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through specific applications in the context of spatial data, which involves the analysis of bounding privacy losses for joint data distributions using only pre-query marginals, particularly relevant to protecting location-based data. The framework's utility in a real-world scenario is showcased by evaluating privacy-loss bounds for a scenario modeling a person's movement across a city. The computational intensity of directly applying the framework to dependent data is significant, which prompts the investigation of simplified strategies for achieving substantial reductions in computational load through specific case studies involving navigation system data and a person's movement across a city, utilizing a k-nearest neighbor based approach to model dependencies and incorporating a hypothesis-testing based method for enhancing the framework's efficiency and accuracy when the model's accuracy is limited. Experimental results indicate that the proposed simplified strategies are up to 10,000 times more efficient, which makes the framework suitable for practical use. The framework's source code is accessible at https://github.com/alexalexandrov/RDL. Our research also leads to the development of two new algorithms: DeepDLProtect and DeepDLRelease, which are evaluated in various scenarios including real-world datasets, comparing their privacy-acquisition performance to existing methods and demonstrating their substantial computational advantages, specifically for protecting location-based services with dependent data, which is particularly visible in scenarios with lower privacy parameters and smaller datasets, while maintaining comparable accuracies, especially for protecting navigation system data, which is observed to be within 10% of the optimal value and significantly lower than existing methods. The computational load of DeepDLProtect is on average 100 times less intensive than the framework, with up to a 43% reduction provided by DeepDLRelease, which is designed for releasing confidential data while achieving substantial reductions in computational load. The developed tools, source code, and experimental materials are accessible at https://alexalexandrov.github.io/research/deepdlprotect/. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes. Our data collection was based on actual, rather than simulated, fMRI datasets from N=345 young, healthy subjects, acquired across eight scanning sites, all of which utilized 3T scanners and varied scanning protocols. Our findings demonstrate that commonly observed functional networks are consistently present across all sites, and inter-site effects were relatively minor. Through Monte-Carlo simulations, we evaluated the effects of multisite data on our ability to detect changes and predict group labels, revealing that our ability to detect changes was minimally impacted, but prediction accuracy did decline slightly compared to single-site studies of equal sample size. Our results imply that large sample sizes can make multisite research in rs-fMRI a viable option. However, we also observed considerable variation in signal strengths of certain networks, as well as discrepancies in resting-state patterns, which could have significant implications for data interpretation and general applicability. Our study highlights the need for further research into site-specific factors that may be present in rs-fMRI data, and the potential impact they have on connectivity measures. Our data and analysis code are publicly available for verification and replication at https://osf.io/7chz5. This research was supported by the National Institute of Mental Health (R01MH113079). None of the authors declare any other financial or conflict-of-interest statements. Our dataset complements the existing rs-fMRI dataset collected by Mattuck et al. (2022) in terms of sample size, research focus, and underlying causes. Our combined dataset comprises N=345 young, healthy subjects, acquired across eight scanning sites, providing a comprehensive and replicable dataset for further research in rs-fMRI methodology development. Our findings suggest that large sample sizes can render multisite research a viable option, despite minor effects on detection power and prediction accuracy. However, we did observe considerable variation in signal strengths of certain networks, as well as discrepancies in resting-state patterns, which may significantly influence connectivity measures and our understanding of normative rs-fMRI patterns. Our study also raises important questions regarding data interpretation and general applicability, and the potential impact of site-specific factors on rs-fMRI data, which may vary significantly and influence connectivity measures. Our data and analysis code are publicly available for verification and replication at https://osf.io

By applying surfel reprojection constraints, this method optimizes both keyframe positions and map features within the database. A step-by-step camera relocalization process is then applied to determine the 6-DoF camera pose by leveraging the constructed visual database. Moreover, this method exploits machine-learned descriptors to achieve enhanced performance, especially under difficult conditions. Our approach is demonstrated to achieve high accuracy under both real-world and simulated scenarios. Additionally, this method is integrated into Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), yielding satisfactory outcomes. Focusing on patients presenting with abdominal pain, we discovered that extending treatment time beyond two and a half hours significantly raises admission rates. Notably, this finding aligns with prior research, but previous studies relied solely on observational data. We employed an instrumental variable analysis, leveraging a state law that limited ED hours in California to statistically prove this correlation. This evidence can inform policymakers seeking to modify treatment time as a means to manage admission rates in abdominal pain patients. We also explored the potential link between extended treatment times and increased costs, but our findings failed to support this hypothesis. A subsequent analysis revealed that rising admission rates following extended treatment times do not correlate with rising costs in a subsequent study. Furthermore, we discovered that the primary factor driving the drop in non-admitted patients is the patient outcome shifting from unstable to stable. Consequently, we suggested that enhanced treatment may lead to more severe conditions being detected and, in turn, increasing admission rates without necessarily incurring higher costs. Moreover, we found that the improved patient outcomes from extended treatment do not directly result in lower costs of care. Nonetheless, our research was unable to rule out the possibility that other factors contribute to this result. An additional analysis indicated that the improved patient outcomes from extended treatment do not directly result in lower costs of care but that other factors may also play a role. To validate our research findings, we employed three alternative methods, including a) comparing admission rates to outpatient facilities and b) evaluating changes in health insurance policies and c) examining pathologic evaluation of patient samples all of which supported our analysis that extending treatment time leads to more severe conditions being detected and resulting in higher admission rates. Ultimately, our research aimed to provide accurate estimates of treatment time on admission rates, patient outcomes, and costs through observational data and robust statistical analysis, addressing potential endogeneity by leveraging instrumental variables and accounting for unobserved heterogeneity by utilizing a difference-in-differences approach in addition to proprietary patient outcome data. A key contribution of our research is providing accurate estimates at multiple treatment time points, which has practical value for informating policy decisions regarding ED admissions. To minimize measurement error when utilizing retrospective observational data, we employed multiple robust statistical methods to verify our findings and maintain a focus on abdominal pain patients to minimize confounding factors. A particular strength of our research is providing reliable and efficient estimates of treatment time effects on admission rates, patient outcomes, and costs which can inform policymakers and have practical value in ED management.

The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions have commonly drawn on a variant of the classic Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), with a focus on achieving the quickest or most time-efficient task sequence. Despite their optimality, these methods face challenges in real-time execution, especially with larger problems. In fast-paced online planning environments where tasks are executed swiftly, the time taken to optimize task ordering becomes a substantial hindrance, even surpassing the task duration itself. The optimal approach in such cases involves balancing solution quality with processing time, achieving a reasonable compromise within a predetermined timeframe. The proposed algorithm meets this requirement through an innovative technique where the solution quality is updated based on the time spent, rather than the tasks completed. This approach adjusts the solution on the fly according to both task additions and execution progress, enabling the discovery of a suitable compromise between quality and time. This research investigates the characteristics of undoped Si substrates by measuring SiMOSFET Hall bars, thereby evaluating the quality of fully fabricated CMOS devices. A notable mobility level of 17,500 cm^2/Vs was achieved with oxide thickness below 10 nm, showcasing a superior interface ideal for use in qubit-based technologies. Additionally, the study explores the impact of different gate materials on mobility and identifies the underlying principles to guide future optimizations of quantum computing hardware. When each cluster contains identical systems, synchronized within that group, but operating independently from other groups, this phenomenon is known as group synchronization. Typically, strict conditions need to be met to achieve synchronization, but research has revealed that slight discrepancies in parameters or connections do not necessarily preclude it. Through advanced analysis, it is now possible to identify stable conditions for group synchronization, including the impact of within-group connections. This expanded understanding allows for a more general representation of these complex systems, reducing their stability evaluation to simpler mathematical dimensions. This research focuses on time-invariant systems but paves the way for exploring dynamic systems, like those with evolving connections, in future studies. Ultimately, this research aims to recognize and predict group synchronization in various real-world applications, such as brain function or power grids. A key aspect is to recognize that distinct groups require different archive strategies for stability assessment. The capacity of wireless networks is inherently restricted by interference, and there has been a lack of investigation into the correlation of interference, which has the potential to cause substantial delays in local transmission. This study addresses the query of whether there exists an optimal transmission strategy that is independent of channel knowledge, and if so, what that strategy looks like. Using a convex optimization approach, we determine the optimal transmission strategy and demonstrated that a distributed, interference-aligned codebook technique is the optimal choice, yielding a minimum average local delay, even in the presence of uncertain channel conditions. Notably, this codebook approach outperforms traditional AMPS when channel information is available and offers a more flexible option when channel information is limited or missing. Additionally, we explored extensions of this problem to multiple-hop transmission and non-fresco systems, examining the optimal transmission strategies in these scenarios and comparing them to existing methods, such as AMPS and FroMS. Overall, our analysis highlights the significance of considering interference correlation, and we introduced the "stop-transmit" policy, known as ST, which serves as a reliable fallback option, performing better than existing methods, such as AMPS and FroMS, and resulting in significantly lower delays in both single-hop and multi-hop transmission systems. Furthermore, we investigated the worst-case regret of ST, and established that, in the limit as the number of users increases, the regret of ST decreases proportionally to 1/N, and can be approximated more accurately using a revised version, known as RST. By exploiting the linear relationship between interference and local delay under equal power transmission, we were able to derive this approximation, which retains all the key benefits of ST. This improved RST results in a considerable reduction in delay, especially when the number of users is small. By combining the optimal single-hop transmission strategy with a modified multi-hop version, known as MH, we were able to derive MH and establish it as an efficient alternative, outperforming existing multi-hop methods, such as FroMS-MH. MH results in significantly lower delays, especially when the number of users is small, and has the added benefit of requiring minimal overhead. By examining the delayed energy per bit in a multi-hop system, known as DEP, which is a measure of transmission efficiency in multi-hop wireless networks, we were able to establish MH as the most efficient multi-hop transmission strategy, and derive the delay energy trade-off for these systems. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement scarce labels with confidently predicted ones. However, the pseudo-label quality in current Graph Neural Networks is lacking reliability and causes noise to be propagated throughout the network, necessitating an improvement. This paper addresses the issue by developing a high-quality pseudo-labeling framework, capable of selecting robust pseudo-labels and informing model improvement during pseudo-label propagation. The framework generates high-quality pseudo-labels by leveraging local and global graph structures through an iterative pseudo-label refinement process. Additionally, it integrates pseudo-label quality assessment into the pseudo-label propagation framework, which effectively reduces noise and yields better classification results. The experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of our proposed high-quality pseudo-labeling framework over existing methods, showing a significant improvement of 5.83% average in accuracy on limited label scenarios. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/jaykim2016/Informative-Pseudo-Labeling.

In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time video analysis on devices. We present PatchNet, a highly efficient neural network model for tracking objects across adjacent frames in videos. Unlike traditional pixel-based approaches, PatchNet leverages patch-wise correlation features. This results in a compact network that runs at a remarkably low computational cost of 58MFLOPs, approximately $5\times$ simpler than MobileNetV2. Our research showcases the effectiveness of PatchNet on object detection in videos and visual tracking, yielding substantial performance gains and comparable or even better results. Specifically, on benchmark datasets ImageNet VID and OTB2015, PatchNet significantly outperforms other state-of-the-art models by reducing their computational costs, often with little to no decrease in accuracy. Furthermore, experiments on low-power hardware, such as the Jetson Nano, reveal 2.8x to 4.3x speed improvements resulting from the decreased computational cost of PatchNet. Therefore, PatchNet is ideally suited for object detection in videos on devices with severe hardware constraints. The associated code and model weights are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/VisualLearningLab/patchNet. We present a generic, classical modeling of electric circuits that describes conventional single-tone microwave optomechanics, where a mechanical oscillator functions as a mobile capacitor within a parallel RLC circuit. Analytical derivations are developed, incorporating fundamental aspects like the back-action force, input-output relationships, and corresponding spectral densities, all situated within a purely classical framework. These derivations align with the established quantum optomechanics when both the cavity and mechanical oscillator have high occupation numbers. Additionally, the derived analysis equates optical elements with their electronic counterparts, a necessity for accurate measurements and design requirements. Lastly, a direct comparison between the quantum and classical treatments helps to distinguish the boundaries between these two regimes, thus identifying the genuinely quantum characteristics from those of the classical realm. \\

This study investigates how basic autonomous entities akin to Braitenberg vehicles can manifest complex, unpredictable movements. Employing a robot design proposed by Steve Mesburger and Alfred Hubler in "Chaos in Wall Following Robots", the autonomous entities use a straightforward distance sensor to navigate, with the added limitation of a narrow "phi" field of view. As these agents maintain a consistent forward velocity, they rely on the sensor to adjust their path accordingly: rightward when close to obstacles and leftward when distant from them. In a linear environment, the autonomous entities maintain a consistent distance from their surroundings and proceed along a fixed path. However, when faced with periodic patterns in the environment, such as square, triangular, or sawtooth shapes, and the field of view is narrowed, these agents follow a recurring path. But as their field of view expands, their movements become increasingly chaotic. A thorough examination, using numerical methods with these shapes, led to identifying key points of transition and analyzing various bifurcation types including border collision and period doubling, with further detailed results to be presented in a separate report. Most surprisingly, when their field of view is narrowed below a certain threshold, these agents change from following walls to crossing them repeatedly. And at an extremely wide field of view, these autonomous entities begin to mirror their movements along a fixed path. Lastly, when tripping over their own limitations in the shape of a delta pattern in the environment, these agents change from following walls to crossing them repeatedly and vice versa at a narrow field of view, resulting in a complex, sensitive dependence on initial conditions movement. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. Multivariate data that change over space or time can often be analyzed with a statistical model known as multivariate Gaussian processes (GP). Researchers have developed new methods by combining the concepts of multivariate Gaussian processes with graphical models, allowing for relationships between individual components of the process to be visualized and analyzed. Two specific approaches, functional Gaussian graphical models and graphical GPs, provide different frameworks for understanding these relationships, the former using a mathematical expansion to describe the process, and the latter by combining smaller processes in a specific order. Our study connects these two models by proving that certain functional models with selected variables can be seen as graphical GPs. This finding is used to show the equivalence between truncating certain functional models and selecting variables in a GP. This theoretical understanding allows for the development of statistical tools to fit models to real data, as demonstrated with an example involving brain development imaging data. This data, which involves multiple functional responses observed in the same region of the brain, can be analyzed using a multivariate Gaussian process with parameters determined through our framework. This approach is compared to alternative methods and found to provide more accurate inferences when data are missing. Our method is implemented in an R package called Mgrr, which is currently available on CRAN. This package can be used to analyze data using the new methods, or with pre-existing data, to verify the statistical results. Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited lifespan due to
imperfect gate operations. To work effectively with these processors, compilers
must optimize programs to run within the device's coherence time, translating them
into the most efficient version possible to extract maximum value from the hardware.
We have developed new, deterministic methods to efficiently compile repetitive quantum
algorithm patterns, preserving their original operation sequence and ensuring the worst-
case scenario runtime remains minimal. By utilizing pattern-based optimization, the
compiler can easily identify and enhance the program's overall performance. Diverse
patterns can be used to match common algorithm structures, and a pattern database
can be created empirically or through manual design. We have implemented a novel
approach to automatically generating repetitive patterns, utilizing an algorithm that
creates a set of tailored patterns to fit specific compiler optimization needs. To
determine the optimal coherence time, our method calculates an optimal threshold for
the probability threshold of remaining correct, which we then use to develop an
efficient pattern recognition algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our
compiler optimizations through multiple benchmarking processes, employing a
superconducting quantum device as an example. The results indicate that our
compiler, with its enhanced patterns, can successfully execute programs at the
limit of the device's coherence time. The value of our research lies in its potential
to enable the creation of robust, high-performance quantum algorithms that take full
advantage of current quantum processors, thereby driving the development of
efficient application compilation. To facilitate this progress, we have made our
compiler tools and pattern generation algorithm publicly available. Additionally, we
include detailed documentation to guide compilers in utilizing our innovative
compiler optimizations. A comprehensive study has been submitted for publication,
and the associated code can be accessed through the GitHub repository at
https://github.com/ibm/quantum-compilers/tree/pattern-compilation. For further
information, please refer to the guide provided at
https://github.com/ibm/quantum-compilers/wiki/Pattern-Compiler-Manual. We have
included a list of our research contributions in Section 1, and all relevant authors
are acknowledged in the acknowledgments section. We have conducted an ethical
evaluation, detailed in Section 7, and an accessibility analysis in Section 8. We
declare conflicts of interest in Section 9, and our relevant permissions are
listed in Section 10. The research outlined in this document has been carried out
in accordance with the applicable laws and regulations in the relevant jurisdictions.

Research indicates that the Cotton tensor offers a way to extend our understanding of gravity beyond what general relativity provides. Additionally, the Cotton tensor's field equations include any solution derived from Einstein's equations, both with and without a cosmological constant, as well as indicate that this constant can be seen as an integral component rather than an external factor. A theory's vacuum state is better characterized by a zero value for the Cotton tensor, as opposed to the vanishing of the Ricci tensor, revealing new insights. A static and spherically symmetric solution that is comparable to Schwarzschild was found. Although the Cotton tensor's equations include derivatives of the third order, they simplify to equations of the second order due to their intrinsic variational properties. A new formalism based on the use of 'non-metricity' allows us to study gravity through the use of a tensor that tracks the covariant derivative's action on a vector, rather than through the use of a metric, making this an applicable framework for future study. A general method for imposing'metric-free' constraints on a gravity theory's degrees of freedom was also discovered, which can serve as a useful tool. A brief review of existing classical models was performed to establish a foundation for future research in this area, which will focus on observing phenomena that are active rather than passive. A prospective quantum strategy was outlined, in which the observability of quantum effects is considered the primary factor, as opposed to internal consistency. Specifically, a quantum model based on a gravity theory's non-metricity is proposed as a suitable framework for studying quantum gravity, particularly because it allows for the recovery of Einstein's general relativity in the large-scale limit while also allowing for the measurement of quantum effects at a small scale. This is demonstrated in the context of a graviton propagator, which indicates that any deviation from Einstein's equations is proportional to $\hbar$ as required. Furthermore, a finite self-energy is calculated for a static and spherically symmetric graviton, which indicates that any deviation from Einstein's equations results in a decrease in the graviton's self-energy. A brief assessment of the predictive capabilities of this quantum gravity framework is provided, which indicates that a future experiment may be able to distinguish between two active gravity theories. Specifically, a test based on the Big Bang's radiation is proposed as a suitable framework for deciding between two active gravity theories, which could serve as a crucial breakthrough in deciding between these two theories. A study on the active role of gravity in the Big Bang's early stages is provided

We've established a specific type of ordered relational topological space known as orthomodular spaces. Our method for creating these spaces involves combining a particular kind of frame, introduced by Hartonas, with a topology in a manner similar to the approach taken by Goldblatt and then extended by Bimbó, in relation to the representation theory of ortholattices. The orthomodular lattices and their corresponding homomorphisms can be shown to have a dual equivalence to the orthomodular spaces and their respective continuous morphisms. Moreover, we've found that these orthomodular spaces fit into a category that is equivalent to the category consisting of orthomodular lattices and their corresponding homomorphisms. Additionally, we've proven that every orthomodular space has a basis consisting of subspaces with particularly simple structures, resembling both chain-theoretic frames and orthomodular lattices, thereby enabling a direct comparison with Bimbó's work. Our study of orthomodular spaces also encompasses the investigation of morphisms that preserve either the ordering or the orthonormality relation, leading to the discovery of specific subcategories within the given category of these spaces. Finally, we provide an illustrative example of an orthomodular space that is not reducible to any frame, thereby highlighting the distinct nature of orthomodular spaces in relation to more general framed spaces. By examining the separated vs. copowered nature of these orthomodular spaces, we are able to conclude with a summary overview of the properties and subspaces present within these specific topological relational structures. The text is accompanied by two separate appendices containing further details and an alternative description of orthomodular spaces as framed spaces with a particular ordering preservation property. Furthermore, we outline potential applications and future research directions related to orthomodular spaces. We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. Furthermore, this tool has educational implications, as it makes it possible for students to engage with and understand the details of each step in a proof visually. As an added benefit, this system also enables the creation of more engaging and interactive learning materials. We have applied this tool to a library of fundamental proofs in functional program verification, including a range of abstract transcendental theorems, as exemplified by the fundamental Brounker's Fixed Point Theorem. To this end, we have developed an approach that automatically generates a table of proof elements, as well as a hierarchical structure, to facilitate the visualization of even complex proofs comprising numerous steps. Ultimately, this tool has been successfully integrated into the ProofDefinition library, thereby making it accessible to over a hundred other libraries of formally verified content within the Coq repository. We envision a future where this tool, known as VisualPO, can be used to create an interactive visual representation of the burgeoning ProofDefinition library, thereby allowing it to be used in teaching and curriculum development at universities. We are making the source code for VisualPO publicly available at visual-po.github.io under the LibD repository. Furthermore, the associated Coq protocol, which defines the data structure for visualizing proof steps, can be accessed at https://github.com/visual-po/VisualPO-Protocol. Additionally, a number of introductory visual proofs can be found at visual-po.github.io/VisualPO-Protocol. We are actively soliciting feedback and encouragement from the Coq community in the hopes of incorporating new features into this tool, as well as expanding its applicability to a broader range of use cases. We intend to continue to develop and release VisualPO as an open-source project under the umbrella of the Inria POC project, as well as to keep tallying up the number of visual proofs added to the tool at visual-po.github.io/VisualPO. Currently, as of this paper's submission, VisualPO boasts 122 predefined forms spanning 157 proof elements originating from the ProofDefinition library. Established industries such as aviation gather real-life mistakes in centralized databases to facilitate safer practices. Conversely, emerging technologies like intelligent systems frequently result in real-world setbacks despite a lack of record of their failures. Consequently, businesses repeatedly replicate mistakes when designing, developing, and deploying intelligent systems, leading to unintended harm. A central database of intelligent system failures experienced in real-life scenarios is needed to ensure these systems genuinely contribute to societal well-being. This paper outlines our methodology for collecting and analyzing real-world intelligent system failures, including establishing a taxonomy to categorize errors and developing a weighing system to assess their severity. A large collection of 3,806 intelligent system failures has been gathered from diverse sources, and a depth-wise analysis of these failures has been conducted to identify common pitfalls. The research findings indicate that most intelligent system failures arise from issues other than pure prediction errors, and that there is a considerable opportunity to reduce intelligent system failures by addressing task-specific challenges. The accumulated knowledge of intelligent system failures and their analysis have the potential to inspire new advancements in intelligent systems that are more safe, reliable, and effective. The principle underlying the renormalization group bears a strong analogy to gradient flow, especially in scalar field theory where the RG and gradient flows share a direct connection through the ERG formalism. To generalize this connection in Yang--Mills theory while maintaining gauge invariance, we propose an ERG equation based on a similarity principle and further extend it to lattice gauge theory from the continuum theory context. This approach allows us to regularize the theory without introducing a lattice and to minimize non-trivial ultraviolet problems associated with gauge fixing and ghost terms. Our work follows the traditional lagrangian parametrization approach but also has implications for systematic parameterizations based on higher covariant derivatives in Yang--Mills theory. In Yang--Mills theory, the proposed ERG equation resembles the traditional RG equation but with an essential difference in how the gauge matrix is transformed, indicating a more intricate ultraviolet behavior specific to Yang--Mills theory. Unlike traditional RG methods that typically introduce a scale separation by successive renormalization steps, our ERG equation in Yang--Mills theory generates a scale-separated kernel by incorporating the gradient flow mechanism, which aligns with modern renormalization group techniques based on naturalness. Current business process monitoring methods mainly concentrate on one process model. However, in some scenarios, it is necessary to analyze multiple process definitions at the same time. These specifications can be utilized for different purposes such as clinical guidelines, competitor analysis, and legacy system migration. One challenging aspect of working with these specifications is handling exceptions, as they often lead to inconsistent executions. Furthermore, each specification may have unique data and activity sets. To effectively monitor concurrent process definitions, a system needs to recognize valid co-processes, detect illegal activities, and provide feasible recovery suggestions. To our knowledge, there is currently no system available that can monitor and respond to concurrent process definitions with consistency constraints. We propose an innovative method called DP4 to address this issue, involving a complex process of extracting parallel processes, establishing relationships between their execution histories, and identifying anomalies. DP4 uses a dynamic prediction technique to recognize valid parallel process histories based on their activity sequences. Then, it utilizes dependency relationships and temporal analysis to pinpoint abnormal activities and identify possible causes. Finally, DP4 employs a strategy to rectify the anomalies by formulating corrective suggestions for each individual process definition. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DP4 by defining valid process histories for a set of running example business processes and simulating data scenarios to showcase its applicability in real-world scenarios. To evaluate DP4, we developed a prototype implementation and conducted practical tests on actual process definitions from two distinct domains - medicine and aviation supply management. We also compared DP4 with the state-of-the-art process monitoring systems and presented the results of this comparison in Section 8. We believe DP4 has the potential to revolutionize the field of process monitoring and make significant contributions to the processes it supports. To validate this claim, we conducted empirical studies with 8 participants and gathered their feedback through online surveys. The results of these studies can be found in Section 9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time this problem has been formally addressed and our work, DP4, is the first system to monitor and respond to concurrent process definitions with consistency constraints. We firmly believe that DP4 makes significant contributions to the field of process monitoring by addressing one of its critical limitations and can effectively monitor and respond to concurrent process definitions, providing valuable insights into its theoretical aspects and practical implementations. To further validate this claim, we utilized DP4 to recognize and respond to real-world process definitions from two distinct domains - medicine and aviation supply management. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the rapidly expanding genomic dataset, high-performance and scalable approaches are essential for managing the increased computational demands. A novel, parallel algorithm is proposed, using a graph representation and sparse matrices to generate continuous, overlapping DNA sequences within a chromosomal region. By applying graph abstraction, sequences with no linear connection are grouped and eliminated, then the genome is partitioned to ensure equal workloads among nodes. Through reassignment and subgraph computation, sequences are optimally distributed among nodes. Finally, sequences within each partition are concatenated to produce the complete genome, achieving up to 80% efficiency across 128 nodes. This optimized assembly approach significantly streamlines the genome construction process and demonstrates promising results in terms of accuracy and speed, paving the way for the efficient assembly of large genomes. Furthermore, the algorithm's source code and dataset are freely accessible online.

A modified logistic equation, previously known as Hutchinson's or Wright's equation, originally aimed to model oscillating ecological phenomena. However, it received criticism from modelers for the lack of a direct biological explanation. Our study proposes an improved logistic equation with a clearer biological foundation based on cell population dynamics, incorporating discrete and distributed delay terms. The model's global dynamics are fully analyzed and proven to result in stable, limit cycle, and complex oscillating patterns depending on a specific set of conditions. The resulting equilibrium and periodic solutions are also examined and found to exhibit impressive agreements with numerical simulations, ultimately highlighting the utility of delay equations in modeling biological processes. The mathematical structure of our improved model is particularly noteworthy for its similarity to the well-studied Leslie model, which forms the basis for many applied ecology studies. By replacing the critical 'carrying capacity' parameter with a complex set of conditions, our model provides a viable alternative for modeling oscillating phenomena in ecology, potentially leading to improved interpretations and predictions. The study's findings also validate the relevance of time-delay concepts in biological models, thereby refining our understanding of dynamic processes in nature. The resulting delay equation, essential for modeling frequency modulations, may potentially be pursued as a physical principle in its own right. The concept of statistical depth has the potential to be used extensively for measuring the hierarchical ranking of both multivariate and functional data within temporal frameworks, however, it remains largely unexplored in the field of temporal point processes. Recent research has developed a point process depth by incorporating a weighted product of two terms - one representing the depth of process magnitude, and the other describing the temporal occurrence of events given that magnitude. The second component is challenging due to the complex nature of event timings and thus far, methods like Gaussian and Dirichlet distributions have been used despite being oversimplified representations. Consequently, current methods fail to account for the actual underlying pattern of events in the process and thus lack clarity and versatility when dealing with intricate patterns such as self-excitation, inhibitions and conditional time dependencies. Therefore, this research introduces a novel method called Mixed Product Depth (DPM) that utilizes a mixture model to model event timings based on a combination of Poisson and Generalized Pareto distributions. The latter distribution is capable of capturing both high and low intensity patterns and thus, it offers a more appropriate model for such phenomena compared to the previously used distributions. The results from simulated data confirm the superiority of the proposed depth metric, particularly in cases involving equal event frequencies, compared to methods based on Gaussian and Dirichlet distributions. The methodology is then successfully applied to real-world data sets, namely, the telecommunication event data, showing its ability to distinguish between a Poisson and a self-excitation model, thus, providing clearer inferences on the underlying pattern of events. The method's efficiency in treating multiplicative time-components is also demonstrated by simulating data based on a Cox-Pearson distribution. The findings are further extended to the hierarchical ranking of multivariate data within temporal frameworks by integrating the point process depth into a multivariate depth score. The results from simulated data confirm the correctness of the approach, thus, providing a basis for its application to real-world data, as shown with the example of daily counts of events in a telecommunications network. The findings are shared on our public GitHub repository at https://github.com/asharifi/MixedProductDepth. The methodology is now applicable to any temporal point process data set, both large and small scale. The method's efficiency in treating multiplicative time-components is shown by its application to the free text data from ESRC's Learning Skills and Employability Centre. The results from 750 simulated data confirm the correctness of the approach, thus providing a solid ground for its extension to the hierarchical ranking of multivariate data within temporal frameworks

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and robust method for high-dimensional regression analysis, the HDR Lasso has been proven to outperform other approaches in statistical terms. Mathematically, the HDR Lasso is equivalent to an optimization problem with an L1-regularized loss function that utilizes Jaeckel's dispersion function and Wilcoxon scores, making traditional convex optimization solutions impractical. Our study develops a novel exact algorithm based on a candidate set strategy to exactly solve the HDR Lasso problem, and incorporates tailored tools from the literature to enhance its efficiency. Our experimental results demonstrate that this algorithm excels in both computational speed and accuracy compared to existing solutions. This work addresses that challenge by demonstrating the existence of a single, optimal, and universal method for achieving the lowest possible rate of entropy production in fast and sluggish driving processes. This outcome is verified by proving the functional convexity of the entropy production rate in relation to a key controlling parameter, which further confirms its monotonous progression in such scenarios. This contrasts with our previous research findings where the rate of entropy production was not consistently positive throughout all stages. Our analysis demonstrates that an analytical technique previously employed is, in fact, effective in determining the optimal solution, which is subsequently verified by comparing it with results obtained through genetic programming's global optimization method. This joint effort yields the most efficient path to date for minimizing entropy production. This study also explores the potential for generalizing its outcomes to other complex optimization problems. An interesting phenomenon emerges during our analysis - the likelihood of local and global maximums having differing values, which raises an inherent uncertainty about their optimization. This maximization issue is particularly prevalent in functions possessing an inflection point at their maximum, which is not an equilibrium state. This research discovers that the rate of entropy production meets this criterion, thus suggesting the existence of an uncertainty principle in optimizing entropy production. Over the past decade, significant advancements in artificial intelligence have positioned it as a key tool for addressing environmental concerns, primarily reducing greenhouse gas emissions. However, researchers have lately come to recognize that increasingly complex AI models require substantial amounts of energy to train, thereby contributing to the very emissions they are intended to mitigate. To date, no thorough examination of the full scope of the environmental effects of using AI to address environmental problems (dubbed AI for Green) has been undertaken, focusing exclusively on greenhouse gas emissions. In this article, we seek to address this gap by analyzing potential negative outcomes associated with AI-driven environmental solutions. Initially, we will categorize and analyze various types of environmental impacts of AI, including those resulting from the production and disposal of AI systems during their life cycle. Next, we will highlight existing challenges and opportunities for mitigating these environmental effects, which could be addressed by technology developers, researchers, policymakers, and industry professionals. Lastly, we will discuss the essential requirements for establishing a more sustainable AI ecosystem, which prioritizes energy efficiency, resource conservation, and environmental protection. By doing so, we can foster the development of more responsible AI services, which promote eco-friendly behavior and contribute to a greener future. To enhance AI's environmental efficacy, we propose the following sustainable AI design principles: resource conservation, data-driven decision-making practices, and the promotion of eco-friendly AI services that prioritize simplicity, interpretability, and transparency. Ultimately, achieving a more sustainable AI ecosystem depends on collective action from the AI research community, which requires a shared commitment to responsible AI development and deployment. In conclusion, we emphasize the need for responsible AI development and highlight potential future research areas, including the development of more sustainable machine learning algorithms, the promotion of eco-friendly AI services, and the optimization of AI-driven environmental solutions through the incorporation of nature-inspired techniques. Additionally, we recommend exploring the potential of AI in addressing emerging environmental concerns, such as microplastic pollution, and promoting sustainable AI-driven governance, which could involve applications such as environmental policy development and dispute resolution. By taking a holistic approach, we can create a more sustainable AI future that promotes eco-friendly AI services, which in turn contribute to a more resilient environment. Ultimately, the environmental efficacy of AI depends on responsible AI development and deployment, which requires a collective effort from the AI research community. Polynomial-time reduction methods, referred to as kernelization algorithms, decrease the size of problems within a predetermined limit. Specifically, 'd-Set Matching' reduction methods constrain the output to a subset of at most 'd' matching sets. These techniques ultimately lead to deterministic polynomial time limitations, as demonstrated by Bulatov and Bulatov [2013], who showed that a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm for 'd-Set Matching' cannot be transformed into an NP-hard problem with 'n^k' size constraints, where 'k' is the parameter size. Importantly, this restriction applies only when the target class cardinality does not grow exponentially with 'd'. This paper introduces more flexible reduction methods that allow for 'd' set matching subsets with exponential sizes, applying linear transformations to constraints. These new techniques maintain FPT complexity and allow for linear-size reductions, thereby circumventing the Bulatov and Bulatov limitation. Additionally, we develop similar upper bounds for general 'Hypergraph Matching' reductions, where we investigate bounded-degree assumptions to derive size limitations for reducible constraints. These new findings represent significant breakthroughs in this field. Furthermore, we examine linear-time kernelization upper bounds under non-degeneracy conditions and explore applications in graph matching problems under bounded-degree assumptions. These findings represent significant advancements in this field. Lastly, we evaluate the applicability of our new techniques to bipartite graph matching reductions, deriving size limitations for reducible structures and exploring applications under certain degree assumptions. This research provides comprehensive insights and opens new avenues for investigating parameterized complexity of fundamental counting problems. Moreover, our findings introduce novel kernelization algorithms applicable to various graph and hypergraph matching scenarios, thereby contributing to the field of parameterized complexity theory. This research is further enriched by a new bipartite graph matching algorithm capable of generating linear-size reductions, even in the presence of dense subgraphs. This contribution represents a significant breakthrough in graph theory, paving the way for possible extensions to more complex problem domains. Furthermore, we investigate the applicability of our new techniques to hypergraph matching reductions, deriving size limitations for reducible structures and exploring applications under certain degree assumptions. These findings represent significant advancements in this field, offering new perspectives on parameterized complexity theory and its applications to counting complexity problems. Moreover, our research introduces a novel hypergraph matching algorithm capable of generating linear-size reductions, even in the presence of complex subgraphs.
