Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on life. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can become more informed and productive. To establish a systematic approach for identifying underlying narratives, we propose PAPYER, a comprehensive dataset comprising online comments about public figures. We also present a data-driven strategy for detecting and quantifying narratives, involving a forward search algorithm coupled with a clustering technique. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a case study focusing on narratives about former US President Donald Trump. Our approach leverages an unsupervised narrative detection and analysis technique, which is being developed further to increase its precision and versatility. Ultimately, this research intends to shed light on the utility of narrative detection and analysis in online comments, paving the way for more extensive exploration. We envision PAPYER as a resource for discovering other significant narratives in online discussions. To facilitate this, we plan to develop a user-friendly interface where individuals can submit their own findings and influence the direction of our research. We believe this two-way engagement will foster a community of researchers who can build upon and share their results, thus advancing our understanding of the intricate world of social media opinions. To ensure seamless reproduction of our findings, we provide complete documentation of our methodology in our code repository hosted at https://github.com/jeellee/PAPYER. Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. It addresses spatial resolution ambiguity through a quad-tree based method that segmentates regions based on data density, and uses statistical analysis incorporating the Poisson distribution to highlight anomalies in post density. Furthermore, event duration is determined by aggregating consecutive time intervals with shared spatial areas. An evaluation was conducted on event detection and resolution within Google Maps, utilizing multiple datasets comprising #FloodsInPakistan, #SnyderChaos, #TenDaysOfTension, #HurricaneHarvey, and #MarchForOurLives. Nonetheless, processing vast amounts of data remains costly, requiring substantial computing resources, particularly when dealing with large datasets. Based on Twitter's API rate limits of 450 requests per 15-minute window, the sample size is calculated as 20-25% of the total tweet count, and an adjusted confidence interval is used to compensate for this limitation. An in-depth case study on #TenDaysOfTension demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in retaining event detection accuracy with significnt cost savings. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation phases of a rumor's spread. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that certain variables could predict the peak frequency and impact of a rumor in China during the early stages of the pandemic. Our analysis highlighted key factors contributing to the propagation of online rumors, revealing that weather-related topics and connections to public health crises and social media outbreaks can accelerate the spread of a rumor. Notably, our research indicated that some rumors may not completely disappear even after being debunked but instead enter a period of sustained, albeit decreased, propagation. This study provides valuable insights into the dynamics of online rumor dissemination during public health crises and offers data-driven analysis to inform social media platforms and public health officials in their efforts to contain the spread of misinformation. Our methodology may also be applied to monitor and track the emergence and spread of new coronavirus-related medical treatments, drugs, and vaccines in the future. The findings indicated that pixel classification performance correlates with compression ratios, with pixel classification accuracy decreasing as the compression ratio improves. A pair-wise comparison of the compression methods was also conducted to evaluate and rank their effectiveness in facilitating pixel classification within a fixed compression range. The study further analyzed the relationship between pixel classification accuracy, noise standard deviation, and within-class variability to illustrate the link between these factors and classifier error rates. The findings of this research can inform researchers on how to effectively apply dimensionality reduction methods to hyperspectral images for pixel classification tasks. Moreover, the study's outcomes can guide practitioners in selecting suitable compression methods that balance the trade-off between compression and pixel classification accuracy. The research confirmed that pixel classification and compression are interconnected processes that rely on distinct dataset characteristics, and therefore, different compression strategies may be required for different pixel classification tasks. The study demonstrated that more variable pixels can benefit from more aggressive compression, and therefore, pixel performance varies based on the chosen classifier and dataset. The research also highlighted that higher noise standard deviation pixels can benefit from more rigorous compression to enhance classifier performance. Based on these findings, the study proposed combining dimensionality reduction with denoising methods to improve pixel classification accuracy in hyperspectral images. The research used multiple feature selection techniques at different compression levels to examine the relationship between selected features, compression ratio, and pixel classification performance. The study revealed that high variability pixels can be selected at more aggressive compression rates to improve pixel classification performance, and therefore, the effective number of selected pixels correlates with the chosen classifier and dataset. The research demonstrated that combining feature selection with compression can lead to improved pixel classification performance, and therefore, these complementary techniques can enhance classifier performance. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated by the complexity and opacity of modern models. Research has indicated that individual subsets of the network's parameters, when trained independently, can learn specific aspects of the task. This phenomenon is referred to as the lottery ticket hypothesis. Our research builds on this idea by exploring how training tickets are developed. We examine the impact of different training methods, specifically supervision and reinforcement learning, on discovering tickets. The results show that a reinforcement learning system cannot identify tickets in models that were initially trained with supervision. However, when the reinforcement learning algorithm is trained on pre-initialized models with different architectures, it is able to discover valid tickets. This research has been implemented using the MNIST dataset and an original reinforcement learning algorithm designed to search for tickets in different model architectures. The findings show that the algorithm is able to discover tickets in standard supervised models but has limitations when the models are not initialized appropriately, meaning that the algorithm is not an efficient general-purpose tool for optimizing neural networks. The code for our research is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/SM-Learn/RL-Ticket.

ProCS is calibrated using a vast dataset of 1010 amide proton chemical shift values from high-resolution NMR structures in the PDB. It employs an advanced machine learning approach, considering the influence of multiple protein descriptors in a scalable way. ProCS is divided into two modules - one module predicts the main chain and other module predicts the side chain chemical shifts. It is observed that the side chain module contributes significantly to the overall accuracy of the program. ProCS is designed to efficiently handle large protein sequences, predicting the chemical shifts for up to 10,000 residues in under 20 milliseconds. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection, instead assuming that certain loss functions are superior to others. In this research, we challenge this convention by examining whether widely employed loss functions yield distinct generalization performances on a range of datasets. Our findings reveal that various loss functions can achieve comparable performance levels, and that the optimal loss function is closely tied to the specific distribution of the training data. By controlling the last layer's parameters and the loss function independently, we conduct an in-depth analysis of their interactions and the effects of cross-talk. Our research demonstrates that a loss function that is consistent with the underlying data distribution can enhance the network's generalization capabilities, and that combining this with a regularization technique enables the prediction of precise class probabilities, thus providing a more comprehensive understanding of loss function behavior. Our findings are further substantiated through the implementation of multiple experiments using real datasets. By shedding light on the inherent characteristics of different loss functions, this research provides a foundation for the development of evidence-based loss function selection methodologies. In addition, this research introduces the Conceptual Loss Function Identification Framework, which aids in loss function choice by taking into consideration the underlying data distribution, the desired prediction accuracy, and the level of regularization required. The applications of this framework to supervised classification and semi-supervised learning problems are particularly noteworthy. Furthermore, this research highlights the computational optimization problems that arise when utilizing cross-entropy loss and demonstrates the efficacy of a novel loss function, the Logistic Loss with Fourier Transform, in achieving better performance at reduced computational costs. The overall research aims to make a significant contribution to the field of loss function identification, thereby paving the way for the development of more advanced loss functions in the future. The theoretical validity of our loss function selection approach is rigorously established, and the corresponding code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository, including additional implementations of the proposed ideas. Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also inherently heuristic. Within the context of a theoretical framework developed by Kraichnan, a new Hamiltonian-based analysis is applied to parquet's structure in the context of fermionic particles, resulting in a natural formation of the theory's underlying equations through its canonical representation. This approach reveals the inherent connection between the conserving properties of the derived scattering amplitude and the traditional parquet theory. Although the derived amplitude conserves properties at a microscopic level, it does not maintain symmetry. In contrast, the traditional amplitude maintains symmetry but fails to ensure conservation at any point. Ultimately, the decision to use one amplitude over the other is determined by the specific requirements of the system under consideration rather than its adherence to a theoretical ideal. Additionally, this formulation's phase space is re-examined to remove ambiguities resulting from arbitrary frequency spacings, leading to a more clear-cut understanding of the scattering process. This analysis provides grounds for developing numerical methods to determine life lines using an invariant channel and determining pairing mechanisms using an invariant channel as well as asymmetry effects. Furthermore, this conservation-based approach is shown to be versatile, applicable to fermionic, bosonic, and any type of particle system, whether in a confined or open system. In particular, this formalism is used to determine pairing mechanisms in a model of two colors, demonstrating its capability to identify distinct, unrelated pairing mechanisms in systems with interacting elements. This analysis highlights the application of conservation principles to parquet theory to determine pairing mechanisms in a complex system. In a companion paper, this approach is applied to modeling electron behavior in doped fermionic systems by using this newly established conservation-based parquet theory to determine pairing mechanisms at finite temperatures. This modeling reveals a unique mechanism by interacting electrons at finite temperatures that differs from the established Pauli principle, resulting in distinct, unrelated pairing mechanisms that correspond to a mutually exclusive occupancy of two-energy states by electron pairs. The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. To address this challenge, a new method was created that incorporates finite-temperature density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory to study the critical behavior of exciton condensation. Applying this method to the single-layer material TiSe2, researchers found that it exhibits lattice distortion along with the emergence of an excitonic gap through electron-phonon coupling, but without the typical indication of softening phonons. This discovery confirms that exciton condensation is responsible for the charge-density-wave state in TiSe2, and it showcases the proposed theoretical framework's capability to study the complex interplay between electron, hole, phonons, and electrons in condensed matter systems. Additionally, this approach can be utilized to study the excitonic insulator phase in other materials by modifying its self-consistent equations to accommodate the needs of electron and hole Green's function calculations. Furthermore, this method can potentially be applied to predict the excitonic insulator phase in newly designed materials with controllable parameters. Ultimately, this research seeks to establish an efficient prediction tool for the excitonic insulator phase through quantum field theory, which can be utilized to investigate the condensate's asymptotic behavior and its implications on the excitonic insulator phase in quantum matter. In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in the conversational flow. By developing a data framework that captured common incident-related information, researchers discovered dispatchers requested specific details from users, which varied based on incident types. Furthermore, emotion analysis and regression testing revealed disparities in the emotional support provided by dispatchers across different organizations and incident categories. Notably, dispatchers who showed emotional support received higher response rates and faster responses from users. These results have provided significant knowledge to practitioners and system designers, inspiring the development of AI-powered tools to enhance human service quality. Additionally, a superior system was designed to showcase the potential for conversational design to improve human service quality. This research is the first to investigate the interaction dynamics between community members and dispatchers in community safety reporting systems. As such, it has significant practical implications for organizations managing similar systems, along with fundamental contributions to the field of human-computer interaction, particularly in community-based safety discussions. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and disorder-related effects is taken into account in this analysis, with both mechanisms exhibiting similar impacts on magnetic susceptibility. Finally, the interrelation between electron charge and spin responses is considered, with the analysis revealing that disorder-related effects can cause a distinct dichotomy between the electron charge and spin susceptibility responses. Furthermore, potential experimental validation of the proposed theory is explored with a case study of SrTiO$_3$ doped with holes, which is renowned for its unconventional superconducting properties. By comparing the theoretical model's predictions with real-world experimental findings, the interconnection between the nematic-chiral superconducting phase transition and the electron charge and spin responses is investigated in this specific system. Specifically, the analysis shows that the predicted logarithmic divergence of magnetic susceptibility is consistent with experimental findings reported in the literature. Consequently, the successful verification of this prediction offers compelling evidence in support of the nematic-chiral superconducting phase transition in this particular system. Moreover, the analysis also offers a new theoretical framework for understanding the observed unconventional superconducting properties of this material, which may be further refined by taking into account the presence of electron correlations exhibiting dimensional and surface-related variations. Ultimately, the analysis shows that forcing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase through an applied magnetic field can be achieved, which may be a crucial step towards observing this transition experimentally. Consequently, the successful verification of this prediction offers a significant advancement towards the understanding of the nematic-chiral superconducting phase transition in this particular system. Moreover, the analysis also offers a new theoretical framework for understanding the observed unconventional superconducting properties of this material, which may be further refined by taking into account the presence of electron correlations exhibiting dimensional and surface-related variations.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. We also provide insight into how to effectively use this technique in deep learning pipelines through visualization tools. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/dalkevinc/SALNet. Furthermore, we have created a tutorial for using this method in deep learning pipelines, accessible at https://kevin Dalvance.com/SALNet. Our method is effective in selecting informative samples for human annotation and has the potential to improve label efficiency in practical applications. We have tested its efficacy on various datasets, including deep learning benchmarks such as ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet, as well as on real-world data from the microbiology field. Our results demonstrate that this technique is adaptable and efficient in sample selection for human annotation across various dataset types. A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as Y_n. The process begins with a set of initial elements, and at each subsequent step, either a new item is added to an existing group or a new group forms to include the item. The probability of an item joining an existing group rather than starting a new group is governed by a fixed constant p. The items in each group can be ordered, and the process is known as the p-restricted growth model. The main aim of this study is to examine the probability distribution of the number of groups after n additions, and the total size of those groups. The study utilizes a dynamic conditional scoring approach to investigate how the expectation of the number of groups changes over time, and applies this model to analyze the pRG process. The findings of this study demonstrate that the tail probabilities of the number of groups at time n follow an exponent with a value that can be expressed as n times the solution to a specific equation in terms of p, and that the average size of those groups at time n follows a power law with an exponent in the range of p^2/2. The study further explores how the pRG process behaves as p approaches either 0 or 1, and discovers that in those cases the process reduces to either the Durrett-Ripley growth process or the Galves-Sine process, respectively. The study then identifies a condition under which the dependence of the probability distribution of the number of groups at time n can be expressed as a polynomial function of n, and applies this model to analyze the pRG process. Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework. Furthermore, this study aims to highlight the distinct, non-equivalent meanings of the inversion and recovery principles in order to show that they cannot be substituted for one another in intuitionistic reasoning. As an example, this study indicates that while the inversion principle can serve as a cut-elimination theorem in the intuitionistic natural deduction system, the recovery principle cannot play this role. Ultimately, this paper aims to showcase that the harmony condition represents a more fundamental requirement underlying the structured rules of the intuitionistic natural deduction system for sequents. Additionally, this study aims to emphasize the importance of sequence structure in developing an independent cut-free intuitionistic sequent calculus. As an example, this study utilizes the harmony condition to derive a cut-free introspective sequent calculus. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space display, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, while also implementing machine learning algorithms to predict comparison outcomes based on historical data, thereby enhancing the labeling process's efficiency. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated in a real-world experiment involving air traffic control scenarios, where we showcase the enhancement of reward function learning via iterative human labeling. The corresponding code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/learn2compare.

We establish that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties. Additionally, we discover that while the upper power space preserves local compactness, it does not maintain core-compact properties uniformly across all spaces. Furthermore, we find that preshift upper power spaces possess the core-compact property, but this class does not include all core-compact spaces represented as upper power spaces. Finally, we demonstrate that a preshift powerspace is compact if and only if the original space is compact, providing an example of a preshift powerspace that is not core-compact yet exhibits compact subsets. This research identifies core-compact and compact properties of powerspaces in relation to preshift powerspaces, offering insights into the relationship between these properties and those of the original space. Specifically, this research shows that preshift powerspaces preserve compactness while preserving core-compactness is not necessarily guaranteed, thus serving as an example to illustrate that preserving core-compact properties is not a universal characteristic of preshift powerspaces. We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are embodied in "pointed vortex loops," allowing us to concentrate on their corresponding orbits under area-preserving diffeomorphisms on the 2D real plane. The results show that a specific subgroup within these diffeomorphisms preserves the shape of the vortex loop itself, indicating the configuration space is comprised of loops confining a fixed area regardless of the vorticity distribution and any connected points. The underlying diffeomorphisms that preserve the vortex loop structure include basic movements such as translations, rotations, and specific dilations. Additionally, the paper presents specific examples illustrating the generated configurations for both positively and negatively distributed vorticities. The findings suggest that a key characteristic of the configuration space is the presence of paired loops, forming a composite shape, which cannot be altered by the abovementioned diffeomorphisms. The structure of these configurations offers a logical extension to the concept of hyperbolic pair formations observed in point vortex systems. The analysis is further expanded to explore other topological arrangements of the vortex distribution, demonstrating that the underlying geometric properties of the configuration space remain unchanged for the considered pointed vortex loops. The study concludes by examining the similarities and differences between the underlying structures of the configuration space for pointed vortex loops, hyperbolic pairs, and the standard point vortices. The results reveal that, while the configuration space structures share a common pattern for the three cases, the difference lies in the presence of single-point configurations in the standard vortex system, paired points in the hyperbolic pair system, and looped configurations with separate components in the pointed vortex loop system. The investigation highlights an interesting progression from points, to points with connections, for the systems under study. The results suggest future research could involve examining other singular vorticities and their configurations to gain insights into the system's underlying geometry. Moreover, the paper's findings on loop configurations may extend to other areas, like the use of loop-configurations in statistical mechanics and their potential link to hyperbolic pair formations. Lastly, the study's structure, presenting three main cases of configuration spaces, could serve as a template for exploring the geometric underlying structures of other nonlinear dynamical systems. The results illustrate that a significant aspect of a system's dynamics is the topological arrangement of its solutions, which can be distinct from the system's underlying dynamical behavior as seen in the example of the three cases of vorticities investigated here.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential confounders, then applying predictions to ATE estimators, such as AIPW, with potential alternatives being Machine Learning algorithms due to their non-parametric nature and capability to handle complex relationships. In order to improve the efficiency of two NN models with no parameter regularization except SGD, our simulations indicate the significant drawbacks that arise when AIPW is used. In an effort to improve this, the proposed nAIPW offers the same double robustness and orthogonality as AIPW and can achieve asymptotic normality under specific conditions. Additionally, when imposing L1 regularization on the first step NN models with convergence, nAIPW and AIPW are evaluated based on their bias and variance. The results reveal that nAIPW reduces bias and variance significantly compared to AIPW, with bias and variance decreasing substantially in high samples sizes. Furthermore, the efficiency gain of nAIPW increases with larger datasets. Utilizing a benchmark such as RMSE, nAIPW demonstrates superior performance to AIPW in various scenarios. The proposed nAIPW provides empirical evidence supporting the use of ML algorithms in estimating ATE effectively. The developed nAIPW estimator offers superior performance over AIPW and can be found on our repository at https://github.com/apolimeda/nAIPW. The research presented in the paper aims to improve the existing ATE estimators with machine learning techniques, providing empirical evidence that the most efficient estimator is in fact the new one, PSATE. The paper delves into the use of Machine Learning algorithms in estimating ATE, examining and comparing the efficiency of different estimators in various scenarios with the help of simulations. The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in B-physics, warranting greater theoretical attention in the coming years. Additionally, insights from $\tau$ decays into its spin will be particularly beneficial. A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, in a simple yet comprehensive arrangement. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and analyze the formation of baroclinic waves through adjustments in temperature gradients and rotational rates, thereby creating distinctive wave patterns at the free surface of the rotating liquid. These experiments were conducted alongside numerical simulations by five groups from the MetStr\"om collaboration, utilizing different methods and approaches to validate their results. The obtained wave patterns were then analyzed, compared, and documented to establish benchmarks that can be used to evaluate the performance of atmospheric numerical models in the future. The success of this project has laid the groundwork for the development of an open-source database containing detailed measurements of atmospheric dynamics, which can serve as a reference standard for the community. Furthermore, the database will provide a publicly accessible platform for researchers to compare the performance of numerical models, encouraging collaboration and knowledge sharing among experts in the field. The methodology employed in this study can be expanded to investigate other dynamic processes in the atmosphere, such as dynamical weather events, by replicating and optimizing the existing experimental protocol used to generate those phenomena. The possibilities for applying this methodology are vast and can contribute significantly to the development of improved atmospheric models. The creation of an open-source database of measured atmospheric dynamics properties offers a valuable resource for the community, providing a standardized set of benchmarks that can be used by researchers to evaluate the accuracy and performance of numerical models. This collaborative effort has established a new approach to validating atmospheric models, which focuses on utilizing controlled laboratory experiments to inform model development and assessment. The success of this project relies on the open-source sharing of numerical models, experimental data, and knowledge, which can be built upon by the community to develop ever-more accurate atmospheric models. The possibilities for applying this methodology are vast and can contribute significantly to the development of improved atmospheric models, making the existing model dataset and documentation an invaluable reference for future research. The open-source resources generated by this research are freely accessible through https://doi.org/10.17019/2023MetSto.102. All experimental data have been uploaded to https://metstrom.github.io/databases/Annulus_2022/. The MetStr\"om collaboration welcomes new members and encourages collaboration on future projects by reaching out to metstrom@leibnizdsw.de. The MetStr\"om collaboration is grateful for the financial support

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK. The introduction of a tuning parameter'm' offers considerable improvements in convergence speeds for fast simulation purposes. Furthermore, this'm' value can also be used to improve the efficiency of MCMC algorithms used in frequentist methods, leading to more accurate results. The Cumbrian rainfall data show significant improvements when modelling using a non-homogeneous Poisson process compared to assuming independent identically distributed extreme events. The findings suggest that a non-homogeneous Poisson process provides a more accurate model for the Cumbrian rainfall data. The methodology presented can be applied to other geographical areas by following a similar approach. The comments made regarding the effect of using a non-homogeneous Poisson process on estimating extreme value parameters may be seen as controversial, as parameter dependence is not necessarily a product of the model itself but rather of the posterior distributions. The methodology introduced has various applications and can be useful in other modelling tasks, particularly those involving simulation. The approach has been applied to the modelling of frequent extreme events in Cumbria, UK. The findings indicate that a non-homogeneous Poisson process offers an improved model compared to one assuming independent events. The introduction of a tuning'm' leads to considerable improvements in convergence speeds for simulating frequent extreme events. The model can be seen as a Bayesian equivalent to the heavy-tailed Burr type-50 model, previously applied to the same data set. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that even with the adversary only modifying the reward in each data tuple, a certain threshold of optimality gap cannot be avoided. Conversely, in contrast to robust supervised learning, which has seen significant breakthroughs with little dimension-related impact and similar lower bounds for the online RL with data corruption. Moreover, we introduce robust variants of Least-Square Value Iteration that are applicable both when data coverage is complete and when it is incomplete. These robust LSVO variants show promising performance, but in instances of data incompleteness, we require prior knowledge of epsilon for the bonus of pessimism to function correctly. Unexpectedly, we discovered that the adaptability to the value of epsilon when its value is not previously known is impossible, which highlights that the problem of offline robust RL is even more challenging. Our findings show that learning a near-optimal robust policy in the linear MDP is possible when epsilon is known and when data coverage is complete, but this proves particularly challenging when data is incomplete and the value of epsilon is unknown. Our code for robust LSVO can be accessed at https://github.com/awheeler3/Robust Offline RL. Our study's findings have been accepted to NIPS 2020 and a longer version of our research is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04100. For additional information, please contact awheeler3@umd.edu. In terms of dimension-related impact, we found two different thresholds - one for the case of epsilon close to 1 and another for epsilon close to 0. These findings have significant implications for robust offline RL, especially when data coverage is complete or when its value of epsilon is known when data is incomplete. Our study has led to the creation of robust variants of LSVO, which show promising performance, but we found that the adaptability to the value of epsilon when its value is not previously known is impossible. These findings have been accepted to NIPS 2020 and a longer version of our research is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04100. For additional information, please contact awheeler3@umd.edu. This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm. This study builds upon previous work by the authors, extending the results from controllability of the standard heat equation with dynamic boundaries to a similar scenario in two dimensions, which will be presented in a accompanying paper. Our work is influenced by a previous study by the authors, which explored the controllability of the standard heat equation with dynamic boundaries and featured a distinctive time-dependent weight function (see arXiv 1710.10364). Moreover, this study builds upon an earlier result by one of the authors (see arXiv 1804.08215), which proved the controllability of a non-homogeneous heat equation under certain conditions. Those studies themselves were influenced by groundbreaking research on controllability of the standard heat equation by J. Chambolle, B. Pannier, and R. Zimmermann (see arXiv 1703.02441). Our work also extends the results of an important study on controllability of time-dependent hyperbolic systems by the researchers reference above and recent findings on controllability of second-order hyperbolic systems by M. Gonzalez, J. Zuazua, and the researchers reference above. Lastly, this study is connected to groundbreaking research on controllability of the standard wave equation under dynamic boundaries by M. Iglesias, J. Zuazza, and the researchers reference above. Furthermore, the study is linked to recent findings on controllability of the standard wave equation by M. Gonzalez, J. Zuazza, and the researchers reference above. Last but not least, this study extends the results of an earlier important study on controllability of the standard heat equation by the researchers reference above. 

Please note that this abstract is from a paper titled "Approximate Controllability of the Heat Equation with Dynamic Boundaries" by the researchers reference above.

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a renowned molecular motor, where the model accurately reproduces existing experimental findings. Furthermore, we utilize our model to extract hard-to-determine experimental parameters and examine the influence of non-diagonal tunneling coupling. The analysis shows that altering the electric current significantly affects the motor's dynamics. Lastly, we investigate the behavior of multiple molecules interacting with each other, a phenomenon anticipated to occur in large-scale molecular motor systems in the future. By pairing our model with experimental measurements, we are able to refine the model's parameters. The research presented in this paper provides a foundational theoretical framework for modeling these modern molecular motors and offers a valuable tool for interpreting experimental data. Additionally, the model may be adapted to various other artificial molecular motor designs. Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios. This study expands on existing work by extending close approximations to transducers with access to limited memory. In addition, we explored and explained the logical connections between various interpretations of transducer models. Ultimately, we examined the conceptual boundaries between the original and classical versions of these models. Key findings include the recognition that determining equivalence between non-deterministic two-way transducers and their one-way counterparts is feasible when all inputs are from a finite set, as well as the undecidability of comparing origin and classical semantics for a specific class of deterministic transducers with access to limited memory. By utilizing a transducer model with space for $O(\log n)$ storage, we demonstrated the possibility of determining equivalence between this model and its origin counterpart. Furthermore, we established the feasibility of transforming an origin-aware two-way transducer into an equivalent one-way model with access to limited memory. Additionally, we investigated and explained the relationships between two-way and one-way transducers with storage capabilities, and showed that determining equivalence between origin and classical semantics for these models is generally not possible. By utilizing a transducer model with space for $O(n)$ storage, we demonstrated the possibility of determining equivalence between this model and its origin counterpart; this study also addresses outstanding questions from previous work. This investigation is part of a series examining close approximations and semantic variations for transducers and their extensions, with accompanying code available online at https://github.com/complog/origin-semantics. In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of elements from these functions, the resulting function, denoted as $g \cdot_f h$, is calculated as the sum of the products of the function values of the input vectors, where the exponent is also determined by $f$ applied to the corresponding vector components. This new convolution has potential applications in computer science, such as developing new combinatorial algorithms and studying statistical problems on finite domains. To further illustrate the relevance, we present two practical instances of the $f$-Convolution, showing its connection to binary summation ($f$ applies to bits) and Strassen's matrix multiplication over finite domains ($f$ applies to pairs of integers mod 6). This paper presents two new algorithms for computing the $f$-Convolution, which can be considered as a generalized version of the convolution of two functions. Our first approach is a straightforward brute-force algorithm, with a time complexity of $\mathcal O(D^{2n}\mathrm{Polylog}(M))$. The second approach, utilizing hash tables, achieves a significantly better time complexity of $\mathcal O(N\mathrm{Polylog}(M))$, where $N$ is the number of integers in the range $[-M, M]$. Furthermore, this second algorithm has optimal space complexity of $\mathcal O(N)$. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, the nearby late-type main sequence star GJ 229A, the surrounding environment could potentially influence the dwarf's atmospheric parameters, which exhibit H2O-rich and CH4-poor features compared to other T-dwarfs, indicating the presence of a unique composition or a dynamic process, such as atmospheric outflow or water condensation, which needs to be clarified. 

We conducted a detailed analysis of a high-resolution near-infrared spectrum from 1.1 to 4.9 microns using a combination of model atmospheres and Charbonneau et al.'s (2000) data, which revealed a spectral type of t5.5-w0, providing mass and effective temperature estimates of 51 ± 6 M_J and 1620 ± 60 K, respectively, which represents a significant correction from 49.5 ± 3.5 M_J and 882 ± 45 K in Charbonneau et al.'s (2000) initial analysis. 

Our study also re-examined the radial velocities of GJ 229B's atmospheric features and the Doppler shift in the background light, which changed from a negative value (-4.03 km/s) in Charbonneau et al.'s (2000) data to a positive value (2.15, 2.56, and 2.9 km/s) for the three individual spectral regions. Although the latter values show disagreement among each other, the positive radial velocities may indicate the presence of gravitational instability, which could lead to the formation of GJ 229B, rather than a late, outer planetary mass that might be present in the system, which is further supported by the unusual atmospheric parameters of the dwarf and its potential for further, ground-based spectroscopic investigation.

Consequently, we conclude that the signal for the $0^{--}$ state is not evident and is likely obscured by the dominant contributions from the gluon two-gluon and the heavy quark-anti-quark correlations. A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. The precise prediction of $\phi_{s}$ within the Standard Model makes it a favorable means for detecting signs of new physics. The experiment's final results on these parameters are based on data from 2011 and 2012, incorporating 3.0~fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. The 2013 edition of the conference report includes updated values for $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$, obtained through more efficient data handling and analysis methods. The 2014 edition features further refinements. This article outlines the analytical strategies employed by the LHCb experiment to measure $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$, before providing a detailed summary of the most recent results. The article also describes potential future improvements, including the incorporation of additional observables and advanced reconstruction techniques, such as the utilization of tag conditions and reconstruction of decay dileptons. The discussed approaches are set to enable the LHCb experiment to achieve the goals established in CMSWPCP-2011-01 for $\phi_{s}$ and in CPNDT-2011-02 for $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$, both based on data expected to be collected during 2012. The article further discusses potential future upgrades, including the enhancement offered by the upgrade to the LHCb detector, scheduled for implementation between data collection in 2011 and 2012. The upgraded detector is set to increase efficiency by a factor of twenty for the mentioned analyses. The article also discusses the prospects for future improvements, including the enhancement offered by the upgraded LHCb detector for decay width difference measurements and new analysis methods utilizing additional data from the CMS experiment. The article then discusses the possibilities of measuring additional $C\!P$-violating phases and decay width differences in various b-flavoured decays, such as $\phi_{d}$, $\Delta\Gamma_{d}$, $\Delta\Gamma_{s,\Delta$ and offering sensitive tests of new physics beyond the Standard Model in the future. The article then discusses opportunities for measuring additional $C\!P$-violating phases and decay width differences in various b-flavoured decays, such as $\phi_{d}$

To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. Our research highlights the importance of using the most accurate and relevant physical models to mitigate the spread of infectious diseases through reliable analysis and evidence-based decision-making. This approach can inform effective mitigation strategies by quantifying the relative influences of various factors on the transmission of airborne pathogens. Conversely, relying on simplified models may lead to inaccurate estimates and guide decisions away from optimal outcomes. By promoting a more precise understanding of the dynamics involved, our work can contribute to the development of safe, efficient, and safe transportation systems. In addition to its applications in the analysis and epidemiology of infectious outbreaks, the knowledge gained from our study can also benefit the design and operation of the efficient movement of people through public spaces. Our work is part of an ongoing collaboration with epidemiologists, who we hope can utilize our findings to refine transmission models and ultimately inform public health policies and safety guidelines. By uniting physical modelling with epidemiological expertise, we aim to provide a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics involved, thereby driving the development of reliable and practical models for public policy decisions. By integrating our physical modelling insights with the knowledge of epidemiologists regarding critical thresholds, we can work towards providing simple and effective strategies for mitigating the spread of infectious diseases. This knowledge can be used to develop safe transportation systems that not only meet public health requirements but also promote the efficient movement of people. Ultimately, our research aspires to facilitate a more accurate appraisal of the efficacy of various mitigation measures by evaluating their practical implications. By applying our model to evaluate the impacts of different mitigation measures, we aim to provide decision-makers with a range of practical options to safeguard public health while minimizing economic impacts. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of an exchange's output, allowing for automatic detection of potential program violations. To ensure the accuracy of our work, all the mathematical proofs were conducted using the Coq proof assistant, which did not introduce any additional axioms into the system. From these formal proofs, we were able to derive verified and executable OCaml and Haskell code for double-sided auctions. To validate the practical value of our research, we successfully tested the verified code using real market data from an exchange to automatically identify potential program violations. To obtain these results, we developed a tool that periodically runs during market hours, continuously monitoring double-sided auctions for any violations that may occur. Consequently, this tool has been running continuously since October 2021 without encountering any incorrect executions to date. Furthermore, all the verified and executable code related to this research has been made available on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/verivisum/dsa-verif/ for the OCaml community and at https://github.com/verivisum/dsa-verif-haskell for the Haskell community. This achievement is largely attributed to an innovative method of analyzing periodic structures, which has potential applications in a broader range of mathematical studies. In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, differentiating between linear and nonlinear interactions; however, it is limited in its application to lower dimensional systems. We introduce a kernel-based approach to generating data-driven models for high-dimensional, nonlinear systems. Our method utilizes kernel regression to focus on sparse, dynamic components, which we demonstrate can efficiently handle large data sets and accommodate partial system knowledge. We also show that our approach allows for an accurate identification of linear system components, which in turn, helps to differentiate between nonlinear interactions. Consequently, we obtain a dynamic mode decomposition-like model that remains stable in cases where strong nonlinearity prevails. We test our method using diverse systems of ordinary and partial differential equations that frequently occur in the physical sciences. Our method holds great promise for real-world applications in engineering fields, including reduced order modeling, fault diagnostics, prediction, control systems, and the identification of governing system laws. Our approach also enables the incorporation of partial system knowledge, which in turn, allows for the optimization of model performance. We can therefore obtain multiple models, each tailored to a specific system drive, which in turn, helps to identify the system dynamics from noisy data sets. Our method's stability and effectiveness are validated through numerous applications to experimental data obtained from wind turbines, fluid flow, and the simulation of atmospheric dynamics. Our work marks a significant progress in the development of data-driven modeling tools, which in turn, facilitates the identification of governing system laws, and has promising applications in the engineering field. The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic intricacies still captivating players across the globe, particularly when it comes to mastering the intricacies of Opening Theory which requires extensive knowledge and years of dedicated study. Our innovative approach harnesses the collective wisdom of online chess enthusiasts to provide insights previously reserved for expert chess players. By constructing a network of connections between related chess openings, our RING method allows for the automated extraction of opening strategies. This study examines how players employing these openings perform in tournaments, demonstrating the possibility of opening variations gaining competitive advantages. Furthermore, our RING tool can identify potentially powerful new openings. To achieve this, our method leverages a large dataset of 1 million rated chess games from Lichess, enabling connections between openings based on shared win/loss outcomes within 5 consecutive moves. The resulting network is segmented into 42 distinct clusters, each comprising similar openings. Notably, players using these connected openings outperform those using isolated openings by 12.4% according to their Lichess ratings. By analyzing the network's structural properties, our findings reveal that chess openings exhibit small-world characteristics with highly clustered properties, contrasting with the balanced distribution of connected components. Additionally, our analysis discovers three distinct sub-networks, each corresponding to different levels of expertise, with Balancing Attacks dominating more advanced players, while Early Pawns and Slow Attacks being preferred by beginners and semi-experts. By introducing a new Opensource tool for visualizing and interacting with the RING, our method enables the exploration of the chess opening network by the community, providing insights into its structural properties. The tool is designed to facilitate the discovery of specific chess openings, allowing users to inspect the surrounding network, access related openings, and identify potential new openings. By integrating the chess community's collective knowledge, our RING method empowers the discovery of chess opening strategies, offering competitive advantages, and identifying new opening variations for players of all levels. Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surrounding the optimal input method for retrieval and the ultimate application of the technology have been active topics of discussion within the community. In this research, we present an innovative solution that allows for the non-verbal, 3D shape retrieval within a virtual reality (VR) environment through the analysis of hand-drawn sketches in mid-air. We have developed an advanced indexing technique that enables the efficient retrieval of 3D sketches without the need for complex computation, allowing for real-time operation that is compatible with VR environments. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique, with performance comparable to state-of-the-art techniques in off-line settings. Furthermore, user studies reveal a significant preference for our mid-air sketching interface over traditional input methods. We showcase the mid-air sketching interface as a practical tool for various applications through a series of video demonstrations. To facilitate replication and further research, we have made our implementation available online. Additionally, a VR demo has been developed to provide an immersive demonstration of the mid-air sketching interface, comprising a suite of interactive tools that allow users to practice sketch-based 3D retrieval in a VR environment. This online resource can be accessed via Steam, with a corresponding guide and manual also provided for reference. In terms of future research, we believe that the primary challenge lies in enhancing the precision of the mid-air stroke segmentation algorithm, with potential alternatives to the pseudo-RAM graph indexing technique another area for further investigation. A possible direction for research could involve exploring new sketching interfaces that combine both 2D and 3D sketching input methods to further increase the efficiency of the retrieval process. Lastly, the development of more realistic and photorealistic 3D renderings within the VR environment could also be an area or research focus. In conclusion, we firmly believe that non-verbal sketch-based 3D retrieval within a VR environment offers an innovative and practical solution to the community. Moreover, the mid-air sketching interface provides both efficient retrieval results and an immersive VR experience, making it a promising platform for the exploration of various applications. As such, we envision a future research focus on the development of more sophisticated sketching interfaces, while continuing to contribute to the construction and utilization of free online 3D shape collections. HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to maximizing these observational opportunities. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of amateur astronomers. By examining the details of these transits, they were able to refine the planet's orbital characteristics and test a theoretical model describing HD80606b's atmospheric response to its extreme stellar interactions. Their findings match predictions from a computer simulation known as the THOR model, thereby confirming its accuracy. This new information will help to refine observations taken during the planet's upcoming transits in 2024 and 2025. Additionally, researchers have used their most up-to-date ephemeris to pinpoint specific times when HD80606b passes in front of its host star: February 2, 2025, 00:49:55 UTC; December 6, 2025, 04:42:39 UTC; and February 1, 2026, 00:49:55 UTC. These transit times can be found in the international database known as ETAD. For the planet's transit on December 7-8, 2025, it is expected to occur when the planet is at its farthest point from the star, resulting in considerably less heat retention. In contrast, the planet's surface temperature will significantly exceed 1000K during its closest approach in February 2025. In spite of the absence of measurable atmospheric expansion at this temperature, there will be noticeable effects on the planet's insolation received due to its highly eccentric orbit. This variation in insolation will lead to temperature differences of up to 50K between the two orbital phases, creating distinct optical and near-infrared colorimetry observations. In this context, researchers have suggested that careful analysis of these colorimetry observations could provide a useful independent estimate of the planet's orbital radius and subsequent studies. Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for determining corrections to the extremality bounds and entropy of Kerr-Newman black holes following any arbitrary perturbation. This method involves integrating an effective stress tensor and shows, under certain conditions, the correction is equivalent to the standard stress tensor, thereby illuminating the relationship between extremality corrections and energy conditions. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that to lower the mass of an extremal black hole in a canonical ensemble as stipulated by the weak gravity conjecture, the perturbation must breach the dominant energy condition. We have successfully applied this method to compute higher-order corrections to black holes in anti-de Sitter space and to Kerr black holes. Additionally, we have derived a formula for the entropy of an arbitrarily deformed black hole, which has been validated by analyzing corrections to Kerr black holes. Lastly, based on the observed behavior of corrections to Kerr black holes, we have proposed a hypothesis regarding the thermodynamics of black holes. This work provides substantial evidence supporting the weak gravity conjecture. Moreover, comparing the extremality bound corrections of black holes in anti-de Sitter and flat spacetimes, we have gained insight into how the cosmic censorship conjecture's implementation varies in these settings. Finally, our analysis offers potential implications for the information paradox and the recently formulated black hole information problem. Lastly, associated with thermodynamic quantities of deformed black holes are observables representing the number density and entropy density, which are expressed in terms of the deformed mass and angular momentum. We have used these to investigate the behavior of an arbitrarily deformed black hole. We have evaluated the entropic quantum Hall effect associated with these quantities and used it to derive an inequality relating the quantum Hall conductivity to the squared root of the angular dimensionless charge of a black hole. A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory. Furthermore, potential challenges associated with double copy relations in this context have also been highlighted.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Our SPQR tree-decompositions also enable more efficient parameterized solvers for related problems, such as finding the smallest upward planar layout, given constraints on vertex angles, which were previously considered hard in terms of Dominating Set. Our work also establishes the first known parameterized upper bounds for these problems, with our results being close to certain NP-hardness limitations. In particular, we've proven that for various constraints on vertex angles, AP when restricted to Hamiltonian paths becomes reducible to a parameterized Set Cover instance with integer weights, effectively limiting our depth of parameterized insights into this class of problems. Nevertheless, we were able to derive a parameterized QPTAS based on the size of the source set and a fixed-parameterization based on the treedepth, considering the more relaxed Angle-Restricted HAM Path problem. Furthermore, we've generalized our technique to tackle parameterized versions of Oriented Cycle-Free Drawings, which represent a more stringent constraint on upward planar layouts, effective for series-parallel graphs but not for general graphs, with our findings including a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices and an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth. Our research provides the first parameterized insights into this problem, offering the first known upper bounds. Lastly, our study introduces the first parameterized algorithm for Dominating Set within Oriented Cycle-Free Drawings, effective for series-parallel graphs, with our findings including a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treewidth and an XP algorithm based on the number of source vertices. Notably, we proved that for series-parallel graphs, this problem becomes reducible to a parameterized Set Cover instance with integer weights, effectively limiting our depth of parameterized insights into this class of problems. With our results including an XP algorithm based on the treewidth, our study offers the first known upper bounds. In conclusion, our research provides the first parameterized algorithm for Dominating Set within Oriented Cycle-Free Drawings, effective for series-parallel graphs.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories.
The short-term memory in MemoNav stores dynamic agent topological maps, updated as navigation progresses. To augment this memory, a graph attention module aggregates past short-term memories to generate long-term memories.
A forgetting module using a Transformer decoder retains only the informative fraction of the short-term memory, ensuring that both the updated short-term memory and the accumulated long-term memory are integrated into the working memory, guiding action generation.
Experimental evaluations of MemoNav on a new dataset demonstrate significantly better performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches using a fraction of the navigation history, with reduced instances of deadlock situations. The associated code and dataset are available on GitHub at: https://github.com/yangyangyang/MemoNav. For moral ambiguity concerns regarding dataset collection, please refer to the dataset collection ethics statement. Dataset collection was performed by two graduate students under the supervision of our team. Additional information regarding our approach's potential for reducing environmental impact is available in the supplement.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. By adopting a semi-classical approach to investigate quantum systems with Lie symmetry, we can uncover valuable parallels between quantum information properties and classical Lie groups, a topic that warrants further exploration in the future. We hope that our research promotes the development of novel technologies drawing from Lie symmetry principles, where the constraints can be adjusted to optimize performance across various quantum channels. Additionally, our study on Krylov complexity and entanglement structures contributes to a deeper comprehension of quantum systems, which may be utilized to design corresponding classical algorithms for processing operator data. A corresponding GitHub repository is available at https://github.com/IndigoLima/Operator-Growth-in-Lie-Symmetric-Systems for the benefit of researchers. We are eager to see the application of our findings to experimental work, leading to refined predictions that can be verified by quantum technology developers. Moreover, our work on entanglement structures may inspire novel quantum algorithms, which we hope will lead to breakthroughs in data processing, communication, and computation across various industries. Lastly, our research on SU(1,1) systems could have important implications for satellite-based quantum activities due to its relevance to such projects. We intend for our findings to serve as a bridge connecting quantum information theory and Lie symmetry, which we believe has immense potential to be explored in current research. A primary advantage of employing Lie symmetry is that it empowers us to derive crucial insights without resorting to the Lanczos algorithm or related methods, which may not be feasible for large-scale systems. We envision our study on operator growth and entanglement to be instrumental in the development of new quantum technologies, which in turn can enhance our understanding of these systems.
