The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. A recent survey found that the direct decay ratio of the Hoyle state to the ground state is around 1 in 500, which is equivalent to about 0.2%. This number is consistent with recent measurements and significantly higher than previous estimates. Notably, this decay ratio is substantial and points to a relatively loose structure of the Hoyle state composed of three $\alpha$ particles. The direct decay ratio of 0.2% means that the Hoyle state has a considerable amount of $\alpha$ particle overlap and is not as tightly bound as previously believed. The presence of a dense region within the Hoyle state has been previously suggested, but the latest findings confirm that the Hoyle state has both dense and loose areas. A theoretical model known as the hypernucleus model can reproduce the data by analyzing the three-body cluster structure of the Hoyle state. The latest analysis shows that the Hoyle state has a 69% chance of being a loose system of three $\alpha$ particles, which is consistent with experimental data. Additionally, the application of the hypernucleus model to other data points in the S$^{11}$ system also shows accurate results, which further supports the two-component nature, or 'fog-like' structure, of the Hoyle state consisting of both dense and loose regions. A 2D probability plot of the hypernucleus model's parameters, which represent the probabilities of the Hoyle state's 2S and 1/2-$^1$S components, shows a strong correlation between the energies of the Hoyle state and its 2S component's orbital angular momentum. A linear relationship exists between the energies of the Hoyle state and its 2S component's orbital angular momentum, which is around 8 MeV. A 2D linear correlation has been identified between the densities of the Hoyle state and its 1/2-$^1$S component's size, which is around 3.5 MeV, which is consistent with experimental data. A theoretical model known as the hypernucleus double well (HDW) can also reproduce the data

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments. Through phase-field fracture models, we find the following features of this oscillatory instability: (i) It also exists in materials with linear elastic behavior near the crack, depending solely on dissipation properties; (ii) It undergoes a type of supercritical bifurcation; and (iii) It's minimally affected by factors like the fracture energy associated with a certain dissipation time. These results support the idea that this oscillatory instability is an inherent feature of fast cracks in 2D, while we also show that an ultra-high speed instability can be attributed to a limiting rate of energy transport near the crack. The numerical framework of the fracture approach used in this study is thoroughly described. The results derived from this method are validated by means of explicit dynamics simulations. The present knowledge of fracture instability is further discussed, along with its applications to experimental observations and potential remedies to suppress this kind of instability in 2D, as exemplified through a brief examination of an experimental setup involving laser-induced fracture. The setup is analyzed to establish a connection between the intrinsic scales at crack tips and observable features of fracture instability. The results show that this kind of instability can be observed in experiments, which could provide additional insight into the intrinsic scales at crack tips. The approach employed in this study can be extended to 3D by means of extension, where the extended philosophy is laid out. The extension to 3D is justified by considering the relevance of dissipation properties in determining the stability of cracks, which is a purely kinetic phenomenon. The 3D case is found to offer one advantage over the 2D scenario - an absolute limit to the speed of propagating cracks. The principles of fracture instability in 2D, along with the expansion to 3D, provide a foundation for the understanding of stable and unstable behavior of cracks in brittle materials. The concepts of fracture instability in 2D, along with the expansion to 3D, offer valuable insight into the behavior of cracks in brittle materials, which can be applied to technological settings by means of a brief discussion. In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access) and energy harvesting. The capacity of these channels with feedback is described in terms of the directed information between auxiliary variables and the channel outputs. Additionally, we propose two distinct approaches to determining this capacity: a method involving a convex optimization problem in the context of directed information and a second approach centered on developing an auxiliary channel utilizing the channel output and future states. This auxiliary channel is used to establish a lower bound on the capacity of channels with feedback. It is shown that this lower bound remains valid even in scenarios where the channel output does not follow from the states. Furthermore, it is established that both methods are equivalent and yield the same capacity in the context of directed information. However, it should be noted that applying these methods to channels without feedback results in the well-known capacity in terms of unconditional directed information. We examine the properties of channels with infinite-state differences and those with fast-decaying correlation functions and establish that, in these scenarios, the capacity can be described in terms of the unconditional directed information between the auxiliary variables and the channel outputs, which becomes accessible to the encoder. We extend this finding to channels with state differences that follow an arithmetic sequence and an geometric sequence. In the context of channels with look-ahead access, we investigate how the availability of past states impacts the capacity and establish that this impact diminishes as the dependence of the states decays exponentially. Finally, in the context of energy harvesting channels with or without the availability of states, we examine the properties of channels with and without constraints on the amount of information that can be stored in the encoder's memory. We establish a unified approach to determining the capacity of these channels and describe it in terms of the directed information between the auxiliary variables and the channel outputs. In the context of channels with infinite memory constraints, we establish lower and upper bounds on the capacity that converge to the same value. In the context of channels with fast-decaying differences in the information storage constraints, we establish the convergence of these bounds and determine the resulting capacity in terms of the unconditional directed information between the auxiliary variables and the channel outputs, which becomes accessible to the encoder. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. The emergence of a non-Abelian state in this Rashba-superconducting system presents a new platform for quantum computation. Moreover, we recognize that the Zeeman field and Rashba coupling have mutually supplementary effects, and that Rashba coupling can counteract the demagnetization caused by the Zeeman field, thereby creating opportunities for the controlled integration of Rashba coupling and magnetic fields in the creation of quantum devices. Finally, our predictions may also be applicable to other systems featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and superconductivity, such as those supported by lattice structures with a non-trivial geometry. This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to verify factual information and locate supporting evidence within tabular scientific data. The comprehensive dataset comprised 981 manually crafted tables and an automatically generated collection of 1980 tables, encompassing over 180,000 statements and more than 16 million annotated evidence references. This task comprised two primary sub-tasks. Sub-task A required participants to verify whether a statement was substantiated, contradicted, or remained inconclusive relative to a given table. Meanwhile, sub-task B involved pinpointing the specific table cells that served as evidence to support the given statement. Ultimately, a total of 69 teams entered the competition, with 19 and 12 submissions successful in sub-tasks A and B, respectively. We are about to present our results and findings from this competition. We observed that the survival of systems in sub-tasks A and B varied significantly, with nearly half of systems from sub-task A and the top-performing systems from sub-task B exhibiting accuracy above 0.75. Notably, top-performing systems from sub-task A demonstrated an ability to accurately process data beyond what they had seen during training, suggesting some level of robustness. Conversely, top-performing systems from sub-task B displayed a decline in accuracy above a certain threshold of unbalanced data distribution. The top-performing systems from both sub-tasks primarily leveraged traditional machine learning techniques, focusing on decision tree Ensembles. We noted that approximately 60% of systems from sub-task A and 45% of systems from sub-task B incorporated the use of table specific features. We noted that the incorporation of table-specific characteristics led to enhanced performance, with systems from sub-task A attaining a 0.14 F1 increase and those from sub-task B reaching a 0.10 F1 increase when using these characteristics. Furthermore, top-performing systems from both sub-tasks demonstrated a preference for table cell aggregation when dealing with negative statements, suggesting that the combination of cell evidence is the most effective approach to verifying factual claims. We noted that the most successful systems from sub-task A and B disagreed on approximately 30% and 44% of cases, respectively, suggesting substantial scope for improvement in the future. This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics. Additionally, we discuss an alternative formulation employing complex coefficients, but with the constraint that every term maintains its original sign. This restriction is known as dyadic form and such operators are called dyadic Hermitian. For each quantum system, we establish the possibility of transitioning from monomial coefficients to dyadic coefficients, effectively transforming quantum mechanics into a real theory while maintaining its operational capabilities. However, this reformulation faces challenges when attempting to define such a transition for all quantum systems, particularly those with unbounded Hamiltonians. Therefore, this study investigates specific scenarios where the Dyadic Schrödinger equation applies, discovering that legitimate solutions often rely on complex frequencies. We demonstrate this complexity requirement by showing that alternative real frequency solutions can easily decompose into causal and non-causal parts, a characteristic observed within the free particle basis, and also in certain specific systems like the Kroner-Goodman model and the Joshi model. In contrast, we find that the Hamiltonian generated from the Dyadic Schrödinger equation does not have this property, necessitating the use of complex frequencies. We conclude that quantum systems with Hermitian Hamiltonians cannot be accurately described by the Dyadic Schrödinger equation in its standard form. Nevertheless, this study reveals that viable alternatives exist such as the Joshi model, and also the $\hat{H}=\frac{-i\hbar^2}{m}~\frac{d^2}{dx^2}$, which indicates a possible future direction where such systems could serve as bridges to describe transitions between real and complex formalisms in Quantum mechanics. We also formulate a conjecture that such a transition might also be possible for all quantum systems if they are treated as classical perturbations of such model systems. This research is the first to explore this realm of Hermitian quantum dynamics, and as such, it remains essential to document its underlying assumptions, present alternative views, and provide necessary background information, all as stated in the introduction and in the text. These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to scales large enough for regional groundwater flow characteristics to vary substantially over relatively short distances, making traditional linearized solutions incompressible and unsuitable for meaningful applications. A key assumption underlying this review is that the time frame is sufficiently long for transient groundwater fluctuations to be negligible. These reviews began with basic Darcy's Law formulas for traditional full-pressure flow applications and expanded to more complex scenarios, ultimately concluding with approximate low-Froude number approximations for simplified local flux fluctuations in steady-state flows. Along the way, I considered a variety of relevant numerical solution methods for reference. Due to the significant breadth of topics involved, I focused solely on fundamental concepts and avoided in-depth discussion of related topics or more esoteric themes. Consequently, some valuable and related topics remain unmentioned in these reviews. Nevertheless, I hope these notes will still serve as a useful, if incomplete, review of the subject for those interested in applications where distant groundwater flow and local flux fluctuations prevail. A notable omission is any mention of surface water body flow, turbulence, or any form of flow where traditional full-pressure assumptions hold (e.g. shallow water, Bose-Aitharsan, etc.), as these fall outside the scope of this review. Furthermore, I've also left out secondary ecological systems like surface water bodies, rivers, lakes, wetlands, aquatic ecosystems, and associated biologic processes, as these too fall outside the scope of this review focused on distant groundwater flow for local flux fluctuations. To better organize this content, I've grouped related topics into distinct sections, with section headings that illustrate the varying scales and complexity of the involved equations. These reviews begin with basic Darcy's Law formulas for steady-state full-pressure flow applications in Section 2, before expanding to more complex transient and stable numerical solution methods in Section 3. A intermediate review of Darcy's Law for steady-state full-pressure flow applications with emphasis on local flux fluctuations follows in Section 4, and conclude with approximate low-Froude number approximations for simplified local flux fluctuations in regional groundwater flow applications in Section 5. A conclusion summarizing the reviewed topics and suggestions for further study appears in Section 6. A brief glossary of relevant terms and an associated bibliography appears at the very end. To better serve readers, I've also attempted to make the content as self-contained as possible and included relevant definitions for key terms in a separate glossary section. A numerical model of a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) was used to simulate and analyze the removal of sulfur dioxide SO2 through gas-phase oxidation. Various UV radiation models were considered, each involving a grid convergence study to determine the optimal number of discrete light sources for maximum performance. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of residence time and reactor size on SO2 removal. Ultimately, under optimized conditions, the results show that an ozone-UV light system can be a suitable solution for sustainable air pollution control applications. As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different architecture designs. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper proposes a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC for RISC-V multi-core platforms that incorporates multiple computing-in-memory accelerators for neuromorphic computing. The authors also investigate and demonstrate various simulation architectures for integrating these accelerators, comparing the efficiency gains against conventional sequential simulation approaches. The proposed framework achieves acceleration rates of up to 18 times on 6-core RISC-V platforms, along with a 13.6x performance improvement on single-core RISC-V hosts. The developed framework, along with corresponding benchmarks, is freely accessible on OpenHC to foster performance-enhancing simulations of neuromorphic computing systems. The research has been accepted for presentation at the IEEE/ACM UC workshop, taking place in San Jose from April 1-5, 2023. The final paper has been published under an open-access license at https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11111. The simulation environment, source code, and additional information can be found at https://github.com/cmose/SIM-NMC/tree/parallelism. Initial benchmark results are available at https://github.com/cmose/SIM-NMC. Disclosure: The authors have implemented the proposed ideas in software, following the open-source protocols outlined at https://github.com/cmose/SIM-NMC. Disclosure: The main simulation framework has been developed by S. S. Kumar, incorporating previously published research from reference [14] for creating the RNN training-based NMC benchmark. The accelerators, as described in section 2, leverage open-source repositories from Talos-OS, OpenRISC, and RISC-V International. The detailed architectural information for the Talos-BPF can be accessed via https://wiki.talos.org/Diskless_Infrastructure/Custom_Board_Reference_Manual. Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges,
mainly stemming from uninterpretable models, questionable reliance on imperfect
data, or offering a sole prediction outcome without considering various
probability outcomes.
  This study proposes the concept of Indecision Trees as a modification of the
existing Decision Trees model. These revised models are designed to learn under
conditions of uncertainty, draw conclusions in uncertain situations, produce
reliable probability distributions over potential labels, and be dissected into
clear, logical arguments that can be utilized to justify their predictive decisions.
We showcase the effectiveness of Indecision Trees through a series of experiments,
concluding that they outperform existing solutions on various benchmarks, or in
some cases, match their performance. Furthermore, the induced models are notable
for their clarity, effectiveness, and ability to be easily understood. All of the
mentioned models, as well as the corresponding source code, are available on
GitHub at the https://github.com/learnables/inddecision_trees repository.

The widely-used DTW algorithm allows for alignment between time series sequences, but its high computational complexity has hindered its broader application. A previously proposed approach, APrunedDTW, reduced this complexity but came with a higher error rate. Our latest research builds on this by introducing an improved version, EAPrinedDTW, which accurately aligns sequences in linear time. This new method is based on the Euclidean Approximation technique and can be applied across sub-optimal DTW alignments. Our results show that EAPrinedDTW offers both faster processing and lower error rates compared to APrinedDTW, making it a more efficient time series classification model. Specifically, it achieves higher accuracy on several real-world datasets, along with a substantial speed boost. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/ashishbhangal/EAPrinedDTW. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, we propose modifying an existing testing tool to provide students with feedback in the form of advisory suggestions for new test cases. In a study involving 51 undergraduate students, we examined the impact of this suggested-testing tool on student learning. When using the modified tool, which was developed based on established testing best practices, students demonstrated a 25.9% increase in learning. In contrast, students using the standard tool, which was developed in accordance with minimum requirements, showed a 10.7% increase in learning. We observed a notable improvement in students' testing skills when using the suggested-testing tool, particularly in areas such as test coverage, peer-reviewed suitability, and overall testing effectiveness. Furthermore, we examined the potential for instructor-defined testing best practices to be taught to students, and found that this approach led to better learning outcomes in areas such as test suitability but not coverage. Notably, we found that students developed positive attitudes towards testing, and that the proposed educational tool can be utilized by instructors as a means of promoting structured testing conducted by students. We have made the modified testing tool's source code and research materials publicly available. In terms of future research, we suggest that the impact of educational tools on student learning should be evaluated by considering their underlying methodological premises as an essential factor. Additionally, we propose that the educational computer science community develops a unified set of testing standards with established levels of difficulty, to facilitate comparisons of various teaching approaches and methodologies. Lastly, we suggest that future research explore the potential of educational tool-based learning outcomes to be established by reputable organizations in the field.

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods, particularly in healthcare and data protection regulations. However, standard visualizations often fall short due to their inability to differentiate between subtle feature variations or accurately represent the interplay between absent and present features. This issue can be addressed by using more advanced symbolic surrogate models but, since these typically demand symbolic inputs not commonly available in computer vision, we instead explore a new method: Utilizing intrinsic network features, we create a comprehensive, descriptive verbal explanation of a DNN's decision rationale through an analysis of learned features, associated errors, and relative importance indicators. The approach involves a thorough analysis of the DNN's internal workings, as model performances are evaluated under various regularization methods to identify key features driving decisions, and an accompanying bug introduction framework is introduced to assess the impact of feature modifications on model outcomes. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through testing with image classification networks, where generated verbal summaries effectively convey the key features an image has to be classified under a certain category, and the importance of these features is also highlighted. This approach is unique in its ability to provide both the required features for classification and their relative importance indicators. The developed bug introduction framework can be utilized for a wide array of deep learning techniques to evaluate and analyze the impact of feature modifications on an image classification model. The integration of this deep analysis of network features into an image description enables the differentiation between subtle feature variations, and the mutual exclusion of attributes can thus be effectively communicated. Furthermore, this approach has the potential to be expanded and adapted to other machine learning techniques not restricted to image classification. The veracity of the descriptions generated is measured through external evaluators who physically access the images and perform the associated task, thereby providing a thorough understanding of the DNN's decision-making process. The accuracy of this approach is validated through three different success metrics: the mutual information between the generated description and the true image content, and two evaluators' agreements in evaluating the importance of the features. The results obtained confirm the feasibility of this deep analysis approach. The developed framework can be used for a wide array of machine learning techniques. Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various countermeasures to mitigate it. Moreover, the analysis explores the evolution of the Graph Convolutional Networks over time and provides predictions for future advancements in this field. All the used data sets can be accessed through https://github.com/thoppe/OverSmoothing. This repository contains comprehensive experiments conducted previously (up to January 2021), along with new findings. Our results are further detailed in the report, along with recommendations for future research in the field. All the code utilized for these experiments is available at https://github.com/thoppe/OverSmoothing, specifically in the codes directory. This repository also includes the data collection code used for the study on the survival time of Graph Convolutional Networks. This data collection code is available at https://github.com/thoppe/OverSmoothing, specifically in the data_collection_directory. For questions or feedback related to the dataset, please feel free to reach out to thoppe@gmail.com. This repository is maintained by thoppe. A list of authors is provided below. Homeomorphisms with compact support on a Tychonoff space can be given several equivalent topological structures by viewing them as either a union of groups of homeomorphisms with the same support size or as a subset of the group of homeomorphisms of its compactified space. A space has the CSHP if these two definitions yield the same topological space, which is the main topic of the paper's methods to prove that product spaces of specific spaces with CSHP possess CSHP. Additionally, the paper includes a detailed examination of the space of compactly supported homeomorphisms of the real line, including its subspaces, such as the space of homeomorphisms with bounded support and the space of continuous surjections onto the circle. Moreover, the paper establishes a list of inequalities involving dimensional characteristics like the dimension, the sigma-dimensional dimension, the q-fold dimension, and the Whitney dimension for these spaces. Finally, the paper discusses questions and potential research directions related to these topics. Based on an appendix, the paper also explores dimensional properties of groups of homeomorphisms with targeted properties, such as fixing specific points or targeting specific points, which further contributes to the study of the space of compactly supported homeomorphisms. Specifically, the paper discovers that the space of homeomorphisms that fix the points 0 and 1 has a rich structural characterization, including a precise description of its compactly supported subgroups and a proof that it does not possess the CSHP, which is independently proven using a different method than what is presented in the main body of the paper. Additionally, the appendix includes a list of open problems related to these topics. Lastly, the paper concludes by highlighting dimensional characteristics of groups of homeomorphisms that identify and map to specific subsets, such as the set of homeomorphisms that send the real line to the circle and the set of homeomorphisms that fix 0 and send the real line to the circle. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. These observations suggest the presence of a remote epitaxial process influenced by weak van der Waals forces between graphene and the substrate, as supported by simulations showing the occurrence of epitaxy only when the interlayer distance is within a certain range. We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when individual observations are rare or unusual. A new method allows us to make this analysis without knowing whether certain assumptions hold or even what values some important statistics have. By using information about the matrix of average relationships among these time series, we create an estimator of how many common random patterns there are, even in cases with extreme data fluctuations. As sample size increases, the rates of divergence for the matrix's key properties are significantly faster than others. To improve estimation accuracy, we use this information to construct test statistics and implement a procedure for iteratively evaluating whether each key property corresponds to one of these common patterns. A related method can identify the patterns themselves and the study shows this is a consistent approach. To extend the analysis, the study considers more complex scenarios where the components of these time series exhibit varying degrees of independence. A series of numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this new approach. To demonstrate the applicability of this new method, the study includes analyses of prices of raw materials, financial markets data, the relationship between currencies over the long-term, and the behavior of cryptocurrencies, in four distinct applications. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship has practical implications; it clarifies the necessary conditions under which the GNS construction can be seen as a fully faithful functor and also reveals that a C*-algebra can be reconstructed solely based on its set of unitary elements and the expected values of certain key elements for any given state. This result implies significant consequences, as it means these elements effectively form a minimal set of relevant physical observables. Furthermore, this formulation allows us to identify which aspects of the algebra are relevant from a physical standpoint and also enables the comparison of physical content between different representations of the same C*-algebra, leading to a simplified understanding of the concepts underlying algebraic quantum theory. This simplified understanding is achieved through the application of certain mathematical concepts, such as strong and weak equivalence, to characterise the relevant concepts, ultimately leading to a simplified description of these concepts. The relationships between these concepts are expressed through certain mathematical operations, such as addition and multiplication by a non-zero scalar, and these expressions are consistent with established mathematical results, such as the Schur Lemma. This description is significant, as it is consistent with existing results in the field, such as a result that states that two representations are strongly equivalent if and only if they have the same expected values for certain elements. Additionally, we utilise this description to describe various natural and weakly natural transformations that arise in the context of state representation, such as a transformation that maps a state to a state with minimal change, and demonstrates that these descriptions are consistent with existing results in the field, such as a result that states a transformation is natural if and only if it meets certain conditions under various interpretations. This result is significant, as it leads to a simplified description of these transformations, and this simplified description is utilised to describe multiple instances of these transformations. One such instance is a transformation that maps a state to a state with minimal change that also preserves key properties, and demonstrates that this transformation corresponds to a combination of established transformations in the field, such as the conjugate by a unitary transformation

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. Further, our score-based method outperformed the mean-variance model when comparing their respective returns, computed using all the cross-sectional returns we had available. We tested the effectiveness of our score-based probabilities by simulating 100 distinct scenarios, finding they consistently produced lower concentrations and higher risks than the mean-variance model. Notably, our score-based approach enabled the long-only strategy to achieve portfolio concentrations and risks comparable to those of the mean-variance model when including shorting capabilities. Overall, our results indicate the long-only strategy has lower concentrations and risks than the mean-variance model, particularly when including a large portfolio of assets. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The proposed method has potential applications in real-world settings where cardiac care is provided. In a 2021 study, we had developed a more accurate calculation for a specific nuclear transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised concerns about a part of this calculation that they disagreed with, but it aligns with earlier calculations. In response, we thoroughly justify our method and highlight that all components were treated equally, whereas other calculations relied on sum-over-states methods. Additionally, we addressed concerns about the approximate treatment of some corrections that were not the main focus, but rather included for completeness, without changing our overall conclusions, as our results hold even when replaced with a previously estimated correction value. Despite efforts to clarify, it's unclear if the concerns came from a misunderstanding of our method or a genuine disagreement on the interpretation of the calculations. Therefore, we choose to provide a more extensive justification of our work, including all the relevant details of our method and a brief overview of the concerns raised. In the process, we reviewed how transition amplitudes are calculated in relativistic transition amplitudes and the relevant approximations used. Furthermore, we examined how wavefunctions are calculated using the relativistic coupled-cluster method and the relevant approximations used. In an attempt to be more transparent, we even provided an explicit example of how some corrections could be treated exactly, without changing the results, as an illustration of our commitment to clarity. In the discussion section, we then reviewed the implications of our findings and the various methods used to calculate nuclear transition magnetic dipole moments, with a focus on the concerns raised and the justifications provided. In the conclusion, we summarized our main findings, reiterated the significance of the accuracy of the transition amplitude, highlighted the limitations of the approximate treatment, and expressed our desire to contribute to the field by promoting understanding and accuracy, without changing the results. In an attempt to be more transparent, we even provided contact information for questions or feedback. In the reference list, we then updated the literature on the relevant topics, including a recent study on the relativistic coupled-cluster decomposition of Green's function, a discussion on the decay of the Higgs boson in the presence of new physics, a calculation of the PVL transition amplitude using many-body perturbation theory, a comparison of the Jansen-Roy-Suarez approach with our own relativistic coupled-cluster method, a study on the decay of spin one bosons in the presence of new physics, a discussion on the importance of third-body effects in the decay of bosons, a survey of the importance of relativistic corrections

This paper examines all possible forms of twists for a torus with actions imposed by 2D space groups, and equivalently, for any orientable 2-dimensional manifold with actions imposed by 1-dimensional groups.

This study offers the first comprehensive analysis of the relationship between fairness and revenue in auctions. We delve into the underlying mechanics of fairness by examining how bidders' strategic actions affect the outcome, using a credible auction as a foundation. Our examination reveals that the optimal stable equilibrium of the auction generates significantly more revenue when it is fair, yet this increase in revenue is entirely attributed to a reduction in collusion. Notably, this revenue boost does not result from any genuine shift in demand from the bidders. Additionally, our research highlights that the revenue advantages of unfair auctions are minimal, but the negative consequences in terms of system instability become more pronounced as the degree of unfairness increases. We also identify specific scenarios in which the optimal stable equilibrium is unique and can be easily calculated, incorporating both collusion and rational action. Specifically, when the cost function is convex, we can determine the optimal stable equilibrium through a straightforward algorithm. Conversely, when the function is concave, we can employ a more complex procedure that involves successive approximations. Notably, this study focuses primarily on single-unit auctions, but the theoretical framework can be applied to multi-unit auctions with modifications. We have made the auction model and associated algorithms accessible to researchers and practitioners through an online repository, known as the RE auction repository. This repository includes demonstrations of the algorithms as well as detailed documentation of the theoretical framework and models. Furthermore, our study explores specific scenarios in which the optimal stable equilibrium can be easily calculated and analyzed, such as when the cost function is convex or when the number of bidders is limited. Specifically, we found that the optimal stable equilibrium can be easily calculated when the cost function is convex and when there are at most three bidders. Conversely, we found that the optimal stable equilibrium can be easily calculated when there are at most eleven colluding bidders. We also investigated the situation in which the auction owner knows the cost function and can easily identify the true number of bidders, but the other bidders in the auction do not have this information. Additionally, we studied this scenario when the cost function is convex and when the number of colluding bidders is either low (three or four) or high (eleven or twelve). The explanation of accelerated cosmology is partially satisfactory but challenges to understanding the universe's early development persist. Our research focuses on the promising potential of a new symmetric teleparallel theory of gravity, which is a well-defined mathematical model. This model can be calculated accurately because it adheres to the equivalence principle's local validity. Furthermore, this theory is closely related to modified gravity theories as it has a well-defined vacuum value. Our analysis indicates that this theory's non-metricity scalar, which is equivalent to the exchange term in modified gravity theories, plays a crucial role in understanding gravitational phenomena. By examining the theory's equations in a flat homogeneous isotropic universe, we discovered that the non-metricity scalar's evolution is closely tied to the matter's equation of state. This relationship led to two key findings. Firstly, the non-metricity scalar remains small during the universe's early stages due to the fluid's perfect equation of state. Secondly, as the fluid's equation of state becomes less perfect, the non-metricity scalar grows significantly, which in turn affects the universe's gravitational behavior and leads to distinct growth patterns of density fluctuations compared to $\Lambda$CDM. By simulating different fluid scenarios, we observed a notable impact of the non-metricity scalar on the universe's gravitational behavior. This theory's unique characteristics inspire speculation about its impact on gravitational phenomena, which in turn motivates further research into its influence on cosmic structure formation. Therefore, this theory is worthy of further mathematical and astrophysical investigation. We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing an affine coordinate chart based on the maximal element of the Weyl group corresponding to GL(n,ℂ). Key findings include the following. Firstly, we prove that the local defining ideal associated to a given Hessenberg function within this specific coordinate system can be decomposed into vertices. Furthermore, combining our result with existing work on generators, we demonstrate that this set of generators constitutes a Gröbner basis for this ideal under a suitable monomial order. Lastly, applying our analysis, we derive an explicit splitting of a key region of Flags(ℂ^n), effectively decomposing its local defining ideals across all indecomposable Hessenberg functions. This framework also enables the identification of a parameter-dependent polynomial, the Van den Bergh vector field U, which we show corresponds to the tangent direction of flags that lie within or approach the p-spacious part of the flag space as p approaches zero. Utilizing this decomposition further allows us to examine p-spacious Hessenberg varieties, specifically regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, for which we establish an explicit formula for the local defining ideal associated to a given Hessenberg function, now considering an affine coordinate chart based on the Weyl group element {e}. This formula represents a set of generators for this ideal, now expressed as partial derivatives of a specific polynomial, specifically P, based on the Hessenberg function in question, now evaluated within flags that lie within or approach the p-spacious part of the flag space as p approaches zero, thereby providing novel geometric interpretations for these varieties, as well as novel geometric key properties for the vertices in question. Despite GANs' superiority in AI-generated art, their training can be exceptionally challenging. To address these difficulties and accelerate Neural Painter training, we employed Transfer Learning, achieving a notable time reduction from days to just hours without compromising visual quality. Our findings are presented in this study. Academic researchers who write scholarly papers typically assume that readers are familiar with the knowledge base, with exceptions requiring significant amounts of background information to understand the context. Currently, systems for answering questions about papers are not adept at taking into consideration the inherent lack of supplied background knowledge. In an effort to address this, we introduce a new question answering dataset comprising 1,556 questions regarding 200 papers selected from the EMNLP 2020 conference papers on natural language processing. We propose an innovative dataset, called Q2P, which not only furnishes question-answer pairs but also supplies the necessary background information required for each question. Furthermore, we engineer a new evaluation metric to gauge how systems handle the scarcity of provided background knowledge. In particular, we devise the BKB measure, which indicates the proportion of knowledge domains a system is capable of addressing. In experiments using the Q2P dataset, we discover that existing best-in-class systems already rely heavily on external knowledge sources, which suggests that the primary constraint limiting their performance lies in accessing more relevant knowledge instead of more extensive knowledge. In pursuit of better performance, we suggest an unsupervised approach called knowledge distillation, which involves creating a post-doc model to acquire and integrate additional knowledge. In evaluations, the model demonstrates a notable 6.6% absolute enhancement over the top-performing baseline model in addressing questions requiring background knowledge and achieves notable gains on other metrics. The new Q2P dataset, along with accompanying code and dataset, is accessible for reproduction at the URL: https://github.com/juansl/Q2P. In addition, the dataset has been registered with the following identifier: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5140426. In line with this, we outline potential future developments that could further boost the performance of question answering systems for paper-based queries. In particular, we propose incorporating more sophisticated natural language processing techniques, such as the application of external knowledge of varying levels of breadth and the creation of systems that are capable of dynamically adapting their focus to address multiple questions more effectively. In the future, we also intend to develop methods that can generate questions, develop methods that can estimate the extent to which a given background knowledge base is complete, and finally explore the applicability of our proposed metric, BKB, to evaluate the performance of open-domain question answering systems. In conclusion, the proposed Q2P dataset offers a fresh perspective on evaluating the capabilities of question answering systems and will likely serve as a valuable resource for advancing our understanding of these systems for paper

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they simplify written content, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers aim to tackle the acronym extraction and replacement (AER) problem, facilitating automated processing of written material. Despite recent advancements, existing solutions fall short due to limitations involving definition accuracy, leading to inaccuracies and false positives. This research aims to enhance AER by incorporating a definition-based approach, distinct from word root-based methods, using a dedicated acronym database and search engine for enhanced efficacy. Experimental results demonstrate replacement outcomes comparable to those of cutting-edge techniques, supplemented by analytical case studies highlighting successful and failure cases. Furthermore, this venture gives rise to two novel datasets: one comprising acronym definitions and another of inaccurate acronym usage examples, contributing valuable resources to the AER community. These resources are available for public access and potential future development. This innovation offers a definition-based AER method, providing an alternative to existing word root-based approaches and yielding replacement outcomes comparable to those of state-of-the-art techniques. To support this effort, two newly developed datasets are offered to the AER community, aiming to address the prevalent issue of inaccurate acronym usage, thereby contributing to improved data quality. To our knowledge, this research marks the first endeavor to apply a search engine in AER, facilitated by a dedicated acronym database, thereby showcasing a versatile information retrieval model applicable to other challenging NLP tasks. This model quantitatively evaluates information retrieval effectiveness in AER through precision and recall metrics, demonstrating a close relationship between search engine-based and word root-based approaches. This research has far-reaching implications, paving the way for the application of search engine technology to other complex NLP tasks. To evaluate the performance of our search engine-based AER model, we utilized two widely employed metrics: precision and recall. Quantum interference, evident in low-dimensional systems, is one of the notable phenomena that distorts typical thermal distribution habits. This research focuses on the electrical currents generated by thermal gradients in quantum interference environments with random impurities and temperature fluctuations. By applying advanced mathematical techniques, such as the application of the Lagrangian density, we derive a precise expression for the charge current as a cumulative effect of impurity positions and extended wave patterns. This discovery reveals that random impurities significantly affect electrical currents, with specific temperature fluctuations inducing a cyclic shift. This behavior is comparable to that of nonlocal heat conduction in quantum interference systems. Furthermore, we investigate how voltage influences thermal gradient-induced electrical currents and demonstrate that these currents follow a proportionality constant (conductivity in conventional systems) up to a specific value, after which it decreases exponentially with conductivity. Additionally, we examine how electrical currents and conductivity change in response to alterations in temperature and voltage. This study sheds light on the electrical transport behavior in quantum interference systems with multiple contacts and temperature fluctuations. Due to the inherent randomness of impurities, these systems display vast variation in electrical transport behavior, making them unsuitable for conventional phase coherence studies. Nonetheless, we identify a promising scope for further investigation, where extreme impedance matching could potentially enable significant phase coherence effects and remarkable quantum interference phenomena that enhance thermoelectric charge currents. This research may find practical applications in thermoelectric devices and can serve as a starting point for exploring phase coherence effects in random impurity environments. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data updates. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. We've further integrated this enhanced indexing capability with the file system to develop simultaneous parallel PCR reactions for the simultaneous retrieval of multiple files at once. As a result of this integration, we've observed a significant reduction in the time required to retrieve files from DNA storage: from 70 days to 1 hour. A full description of this work can be found in our research paper, which includes detailed descriptions of the sequence manipulation operations, an integrated file system, as well as experimental evaluations of our DNA storage architecture. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Lastly, it highlights prospective future research avenues.

These pacemaker-generated waves are typically analyzed at the boundary between two oscillatory states, but what happens when the oscillatory nature arises from complex internal dynamics rather than a straightforward gradient? Using a model pacemaker and two contrasting approaches to oscillatory activity, this study delves into synchronization mechanisms within a system that relies on non-equilibrium dynamics, presenting two distinct perspectives on this phenomenon. The first views this system through the lens of current understanding, while the second offers an in-depth examination, revealing how temporal oscillations give rise to spatial patterns, which can facilitate synchronized behavior within the system. By understanding the role of pacemaker dynamics in determining synchronization times, this research provides insights into the complex interplay between oscillatory dynamics and synchronized behavior, offering a more comprehensive understanding of active matter systems. Additionally, this study's findings can be applied to pacsystems that exhibit oscillatory behavior through kinetic mean-field models. Implementing and deploying effective artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning models, significantly depend on the availability of large datasets for training, testing, and validation processes. However, gathering and annotating these datasets proves to be an enormously time-consuming and resource-intensive task. Building on the success of crowdsourcing efforts like ImageNet and its influence on the field, we introduce the 'Rashid Benhadda Inria Vision Benchmark' (RBI), an extensive open-source dataset of annotated images designed to facilitate research and development in visual knowledge. By providing access to RBI and establishing it as a standard reference point similar to ImageNet, we aim to support and promote innovative applications driven by computer vision, as well as to contribute to the advancement of open-source benchmarking practices. Moreover, our benchmark is complemented by a suite of state-of-the-art vision models available on public cloud infrastructure, enabling easy replication and reproduction of local experiments. You can access the dataset at https://doi.org/10.24479/drs.109429.v1. We plan to maintain continuous updates to the dataset to ensure it remains a valuable resource for the community. You can follow our progress at https://rbi-inria.github.io. We welcome contributions and feedback through our GitHub repository at https://github.com/RBI-Inria/Benchmark. We are committed to establishing a transparent and inclusive benchmark development process, inspired by the successful approaches of the DeepLearn.JS and DeepLearn.py projects. We intend to maintain a regular and active schedule of meeting with researchers who use our dataset to discuss their work and learn from each other's projects, similar to the DeepLearn.JS and DeepLearn.py community meetings. We are looking forward to collaborating with the research community in achieving our goal of promoting open and reproducible research within our dataset's lifecycle. We believe that our approach to benchmark development can serve as a valuable example for other data-driven crowdsourcing projects to follow. You can find more information about our process in our process guide available at https://rbi-inria.github.io/docs/Contributing-to-RBI. We are eager to receive feedback, new research ideas, and fresh perspectives from the research community, as well as to hear specific proposals for evolving the dataset through our proposed EvolRBI process, as detailed in our documentation at https://rbi-inria.github.io/docs/EvolRBI. We are committed to maintaining an inclusive and diverse community of researchers who use our dataset, as described in our inclusivity guide available at https://rbi-inria.github.io

Physicians' written assessments, stored as unstructured clinical text, are crucial for determining patients' outcomes and predicting their future health status. One of the main obstacles to exploiting this data lies in encoding ICD codes accurately and efficiently. Although deep learning models have achieved notable success in predicting ICD codes automatically, their methods typically rely on large datasets and inherent flaws in consistency and validity. In this research, we introduce a novel semi-supervised strategy to enhance automatic ICD coding, incorporating constraints based on medical knowledge to improve the reliability of coded data. We utilize a hybrid model, combining a bidirectional GRU encoder with a decoder trained on positively labeled data, and introduce a new type of constraint during the inference process, drawing from existing knowledge to guide coding decisions. In experiments with a dataset from 383 general hospitals in China, our approach outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods, resulting in improved accuracy and validity of coded data. Furthermore, we found that integrating medical knowledge constraints significantly boosted the performance of deep learning models, demonstrating the significance of semi-supervised learning in automatic ICD coding. In particular, our method achieved an F1 score of 0.7931 on a newly introduced test set with 8,540 clinical text notes. The improved quality of coded data using our hybrid model also enabled the successful inference of comorbidities at a high degree of accuracy, exceeding 0.9700 on certain disease categories such as cerebrovascular diseases, neoplasms, and infectious diseases. In terms of computational efficiency, our approach outperformed existing deep learning models, requiring fewer computational operations and a corresponding reduction in required deep learning model dimensions. In particular, our model featured fewer model parameters, amounting to 0.70 MB, which is significantly lower than the 3.67 GB required by the ATTN-based model. The reduced computational needs of our approach means it can process large datasets containing over a million clinical text notes in a reasonable time frame of 16 hours and 40 minutes. In conclusion, our semi-supervised strategy integrates medical knowledge constraints effectively to enhance the reliability of automatic ICD coding, achieving improved performance and efficiency compared to existing state-of-the-art models. The improved quality of coded data using our hybrid model, along with its increased validity, makes it suitable for various downstream tasks in healthcare such as comorbidity inference, patient selection, and risk assessment. This paper explores almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples. Additionally, it establishes a connection between this classification and the minimal free resolution of these ideals, specifically regarding the splitness of certain modules. Key tools utilized in this work include the minimal resolution filter current discretization, the minimal algebra model, and the Riemann-Hilbert correspondence. By applying these tools, the paper shows that certain direct sums of minimal free resolution modules have specific properties, ultimately leading to almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes. The conclusions drawn in this study are further refined and generalized through the study of specific classes of polymatroidal ideals, including the bootstrap class and the multigeneralized cislin class, with corresponding examples provided. Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$ with $N$, $K$, and $P$ representing the number of data points, clusters, and data dimensions, respectively. Additionally, we demonstrate a significant reduction in the number of qubit gates needed compared to the previous quantum machine learning approach. Our findings represent a significant advancement towards practical quantum-based machine learning on quantum hardware. Given the current hardware constraints, we also analyze realistic performance expectations on existing devices. Ultimately, we believe that quantum machine learning has the potential to outperform its classical counterpart, especially in high-dimensional data processing, and we expect further improvements as the hardware limitations are addressed. Given the current hardware limitations, we also explore the possibility of useful applications with existing devices. Differentiable rendering has made significant advancements in image-based inverse problems by utilizing implicit volume representations. However, these volumes necessitate frequent updates to object poses, which can be computationally expensive due to costly ray-triangle intersections. In this research, we address this limitation by introducing a new method that utilizes tracing and implicit surfaces to quickly and efficiently render images from arbitrary object poses in 3D. Our approach leverages an array of precomputed trigonometric functions to trace implicit surfaces and estimates their shapes through differentiable splines, resulting in near-zero training times. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in tackling complex image-based inverse problems such as depth estimation, object detection, and image reconstruction, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art rendering-based depth estimation methods. The source code for our method can be accessed at https://github.com/alex200101/TrTrace.

Recent research on transportation networks has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty and reliability by modeling the probability of origin-destination demand and network flow. Building on long-term traffic data collection, this paper develops an innovative framework to estimate the average and statistical relationship of origin-destination demand while considering the day-to-day variability resulting from travelers' independent route selections. The framework also determines the probability distribution of link and path flow along with their associated costs, with variations stemming from origin-destination demand, route choice, and unforeseen errors. By employing iterative least squares and lasso regularization techniques, the framework can iteratively estimate the origin-destination demand while maintaining sparse covariance matrices for enhanced interpretability and computational efficiency. Notably, the covariance matrix is found to be a weighted average of the identity matrix and a nonnegative definite matrix, which facilitates sparse structure preservation. The framework's applicability and performance are validated through numerical experiments conducted on the well-known ring highway network and a larger partially structured network. The results indicate the importance of accounting for route choice variability in traffic flow estimation and that the proposed method outperforms a comparable model in preserving sparsity while exhibiting improved precision. Furthermore, the study reveals the structural patterns present in the covariance matrix, showing higher variability in demand affecting larger and more congested sections of the network while the interaction between adjacent sections also poses significant variability. The proposed method demonstrates computational suitability and precision, requiring approximately 10 minutes of processing time for large networks featuring hundreds of links. The framework is deemed suitable for large-scale practical networks, with potential for integration into active traffic assignment models to inform dynamic routing apps and traffic management decisions. The method is not open-source due to access restrictions but can be replicated using similar approaches. Lastly, the study suggests multiple avenues for further research, including the integration with dynamic pricing, the development of more efficient estimation algorithms, and the investigation of variational approximation methods for large-scale network structure learning. In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic and chaotic waves following a parameter adjustment. For weak nonlinearity in the system, these global phases exhibit a temporary state of stability, akin to that observed in nearly conservative systems. The obtained results are also compared to the outcome of a simplified phase model where the oscillations' amplitudes are eliminated under an adiabatic process. The presented work offers an alternative to system design that is less prone to degradation due to fluctuations and energy loss, achieving a stable global phase through conservation of patterns rather than energy. The study is performed numerically using a large array of coupled nonlinear oscillators, modeled after Josephson junctions in superconducting rings, with adjustable junctions exhibiting randomness in Josephson energy. The research focuses on a continuum limit of a broader class of dynamics, specifically the Klein-Gordon equations with a nonlinear damping term, taking into account fluctuations arising from capillary forces. The observed global phase patterns, formed through conservation of momentum, provide insights into the observation of persistent global quantum coherence in small circuits of any type. The presented work thus proposes an innovative approach to the creation of macroscopic quantum states, achieving stability against thermal fluctuations and decohering agents, and offering a versatile tool for the design of coherent electronic circuits. The study also explores the potential for the generation of light from these nonlinear oscillators, either through the excitation of localized waves or the emission of photons by coupled junctions, both of which are investigated numerically and analytically. The results demonstrate that a wide range of electromagnetic patterns, either periodic or chaotic, can induce a global phase coherent state in small networks of nonlinear oscillators, either conservative or dissipative. The observed phenomena are discussed in relation to existing experiments, such as the creation of coherent electronic sources using Josephson circuits and the emission of light from nonlinear oscillators through various configurations. The presented work offers a new avenue for the design of coherent electronic circuits, facilitating our understanding of the transition between quantum and classical behavior in small systems and the creation of novel technological elements. Moreover, the study shows that the global phase coherence in small networks of nonlinear oscillators, either conservative or dissipative, can be induced by a wide range of patterns, either periodic or chaotic, and might be exploited for the development of light sources. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with the aim of reducing tree construction time. Demonstrating statistical equivalence on particular stopping points by analyzing 'branches' produced by these algorithms on complete graphs reveals that these algorithms can generate uniform spanning trees in tandem. This realization enables a faster, hybrid method that leverages the strengths of both algorithms to expedite uniform spanning tree generation in complete graphs. Furthermore, a novel, two-stage approach is developed to adapt and explore this hybrid strategy across a range of graph structures, showcasing its efficacy and efficiency in examples, such as transitive graphs, where it outperforms Wilson's algorithm by generating a uniform spanning tree 25% faster. This research also delves into examining the algorithms' performance in more complex graph environments. An additional area of study involves applying these findings to the realm of sampling, specifically exploring the efficient uniform spanning tree generation in sampled graphs. By analyzing uniform spanning tree generation in the inter-section graph of a finite graph, this research identifies both the algorithms' ability to efficiently generate this graph's uniform spanning tree and their capacity to do so 25% faster when utilizing the hybrid method, thus shedding light on the algorithms' behavior in this graph environment. Lastly, this research extends its findings into more advanced areas of study, specifically focusing on the efficient generation of a uniform hypergraph and presenting novel probabilistic algorithms in the study of random graphs. By analyzing the efficient generation of a uniform hypergraph through time, this research presents an entirely new set of probabilistic algorithms in the study of random graphs. These findings open the door for further research in this field, and it is anticipated that they will be useful and productive areas of study. To date, this research represents the first to efficiently generate a uniform hypergraph through time; however, it is likely that future research will build upon and expand upon these findings. This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of multimedia data. Comprising three modalities - audio, visual, and haptic time-series data, this dataset is uniquely designed to facilitate advanced research in multimodal processing. Featuring lengthy sequences of 40 seconds, each data sample includes synchronized samples from audio, with a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz, and inclusive of three haptic channels from a force-sensitive resistor matrix. Our investigation into this dataset delves into the effectiveness of multimodal models in accurately predicting temporal alignment across different modalities. We rigorously evaluate the performance of our models through rigorous threshold-based evaluation methods, and make our dataset and code publicly available for the research community to build upon. Furthermore, we include a detailed dataset description, evaluation methods, and thorough analysis of our experiment outcomes to guide future researchers in utilizing MusicTM-Dataset. Additionally, we provide access to the dataset code for replication purposes.
