This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second challenge, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is realized through a temperature function reduction technique borrowed from the point set registration process. The objective of this reformation process is to rapidly eliminate disturbances, thus minimizing the time required for the swarm to reach its destination and ultimately lowering the energy consumption of this process. To quantify the extent of formation disturbance triggered by collision avoidance, deviation in the centroid of the swarm formation is measured, drawing inspiration from the concept of center of mass in classical mechanics. The study's experimental outcomes validate the efficacy of the proposed technique in terms of performance and energy efficiency. Specifically, it has been observed that the time taken for the swarm to reach its destination after completing collision avoidance is merely 7% of the original time, while the energy expenditure is also significantly reduced at 12%. Moreover, the technique shows remarkable applicability in scenarios involving non-uniform drone formations, demonstrating a versatile aspect of the method. The successful implementation of the technique has been verified using simulations in an environment that mimics real-world conditions by using 50 drones in various formations. Furthermore, the technique has been tested in an actual drone swarm consisting of 55 drones, showcasing its ability to effectively avoid collisions through simulation. The use of 50 green drones in the simulation represents the formation's original state, while the blue, red, yellow, and purple drones indicate the various formations employed after successful collision avoidance. It is evident that the proposed technique has great potential for application in autonomous drone swarms. This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions. Furthermore, this study compares the efficiency of the Seidel matrix algorithm to the Cassidy-Liu algorithm. We introduce an efficient method of computing the Seidel energy for chain graphs, which runs in $O(n\log n)$ time, utilizing the Cassity-Liu algorithm. We establish the efficiency of this new method, which runs in $O(n^{3/2}\log n)$ time in the case of a random oracle, based on Akivis' model. We test our new method on chain graphs with orders $n$ ranging from $10$ to $50$, which confirms its efficiency relative to the Cassity-Liu algorithm. We conclude by presenting further research opportunities in graph theory and algebra. We verify our theoretical findings through random experiments, which include computations of the Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting the corresponding eigenvalues of the Seidel matrix. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues. Interestingly, a specific set of these eigenvalues corresponds to the discrete spectrum of the original Dirac operator, derived from the solutions to an associated non-self-adjoint eigenvalue problem involving the Heun equation. This reveals a unique connection - the solutions (eigenvalues) are symmetric about the real axis. Conversely, another set of eigenvalues originates from the self-adjoint Dirac operator, possessing real eigenvalues that correspond to the solutions of the classical Hill's equation. Consequently, a set of eigenvalues is produced that correspond to the quasi-periodic solutions of the focused Dirac operator, essentially merging the approaches of "direct" and "indirect" methods for determining discrete spectrum. This research, therefore, offers a more comprehensive understanding of the directed spectrum by utilizing "indirect" methods, encompassing connections to the Heun equation, tridiagonal operators and corresponding eigenvalue problems. This mathematical framework may be viewed as a "non-self-adjoint" extension of a previously established "self-adjoint" framework, specifically Atiyah-Patodi-Singer's work on the signature operator. This non-self-adjoint framework may be used to investigate specific, non-standard homology theories on the circle group, by exploring the relationship between the directed spectrum and homological features. This research thus initiates an investigation of the directed spectrum via homological lens, aiming to determine if the directed spectrum can be related to homological features, or if not, to establish a counter-example as a result. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality. Prior research used automated labels derived from page views and user comments, but these indicators are insufficient to efficiently label all articles. To address this issue, we developed a model that leverages Wikipedia's hidden data to automatically identify high-quality sentences. Our model relies on the analysis of paragraphs and their modifications over time, enabling us to accurately identify high-quality sentences with an accuracy of 42%, nearly double the classification accuracy achieved with automated indicators. By utilizing this model, we successfully scaled the labeling process, enabling us to analyze the article structure and evaluate the effectiveness of existing quality indicators. Our findings indicate that Wikipedia's quality indicators are largely ineffective in retaining high-quality content. To improve article quality, we propose rewriting Wikipedia's quality scale to prioritize contributors' subjective evaluations and the page view-based quality indicator, which correlates with our model's predictions. This new scale demonstrates a more robust correlation with objective criteria and provides 25% more accurate predictions than our model in isolation. To facilitate the adoption of our model and proposed quality scale, we provide an open-source implementation and the Wikipedia sentence-level quality data. Both resources can be accessed via GitHub at https://github.com/your-username/wikipedia_quality. To view our model and findings in action, please visit our demo website at https://your-website-url. We are excited to share our work with the Wikipedia community and the broader research audience, and we hope it helps advance Wikipedia's quality and accuracy. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, where a compact model is trained to replicate a network's decision function using nothing but the network's input-output pairs. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with performance comparable to traditional methods when all data is available, and superior to alternative black-box methods when only a limited amount of data can be accessed. The accompanying code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/SingleTask/BBKD. The PyTorch model implementation is accessible at https://github.com/SingleTask/BBKD-PyTorch. The Caffe implementation can be found at https://github.com/SingleTask/BBKD-Caffe. Additionally, the Google Colab notebook at https://github.com/SingleTask/BBKD-GoogleColab provides a portable version of the experiment. The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, offering clear group-theoretic criteria for classifying classical T-duals and providing explicit, continuous-trace algebra computations for the resulting non-trivial Dixmier-Douady classes. Ultimately, we demonstrate that any solvmanifold can be represented as a $C^*$-algebra bundle of noncommutative tori, which we explicitly compute, while the monodromy of the original torus bundle is translated into a Morita equivalence among fiber algebras. Our findings serve as a foundation for future research on topological T-duals of compact manifolds, though the associated nontrivial $C^*$-algebraic structure necessarily deviates from classical topological properties, revealing an inherent discrepancy between the geometric and algebraic frameworks. Specifically, we observe that the first integer cohomology of the $C^*$-algebra bundle's total space no longer reflects the group ${\rm Diff}_{{\rm diff}}(G)$ of diffeomorphisms representing the monodromy of the torus bundle on its fiber algebras. Though the algebraic structure of the $C^*$-algebra bundle captures this diffeomorphism, the resulting quasi-isometry between the Heisenberg groups' algebras fails to directly encode the properties of ${\rm Diff}_{{\rm diff}}(G)$. Our work is an extension of an earlier article by Mathai, Rosenberg, and Zettler, with additional contributions including the classification of classical T-dual models for nilmanifolds and other examples from string theory, such as the Heisenberg algebra's quasi-isometry representing the monodromy on an example by Moore-Seiberg. Moreover, our $C^*$-algebra formalism offers a versatile framework for tackling future research questions, like topological T-duality on compact manifolds with a diffeomorphism representing the monodromy. Reinforcement learning efficiency can significantly be improved through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. The associated code is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/qianzhengf/co-imitation-learning. Additionally, a video demonstrating CoIL's performance can be found at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4vR_H1XmTmM. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric function, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve the average computation complexity of search-limited decoding. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited decoding can be nearly as efficient as hard-decision decoding, particularly when the polarization-holes are shallow. We further introduce a semi-public anagram decoding method for PAC codes, which involves selecting the most frequent frequency pattern as the correct path. By applying this frequency-based semi-public anagram decoding, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes, which confirms the proposal's effectiveness. Moreover, we investigate the optimal code design for frequency-based semi-public anagram decoding, which involves balancing the code's polarization-holes and the frequency-diversity, for both random and structured frequency matrices. Furthermore, we generalize the frequency-based semi-public anagram decoding to the entire polarization matrix, introducing two new decoding methods: the frequency-based public anagram decoding and the frequency-based private anagram decoding. By analyzing the decoding computations, our results indicate that the frequency-based public anagram decoding outperforms the current best frequency-based semi-public anagram decoding, which was previously confirmed by Monte-Carlo simulations. Moreover, we investigate the optimal code design for frequency-based public anagram decoding, which involves maximizing the code's frequency-diversity, for both random and structured frequency matrices. To achieve this, we introduce the maximum frequency-diversity ratio and the high-rate frequency-diversity ratio, which involve removing redundant frequencies from the frequency matrices. Our results indicate that the maximum frequency-diversity ratio and the high-rate frequency-diversity ratio yield nearly identical results. Furthermore, we investigate the optimal code design for frequency-based private anagram decoding, which involves both polarization-holes and frequency-diversity, for both random and structured frequency matrices. This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to calculate hand joint movement between frames. Our novel hand pose canonicalization module simplifies this task and enables accurate tracking of hand joints. By converting these joints into a template-based hand model called MANO, our system can reconstruct the entire hand. To track objects, we use an efficient module that generates object SDF data from the first frame and performs optimization-based tracking. Then, to resolve ambiguity caused by occlusions, our system adopts joint optimization for both hands and objects. In testing, our system demonstrates significantly better performance than existing approaches, with a notable speed advantage. Code and model will be publicly available. \\

This study applies the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram containing four vertices, aiming to examine how the group's elements are curbed by taking the reduction. We undertake a detailed analysis of the properties of the reduced algebra and the representations within this context. A key observation derives from the conjecture that the reduced algebra is comprehensive. We have also discovered that the reduced representations constitute a full set based solely on the group's star diagram and the intersection of the branching graphs corresponding to the groups' subdiagrams 01 and 10. This full set is unaffected by the group's finite index k. An independent verification of our findings through computational methods has been carried out. In addition, the current work implements a computer program designed to identify the reductions of Coxeter groups of rank 4 containing a general star diagram with four vertices, which involves a detailed examination of the properties of the first 80 irreducible representations in the reduced algebra modulo p for p = 5, 7, 13. A key application of this program has allowed us to pinpoint the reductions of five notable Coxeter groups: G4, G25, G33, G42, and G45. Specifically, the program confirmed that the reduced algebra of G4 modulo 5 is isomorphic to a direct product of two altered Weyl loops, whereas a previous study had already established this isometry. Furthermore, the program has independently verified a number of key reduction cases, including the complete set of representations in G25, G33, G42, and G45. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically calibrate camera parameters, offering a fast and reliable solution. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through extensive empirical testing across various real-world scenarios employing different moving methods and devices with unique optical characteristics. Compared to alternative approaches, our method yields superior performance in terms of accuracy and reliability. The benefits of this innovative solution include the elimination of time-consuming marker placement procedures, reduced reliance on imperfect simulation environments, and the ability to produce high-quality results in complex fiducial-array designs commonly found in industrial settings. The accompanying code and calibration datasets are publicly available for replication purposes. The proposed calibration technique serves as a versatile tool for optical characterization in various applications, including, but not limited to, robotics and augmented reality. A related video showcasing the method's performance in different scenarios is available at: https://youtu.be/pxasfMtO5Vw. The figure shown in this abstract is from that video.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods. Moreover, we establish procedures to identify specific units where treatment effects are significantly impacted and where changes in one unit's outcome are significantly affected by the treatment status of its neighbors. Simulation results indicate that existing methods often fail to detect treatment interference when units are highly similar, leading to the discovery of unobserved factors contributing to treatment interference in networks. Moreover, we introduce methods to eliminate the influence of these underlying factors so that active treatment interference can be more effectively detected. When applied to the data from the Job Training Partnership Act, we found treatment interference in some sites but not others, leading to partially effective treatment interference. Furthermore, we examined active treatment interference and discovered that changes in one site's outcome were not significantly affected by the treatment status of its neighbors for some treatments but were for others. Finally, underlying factors contributing to treatment interference were discovered in sites where treatment interference was not entirely effective. Additionally, we discovered sites where treatment interference was not effective but underlying factors were partially effective. These sites were rare. Moreover, we discovered sites where treatment interference was not effective but underlying factors were not effective either. These sites were even less common. To our knowledge, this is the first study to account for underlying factors when detecting treatment interference and active treatment interference and the first to establish methods for partially effective and active treatment interference. Moreover, this is the first study to establish sites where treatment interference is not effective but underlying factors are partially effective and vice versa. Furthermore, we discovered methods for identifying specific units where treatment effects are significantly affected by the treatment status of neighboring units and changes in one unit's outcome are significantly affected by the treatment status of its neighbors. We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about 0.1 Kelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the experimentally determined parameters are employed to determine the critical temperatures associated with BKT transitions as well as long-range order. Finite-size scaling of the spin stiffness based on our in-plane theory shows a perfect match between theoretical and experimental critical temperatures, clearly indicating the complex nature of the phase diagram of our material and the manifestation of BKT correlations in laboratory magnetic fields. Moreover, the observed critical temperatures reveal critical field values that follow a scaling law proportional to the critical temperature of the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, thereby providing practical applications in field-induced quantum spin liquids. Lastly, a comparative analysis with another weakly coupled Heisenberg material called BaCu2(PO4)2(PO4) shows that the critical anisotropy required to enter the BKT regime decreases exponentially with the critical temperature of the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in lower-dimensional systems, thus supporting our experimental observation. This comparative analysis, coupled with our theoretical model, suggests that the BKT regime is universally accessible in weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg systems subject to laboratory magnetic fields. Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis of dark matter production to ensure its consistency with observed data. The examination, which encompasses both the spin-independent and spin-dependent dark matter scattering as well as direct and indirect dark matter detection, reveals no significant hurdles within the model's parameter space. Furthermore, a detailed study of axion decay and neutrino less double beta decay provides additional constraints helping to refine the model's parameter space. The analysis of lattices spanning $10^4$ points shows that these experimental constraints effectively limit the model's parameter space despite the presence of multiple degrees of freedom. The constraints on the model's parameter space also have significant implications for axion dark matter and neutrino less double beta decay experiments as well as future colliders, such as HL-LHC and ILC, to further restrict the model's allowed parameter space. The predictions made by the $a\nu$MSM model for long baseline neutrino experiment are also analyzed, which may provide additional constraints on the model's parameter space. The analysis shows that future dark matter direct detection experiments such as LDMX, who is currently on track to operate near the axion saturation boundary, will likely be the most stringent constraint on the model. The constraints imposed by the dark matter direct detection, on the other hand, will eventually be bettered by axion decay unless an axion decay into masked neutrinos is involved. The constraints imposed by the dark matter indirect detection, on the other hand, will not be able to compete with the future dark matter direct detection and axion decay observational limits for a general case. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating single random numbers at a time. In order to overcome these drawbacks, this paper presents a new approach, called SRAM-GATE, which enables high-throughput generation of multiple random numbers simultaneously. SRAM-GATE achieves this accomplishment by incorporating two distinct access methods to the SRAM array - rapid, narrow reads during a short period, followed by a longer period of wider data transfers. The design incorporates two parallel circuits that handle input/output operations, enabling the simultaneous processing of requests in conjunction with reduced bus contention. The effectiveness of SRAM-GATE has been verified through EM-simulations that demonstrated its capability to produce 40 million random numbers per second while consuming less than 0.2 mW of power, thereby exhibiting significantly improved performance compared to current SRAM-based TRNGs. The research demonstrates that SRAM-GATE provides an efficient, low-power solution for embedded systems requiring high-quality random numbers for various applications, such as, security, science, and statistics. Additionally, a fully-functional hardware driver was developed to facilitate the integration of SRAM-GATE with Linux-based platforms, thereby simplifying the access to random numbers generated by SRAM-GATE. The performance of SRAM-GATE has been quantitatively evaluated through the measurement of its latency, throughput, energy expenditure, and bit disparity in over 101 trillion random numbers, thereby ensuring its high-quality as per random number generation standards. Furthermore, a detailed economic assessment revealed that the cost per random number produced by SRAM-GATE is significantly lower than that of state-of-the-art TRNGs built with dedicated hardware. In conclusion, the research presents SRAM-GATE as an advanced SRAM-based TRNG offering superior performance, versatility, and reliability for random number generation in various embedded systems. The technical merits of SRAM-GATE have been validated through extensive analyses and experimental evaluations, thereby ensuring its suitability for various applications including, security, scientific research, and statistics. The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals novel possibilities in theoretical research. This study explores the impact of $q$-deformation on phase transitions in optomechanical systems, using the deformed parametric amplification process to investigate the limitations it imposes. By applying the generalized bosonic field representation, we develop a theoretical model of $q$-deformed optomechanical systems and examine the stability of stationary states. Through analysis of the stability conditions, we identify how $q$-deformation influences the phase transition, finding that it alters the threshold for parametric amplification and introduces a new type of phase transition. Additionally, we evaluate how $q$-deformation affects the optical cavity frequency and find that it is determined by the transverse wave velocity of the underlying medium. Finally, we evaluate key parameters in the optomechanical system to gain a deeper understanding of the effects of $q$-deformation. This study provides a foundational theoretical model for $q$-deformed optomechanical systems and sheds light on the broader implications of $q$-deformation for optomechanical technology. \\

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on years 2020 and 2021. The logarithmic US dollar price returns of this network are examined using Granger causality and O-information to quantify both pairwise and high-order statistical relationships. The Granger causality results indicate peaks in significant events, while the corresponding network structure exhibits stability, with most influential nodes being cryptocurrencies. Contrasting with pairwise analysis, stable coins appear in few synergistic connections but dominate high-order statistical dependencies, suggesting a complex role in cryptocurrency markets. Moreover, a significant surge in synergistic connections among cryptocurrencies occurs in 2021, indicating increased information dissemination effects that could be attributed to the widespread adoption of Bitcoin by institutional investors. The study also demonstrates that high-order synergies offer superior predictive power for future log returns, as confirmed through a significant correlation in 2021. Nonetheless, this relationship becomes non-significant in 2021, indicating a possible decrease in information dissemination effects. Furthermore, the study reveals that high-order synergies related to cryptocurrencies are more informative than those involving traditional financial assets like S&P 500 index components. The potential applications of this research are diverse, offering tools to navigate cryptocurrency markets based on network structures and information measures, which can be used to develop informative causal graphs for investors and financial analysts. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based models like BERT and RoBERTa in this context, particularly with multi-task training methods that integrate data augmentation techniques to grade essays more effectively.  To assess the efficacy of these approaches, we selected two popular essay grading datasets: the Dataset A from the University of Massachusetts Amherst and the Dataset B from the Allenni research platform.  Our experiments involved pre-trained transformer models, such as BERT and RoBERTa, paired with data augmentation strategies like paragraph-level and sentence-level replacement, as well as a multi-task training method that combined these approaches.  Our findings indicate that the combination of pre-trained transformer models and multi-task training with data augmentation significantly outperformed the baseline models by 4% and 5%, respectively, on Dataset A and 2% and 3% on Dataset B.  With these results, we developed a high-performance automated essay grading model that achieved an F1 score of 0.73 on Dataset A and 0.67 on Dataset B, paving the way for practical applications in this domain.  Our hope is that these findings will inspire further research in automated essay grading, a critical and ubiquitous NLP application. We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities. 
Therefore, Delegated RingCT can be considered a suitable solution for DPoS-based cryptocurrencies that require anonymous transactions. 
The source code of Delegated RingCT is publicly accessible on GitHub at the address https://github.com/Blockchain-Experts/DelegatedRingCT.

These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 7.4 standard deviations above background noise.  Specifically, signals for individual W boson variations have a significance of between 3.3 and 3.4 standard deviations, while separate background noise estimates indicate that events with two identical bosons make up about 35% of the total boson creation signals.  These findings enhance existing knowledge of four-boson processes in high-energy collisions.  Furthermore, direct searches for non-standard model physics have been done using the same data set, focusing on events with unusual patterns of missing energy and heavy top-quark presence.  Two separate scenarios of beyond-standard model physics have been ruled out with confidence levels greater than 90%, based on analyses looking for single top-quark production with additional boson creation or in double top-quark creation with additional boson creation. This data set remains compatible with limits on various beyond-standard model physics hypotheses, including a hypothetical particle acting as a vector-like doublet. Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using automated tools, and achieves new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining advanced language models with innovative approaches. Additionally, the project updates and releases the existing UD HTB annotation scheme, incorporating the improvements from the new Hebrew corpus. This updated scheme serves as a model for developing high-quality UD annotations in other languages with limited resources. As such, it is itself incorporated into the UD Hebrew repository. Lastly, the paper discusses its findings on the UD Hebrew corpus's composition, NLP tasks, and NLP research methodologies. This includes a statistical analysis of the corpus, findings on topic shift detection, and a exploration of the challenges and opportunities presented by the diverse topics and registers in the corpus. This research aims to contribute to the UD Hebrew corpus as a valuable resource for further research, NLP task development, and to promote future advancements in the field. An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design approach are demonstrated through comparative evaluations using a mass of aerospace systems. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may facilitate the development of in-context learning, even when each domain doesn't result in in-context learning alone. Lastly, a pretraining corpus related to a downstream task may not always ensure a high in-context learning performance for that specific task, especially when it comes to the few-shot setting, and that language modeling performance and in-context learning do not always correlate as one might expect. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel consonant pairs, while steady-states represent sonorants. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot. The associated video demonstrates the results, highlighting the potential for this method to underpin real-time planning applications on multi-limbed robots. The accompanying code is accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/tu-berlin-mpi/MPODE.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and errors in the distillation of quantum resources from general quantum states.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods in the specific resource theories of quantum entanglement and quantum coherence. 
In the context of entanglement, we derived tighter bounds on the probability of successfully generating a desired entangled state from an arbitrary entangled state through multiple copies.
In the context of coherence, we found that the trade-off between success probability and error tolerance followed a distinct exponent characteristic of resource metric's norm, which held universally across previously established resource metrics, but was particularly verified to be valid for the path-deformation metric. 
These findings provide novel insights into the characteristics of resource metrics and offer practical guidance for the efficient transformation of resources in quantum information processing. 
In addition to its theoretical significance, our methods have practical applications in the ongoing development of quantum technologies, which rely on the available resources to accomplish specific tasks with high success probabilities and minimal errors. 
Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between quantum resources and their utilisation in probabilistic protocols. 
As such, it may be applicable in the context of real-world quantum devices which regularly encounter limitations in their available resources.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques. Additionally, this study aimed to replicate key findings from a renowned study on coffee dynamics using these analytical methods. Our approach resulted in simpler equations that still accurately captured the phenomenon, allowing for further advancements. Ultimately, we took our analysis a step further to establish correspondence between the physical system and its mathematical representations. Despite the apparent simplicity of our model, we discovered that simplifying the problem led to the loss of crucial features essential for accurately modeling coffee dynamics. Therefore, this study suggests that an effective modeling strategy should strive to balance the level of approximation with the level of complexity. Furthermore, we reflected on the broader implications of our research for engineering applications, emphasizing the significance of considering excitation and non-linearity in modeling dynamics. Finally, we explored potential avenues for extending our model in the future, such as incorporating vertical motion and using the method of multiple scales to analyze dynamic phenomena in a system with a weak detuning parameter. Nonetheless, our current model is still applicable for designing practical purposes, allowing for instance to derive an expression for the maximum stable angle of a mobile nonlinear pendulum subject to parametric excitation. Conversely, we observed that excitation in the horizontal plane did not reveal any notable findings for the dynamics of a free swinging cup. Therefore, we concluded that this type of motion does not significantly influence the dynamics of a coffee cup being carried. In a rare instance of a perfectly conservative system, we found that introducing dissipation had a surprising effect - it facilitated the creation of a stable equilibrium position for the pendulum even in the presence of parametric excitation. However, this phenomenon came at the cost of altering the phase space structure, as observed through the application of two analytical methods. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. Moreover, the merits of DR-DSGD extend to applications in synthetic data collaboration and distributionally robust classification under covariate shift. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to quasi-particle RPA results. The accuracy of the dipole-based model in capturing non-particle-like interactions and excitations serves as evidence for the potential of this model in modeling light-matter interactions. Moreover, we highlight that certain properties, such as fractional orbital occupation, can be detrimental to describing interactions in small systems. We suggest future directions for developing a unified description of light-matter interactions within TB models. Moreover, we apply these models to simulate optical spectroscopies under non-resonant and strong excitation conditions, achieving consistency with first-principle predictions. The models are utilized to investigate transient optical responses in dielectric and metallic systems, including nonlinear effects that manifest in the frequency-domain through the modification of emulated bands. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a multi-step nonlinear excitation process in dielectric systems yields an accurate description of frequency-domain optical responses, such as inter-band transitions and excitonic effects, thus providing a viable approach for such applications. Moreover, we utilize this model to explore the design of optical responses in 2D systems subject to strong excitation, exploring multi-photon processes and examining coherent effects among quasi-particles to assess their relevance in optical spectroscopy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing. The success of this modified control design is confirmed through notable improvements in its ability to reduce positional error, maintain desired trajectory integrity, and compensate for dynamic fluctuations, all without compromising its original stability and performance characteristics. The control design is further validated through an experimental verification conducted on a precision stage built by Velmex, an industry leader in high-precision motion systems. The experimental validation, complemented by numerical simulation results, comprehensively evaluates the effectiveness of this innovative control strategy in navigating complex trajectories, both in the presence and absence of unexpected disturbances. We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside learned keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently predict keypoints and correspondence across varying views and objects, while its geometric representation is also transferable to classification tasks. Furthermore, PRNet's keypoint and correspondence predictions serve as a strong baseline in partial point cloud registration tasks. The proposed framework is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexeydykin/pronet.

This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to those predictions, our results indicate a nonzero longitudinal distribution amplitude. Furthermore, we find that the transverse distribution amplitudes for the vector mesons are nonzero, contrary to the predictions of perturbative QCD. Our study employs a lightfront truncation scheme and a set of kernel functions derived from quark distribution amplitudes, utilizing renormalization group equations to determine the parameters of those kernel functions. The distribution amplitudes for the distribution functions of the distribution amplitudes themselves exhibit a distinct shape compared to those of the parton distribution functions themselves, suggesting that our truncation scheme is suitable. The matrix elements of the hadronic vector correlators are also essential for understanding rare decays and electroweak precision tests. Our results indicate that the decay width of the Higgs boson into a vector meson and a photon may be non-zero, which could be confirmed or refuted by experiments. Furthermore, the full momentum dependence of the correlation functions can be probed experimentally by measuring the momentum-dependent transverse distribution amplitude of the vector mesons at large momentum transfer. Finally, we calculate the full momentum dependence of the decay width of the Higgs boson into a vector meson and a lepton pair, which could be measured in experiments. The full details of the calculation and the relevant parton distribution functions can be found in the associated documentation and public code releases. The numerical results of the study are as follows: The decay width of the Higgs boson into a vector meson and a photon is less than $7\cdot10^{-6}$ times the square of the unitary phase space, at a 95% confidence level. Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a known dataset or make general predictions, but our focus lies on a specific, critical challenge: can we successfully segment novel, unseen imaging modalities? To this end, we introduce a groundbreaking task called cross-domain instance segmentation, involving the separation of distinct objects within images obtained from a different modality. To tackle this challenge, we have developed a unique dataset comprising 400,000 instances of salivary gland pathology ultrasonograms paired with CT scans. Our initial findings reveal that deep learning models struggle to adapt to new modalities and significantly underperform basic segmentation methods. We then developed an innovative multi-stage approach called DeepStage, comprising self-supervised learning, domain adaptation, and pseudo-labeling, demonstrating the feasibility of cross-domain instance segmentation and achieving respectable accuracy rates of 0.814~AUC and 0.701~AUC on salivary gland pathology and CT scans, respectively. DeepStage has shown significant potential and now serves as a benchmark for cross-domain instance segmentation, with its code and dataset available for public use at the link provided. https://github.com/SingleCellAI/DeepStage. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers robust defenses against malicious transformations by incorporating specific tasks to counter rotation, stretching, and positioning attacks. TPC employs an iterative process involving the reliable estimation of the scale factor, rotation matrix, and a random vector within a bounding box. It then updates the estimate of the target point cloud using a weighted average, calculated from the estimates produced by multiple networks, each trained separately on distinct transformation categories. TPC also incorporates supervision during training, aiming to minimize the discrepancy in estimated shapes resulting from different rotation and stretching movements. Moreover, we develop and release SiSpA, an innovative dataset consisting of artificially crafted sets of points that mimic the features of RealWaymo, but with added stretches and rotations. The results from our experiments reveal that SiSpA presents significant challenges for the point cloud models to distinguish the front of a car, while the models' performance is notably improved when trained with TPC. Given its general applicability, our proposed framework can be applied to various 3D detection benchmarks. We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency, while developing optimization strategies to maximize system efficiency. We introduce a clear channel assessment process to CSMA, allowing radar units to detect and minimize interference, while implementing expected throughput metrics to evaluate the efficiency of both ALOHA and CSMA protocols. Numerical evaluations demonstrate the impact of parameters such as system efficiency, interference probability, and system load on the performance of both medium access techniques. In scenarios where system efficiency is low due to high load or long interference probability, CSMA exhibits better performance, while ALOHA performs better at high system loads with low interference probability. These findings can guide network planners in choosing the more suitable medium access technique for their FMCW radar networks. In addition, we identify key parameters that require adjustment to further optimize the performance of both ALOHA and CSMA protocols. In the case of CSMA, we examine the impact of system load, clear channel assessment probability, and radar unit characteristics on network performance, identifying opportunities for improvement through adjusted parameters. We also explore the potential of combining ALOHA and CSMA into a hybrid medium access technique, allowing radar units to switch between the two based on different system conditions or detection outcomes. By switching to CSMA when detection outcomes indicate clear channels and using ALOHA in scenarios with high system load and interference probability, we discover that the resulting hybrid policy leads to higher system efficiency, 9.1 dB on average, compared to using CSMA or ALOHA alone. Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically when a heavy object strikes a soft surface and when the point of impact is positioned at a shallow angle relative to the listener's location. Furthermore, an approach to create a simple and effective sound synthesis technique is developed, which produces a realistic sound simulation ground surface using a numerical solution, with the ability to adjust for different material properties and impact conditions. A comprehensive example is provided, demonstrating the calculation of the ground surface acceleration for a 2 kg ball dropped from a 5 m height onto a 10 m radius, soft and flexible surface with a 3000 kg/m^2 mass density and a 50 N/s^2 gravitational acceleration. Additionally, the paper includes supplementary materials with more detailed mathematical derivations, relevant code snippets, and an additional demonstration example comparing the accuracy of different numerical schemes in generating audible ground impact effects. Based on these findings, the method of second order upsampled interpolation is recommended as the most effective approach. To facilitate further research, the ground sound model, sound synthesis technique, and demonstration code are made accessible through online repositories at https://indigomind.github.io/GroundImpactSound/ for downloads and https://groundimpactsound.github.io/ for online exploration. Lastly, future prospects for improving the accuracy of ground sound synthesis in rigid-body impact scenarios are identified and discussed. A key area of improvement identified is the incorporation of the impact sound produced by the ground itself, which remains an unsolved problem in this field. Ultimately, the potential for developing applications such as soft and hard ground sound effect libraries and impact vibration transmission assessment tools is also identified and presented. Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold the standards set forth by ISO 26262, rigorous testing of this logic is mandatory. Through this validation, one can confidently ensure the reliability of system responses in times of crisis and prevent aberrant system states from materializing. Traditional safety assessment tools are often inadequate in this capacity, prompting us to propose an advanced method centered around formal verification, leveraging model checking in particular. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, we carefully recreate the driving system's dynamics, define and formalize key safety criteria, and scope the analysis within the guidelines specified by ISO 26262. Upon successfully verifying a high-automation fail-safe logic aligned with industrial standards, we discovered critical errors previously unaccounted for in more conventional evaluations, thereby significantly enhancing the reliability of automotive safety-critical systems. To efficiently facilitate verification for complex systems, we advocate for the utilization of state-of-the-art formal verification tools and methodologies as an alternative to conventional testing methods for safety assessment. Furthermore, we provide and publish a verified model of the fail-safe logic used in highly automated driving systems, promoting replication and validation as an essential step towards validating this approach within the broader formal verification community. This model, along with the associated documentation, is accessible at https://github.com/verification-of-driving-systems/failsafe-arbitration under an open-source License. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle. Furthermore, even though a conservative addition, the theory developed from a conservative expansion of Robinson's LHR still violates classical logic's distributivity law, a phenomenon observed in other approaches such as SIA and also by Boolos in a purely transfinite context. Finally, even though Arthur's comparison of SIA to Leibnizian calculus may be well-intentioned, it remains fundamentally flawed and thus unable to contribute accurately to the ongoing discussion on the nature of Leibnizian calculus. In contrast, this paper's conservative expansion of Robinson's LHR provides a more accurate and faithful representation of Leibnizian calculus. Moreover, even though it is conservative with respect to Leibnizian logic, it necessarily leads to a violation of distributivity, a consequence which cannot be avoided. Instead, this violation is now argued to be the key to resolving the famous paradox of the third norm, a problem which had intrigued and challenged even Leibniz, leading to a hopeful conclusion that a more accurate understanding of Leibnizian calculus may now be within reach. One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Our research integrates these methods with context-aware document models by taking into account users' perspectives on these items. Additionally, our model offers the advantage of online personalization where the system can adjust the user and item representation profiles upon detecting new user interactions without requiring model retraining. Our proposed algorithm has been successfully tested and validated on three real-world datasets by comparing it to state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating notable improvement in accuracy and variability balance. Furthermore, our experimental analysis examines the effects of several key factors on model performance. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The key innovation of our algorithm is the transformation of the estimation task into a more accessible problem by introducing artificial constraints, specifically limits on the malicious nodes' degree and the distance to them, through the utilization of a novel graph class with properties suited for our design purposes. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our findings indicate that this method is a reliable tool for a broad range of simulations in numerical relativity. Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of an Atmospheric Dispersion Corrector. Current designs of the corrector, typically involve shifting mirrors or using prisms, are examined in relation to various off-axis observations. By applying wavefront propagation algorithms, it's possible to determine whether a telescope's image is significantly distorted and decide if a prism is necessary to correct dispersion. Instead, a digital correction could be employed before analysis of the captured image. Notably, this approach can be particularly beneficial for telescopes with small apertures or those operating at low signal-to-noise ratios. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. We have made our code publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/apachecn/PILE.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore be used to detect these low-frequency fluctuations, making it effective in cases where its sensitivity extends below the Compton frequency but not necessarily reaching its exact frequency value. A network of sensors making up a distributed system can enhance a detector's sensitivity to these fluctuations by up to ten orders of magnitude, depending on the number of detectors and their geographical distribution over a surface area. By considering the sensitivity of detectors to low-frequency fluctuations as an effective lower limit to their overall sensitivity, by taking into account their total active time, a collective group of sensors can also be used to find the average Compton frequency through regression analysis, potentially providing a value for the Planck constant, or at least refining existing estimates. A numerical example using over two years' worth of data from twenty detectors shows how this technique can be used in practice, offering a new and powerful method for investigating ultralight bosonic dark matter interactions. A comprehensive set of technical papers will be published that explain in detail how this technique works and what insights it provides about bosonic dark matter interactions. Those papers, along with related software and data, can be found at https://bosonicdm.github.io/. This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively. The study of BPC's solutions and the associated matrix properties offers an intriguing area of research, providing both mathematical and computational insights. The associated matrix, dubbed the Fourier Toeplitz matrix, shares properties with positive or negative semi-definite matrices, but not necessarily those of positive or negative definite matrices, particularly when it comes to the infinitesimal perturbations of its zero eigenvalues. The number of zero eigenvalues, denoted as N0, also plays a crucial role in determining the weights and locations of the Dirac masses. The possible range of N0 is from 0 to K+1, where N0 equals 0 when the matrix is positive definite, positive semi-definite but not positive definite, or infinite when the matrix is negative semi-definite. The proposed algorithm, basis pursuit in the continuum, is computed through an optimization package, resulting in various sparse solutions of an infinite-dimensional nature. The study expands on the previous work of Ref. [1] and timely addresses the comments raised in Ref. [2], particularly when Kc approaches the problem's dimension, denoted as K. The problem also finds analogies in the mathematical fields of Radon measures and functional analysis, as well as the computational field of basis pursuit, which motivates the construction of a matrix that has unique positive or negative semi-definite properties for sparse solutions. The proposed algorithm offers a computational approach that complements the theoretical analysis of Radon measures and provides valuable insights into their low-frequency Fourier components. The study establishes a timely connection between the mathematical and computational fields by addressing wide-ranging sparse solutions, thus providing relevant and valuable results. P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping algorithms to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows rapid prototyping of different mapping approaches and provides resource usage metrics for comparison. The compiler backend is now included in the P4.github.io website as an open-source repository. Our efforts promote reproducibility in research by offering a flexible frontend for P416 programs and various mapping algorithms, enabling researchers to develop and integrate their own mapping strategies. A dataset with benchmarking results is accessible at https://github.com/p4society/p4-malos-dataset. MalOS is an acronym for "Open Switches," representing the concept of freely accessible and modifiable switch software. The P4 repository on GitHub includes a collection of V1Model-based switches from different vendors, along with P416 programs, benchmarks, and evaluation information. Our research uses MalOS as an innovative tool for advanced research in programmable switching, enabling developers to modify the P4 code to test new hardware features and configurations. By offering a flexible dataset and research environment, MalOS promotes collaborative research among researchers, and its P4 repository serves as a resource for cutting-edge research in the field of programmable switching. Additionally, our research includes a new protocol suite, HTTPoA, addressing the problem of timely resource management in data centers by utilizing programmable switch technology. This innovative protocol enhances packet processing speed while maintaining privacy and is included in the open-source P4 repository on GitHub. HTTPoA's development marks a significant step in leveraging programmable switching technology to optimize data center efficiency, and its implementation is now accessible through the P4 consortium's benchmarking tools. Our research into programmable switching technology within data centers is an ongoing area of study in our ongoing work. More details can be found at https://p4society.github.io/malos/.
