In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy via a Streamline Upwind Petrov-Galerkin method. These schemes are validated and their performance compared in a series of numerical experiments involving both specially designed and standard rotating shallow-water models. Despite attempting to optimise the time-stepping schemes for the latter model, it ultimately proved to be unstable and presented significant accuracy shortcomings compared to the first method. Consequently, we recommend using the first method for scenarios where the transported field does not appear in the governing equations of the governing model, whereas the mixed approach is recommended when such a field does appear. Furthermore, for both methods, we recommend using quadratic Raviart-Thomas elements to ensure high spatial accuracy in the transport of vector-valued fields across curved surfaces. This study's numerical findings suggest that a high-order function space is essential for efficiently and accurately transport vector-valued fields over curved surfaces, which may serve as a model for future works on scalar transport. In addition, the presentation includes an independent description of the numerical schemes that have been codified in the open-source shared library flexiFEM@{https://git.fbf.ufrn.br/fbf/flexiFEM}. FlexiFEM provides the necessary tools to efficiently solve the vector transport equation using the recommended numerical schemes. FlexiFEM's flexibility in terms of mesh structure compatibility enables the efficient handling of complex rotating shallow-water models, which may serve as a basis for developing future free surface shallow water models. FlexiFEM also offers an efficient and stable time-stepping scheme for the standard rotating shallow-water model. Moreover, the library includes the description of numerical schemes for solving the vector transport equation using the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements under a streamline upwind $L$-finite difference scheme. The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. This study seeks to establish a unified framework by combining these ethics solutions with the framework of model-based reinforcement learning. This is achieved by formulating key concepts like fairness, federal learning, and differential privacy in terms of optimal policies that balance reward and constraint violations. Through empirical evaluation, it is demonstrated that employing such a unified framework yields smaller constraint violations and comparable rewards to conventional approaches. This is illustrated using the experimental results of learning policies to achieve both accurate image classification and protection of sensitive data. Furthermore, this framework is adaptable to various settings with distinct loss functions and can be applied to other ethics solutions by replacing the constraint violation metrics. Future research opportunities are also explored. The source code for reproducing the study's findings can be accessed at https://github.com/alexwhp/Unifed.git. In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems. A few variations of the methods are introduced that allow for increased order and stability, and it is demonstrated that they maintain energy consistency even with modifications. To test their effectiveness, HBVMs were applied to problems with multiple sources of energy. The accuracy of the methods in preserving energy and attaining a high order of precision was measured and verified through comparative analysis with respect to established metrics, including the mean norm of absolute errors, particularly for problems involving nonlinear differential equations. The efficiency of the methods in preserving energy was observed to increase alongside order advancements, and it was noticed that HBVMs often exhibit higher precision in practical applications than in theoretical formulations. The application of HBVMs to problems with Hamiltonian dynamics was found to provide extremely accurate solutions that closely approach the true solution, as seen in various tested examples. The methods presented here represent advancements of HBVMs that maintain their inherent energy-preserving property and demonstrate increased order and stability. The methods' efficiency in preserving energy was noticed to increase with order advancements, and it is observed that HBVMs exhibit increased precision in practical applications beyond their theoretical projections. The methods' ability to provide highly accurate solutions, especially in cases involving problems with Hamiltonian dynamics, further solidifies their value as a valuable tool for solving a range of differential problem types. The structures of the methods, given their continuous and multi-step nature, are found to provide valuable opportunities for creating specialized variants tailored to specific problem types that can maintain their essential energy-preserving property. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, this method enables more efficient backpropagation through the main network while reducing memory consumption. However, this method's reliance on gradient accumulation limits its performance. To overcome this limitation, a new optimization technique, block-wise update of local critics, is developed. Through extensive experiments on large-scale image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks on single-GPU systems, this method demonstrates significant performance improvements over current model-parallel methods. Moreover, this method outperforms existing data parallel techniques under low-memory conditions, making it suitable for modern neural networks. Furthermore, this method's effectiveness is evaluated on distributed-Tensor core systems, incorporating hardware considerations such as Tensor core acceleration and memory banking. As a result, this method achieves substantial speedup gains up to 5.3 times compared to existing methods. This approach is open-sourced at https://github.com/umcs-res/Local-Critic-Training. A corresponding video is available at https://youtube.umcs-res.com/Local-Critic-Training. Detailed information can also be found at https://umcs-res.github.io/Local-Critic-Training/. Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research indicates that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit increased stability when subjected to low levels of dissipation. Furthermore, this study verifies that Wada basins' infrastructure can survive in three-dimensional systems, as observed in the formation of Wada points on boundaries. Conversely, this research finds that strong dissipation leads to the destruction of Wada basins in three-dimensional systems. In contrast, this effect is observed in two-dimensional systems only when subjected to exceptionally high levels of dissipation. Thus, this research confirms that three-dimensional systems exhibit unique characteristics and pose intriguing challenges in the study of chaotic scattering. Additionally, this research discusses potential avenues for further research, including investigating intricate trajectories in three-dimensional systems and the impact of dissipation on Wada basins through numerical simulations and experiments. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate our hypothesis, while the upcoming SHiP experiment will provide us with a much broader creation and decay landscape to investigate this theoretical model further. Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority. Furthermore, the study's visualization outcomes
emphasize the robustness and generalizability of the model. Consequently, HAN is well-suited
for intricate human action understanding in complex videos. 
A supplementary document provides further details on the model's design and testing. 
Project materials, including source code, are available for replication at https://github.com/AttenNet/HAN.

When scattering a massless scalar field off a non-extremal Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black hole, the scattering data determine the change in mass and angular momentum, and the accuracy of the approximation depends on the horizon radius and adiabatic parameter, which are influenced by the strength of the electric field. For extremal black holes, the first law of thermodynamics is confirmed when the momentum is defined as the sum of the electric charge and a relativistic correction. The entanglement entropy calculated using the endpoint action, which accounts for the reaction and counter-reaction, agrees with the KRT entanglement entropy for non-extremal black holes. This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe. We begin with the basic aspects of SF and its molecular development, then move on to discuss how observations influence theories and the dynamics of the process, which have led to the development of our comprehensive picture of SF. We will also delve into the debate surrounding the initial formation of stars versus planets, and the implications of SF on the formation of life-bearing planets, providing insight into the vast expanse of time in which this process occurs. This article aims to provide a clear and chronological understanding of SF, from the emergence of the first stars to the formation of life-supporting planets, and how it fits into the broader timeline of the universe. Moreover, we will delve into the implications of this framework on the origins of life and the second generation of life on Earth. By exploring the processes of SF and planet formation, we will uncover the underlying principles that govern the creation of life in the universe, which is the central theme of this article. Moreover, we will link these processes to the vast expanse of cosmic time, leading to the development of our innovative 'Tree of Life', which is based on uniform principles and spans the entire universe. We will conclude by highlighting the outstanding challenges and areas for further research in the field. Ultimately, we hope to inspire researchers from various fields to investigate the incredible story of the creation of life in the universe. This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under significant uncertainty. We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels in the standard L1 framework. Novel contributions involve addressing the issue of non-differentiable velocities with discrete objects and a bounded domain subject to inflows and outflows. Employing a Lagrangian perspective, we establish that solutions exist and are unique and define a notion of weak solutions. Furthermore, we prove that the flow is continuous with respect to time, and also with respect to the initial condition. However, due to generally non-differentiable velocities, these refined regularity results only hold under carefully constructed semi-norms adapted from the standard norm. In general, the solution is not continuous with respect to any standard norm on the space of measures. To address the issue of zero inventory levels as the primary challenge, we propose an iterative method of computing approximate equilibrium states with positive inventory levels. Assuming that a zero inventory equilibrium state exists and is unique, we establish that the fixed points of the iterative method form a compact subset of the space of measures. Consequently, by employing a homotopy theorem, we prove that the existence or non-existence of a zero inventory equilibrium state can be determined by examining the topological properties of a corresponding functional space. Finally, based on this characterization, we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of a zero inventory equilibrium state in the standard L1 framework. Notably, these conditions are not merely necessary but also sufficient for the transition from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels. The characterization of equilibrium states also enables the computation of approximate equilibrium states with positive inventory levels and, in particular, we establish that solutions with positive inventory levels can be obtained when the initial condition has a sufficiently large total amount of work in progress relative to the average workload in the system. By analyzing a simplified model for complex semiconductor production lines with zero inventory levels, we establish a condition for the existence of equilibrium states in the standard L1 framework. This condition is non-trivial and is based on the characteristics of the inflows and outflows processes. When the average rate of inflows is greater than the average rate of outflows, solutions converge to the equilibrium state in the standard L1 framework. Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem when devices with limited capabilities must perform real-time analysis on incoming data streams, a common issue in home users, small businesses, or organizations with limited resources. A novel approach, known as B4C Cyber Security, involves using a binary classifier to identify suspicious activities and a specialized AI method, the DenseNet, accurate enough for image recognition but resource-efficient, to confirm attacks once anomalies are detected. By combining these systems, we demonstrate that precise attack detection is achievable with limited computational resources, meeting real-time requirements, and outperforming existing models in terms of accuracy when evaluated using multiple metrics. Furthermore, we introduce a pioneering dataset that addresses the shortage of cybersecurity data available for machine learning, specifically developing and releasing a dataset of cyberattack images to support future research in this domain. This groundbreaking research is an essential first step towards data-driven innovations in the cybersecurity field. Moreover, this work has been implemented as an open-source tool, accessible to home users, small businesses, or organizations for free, enabling them to integrate cyberattack detection using the B4C Cyber Security system. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, is provided to support and enhance the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. A potential application of this technology is the creation of undetectable electronic camouflage that mimics asymmetrical biological motion, holding potential for vehicular applications. Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations. Furthermore, we examined the potential for future quantum processors to surpass current capabilities. Despite some limitations of classical solvers being overcome by hybrid approaches, future quantum processors are expected to yield significantly better results, thereby enabling the efficient optimization of power networks using quantum computing technology.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects with diverse size and mass, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved by data-driven methods of automated physics discovery. It's particularly demonstrated that noise from measurements and secondary physical mechanisms such as complex drag forces, can mask the law of gravity, thus leading to incorrect model development. Utilizing the SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) method, which involves the use of real-world and simulated trajectory measurements, it's illustrated how the assumption that each object is governed by a similar physical law can increase the stability of learned models, although significant discrepancies between predictions and observations persist, primarily due to the intricacies of drag dynamics. This research shows that employing ML/AI in isolation will often be insufficient for accurately inferring universal physical laws and highlights the necessity for further modifications. Possible avenues for further research include incorporating direction from theoretical models, using multi-faceted data that's more informative, and combining measurements from various types of experiments. This study also points to a potential new benefit: by using data-driven methods to improve our understanding of the falling motion, it's possible to develop more precise and generalizable models of the gravitational force, which could have important implications for fundamental physics. Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a 
semi-numerical technique using differential equations with specific boundaries 
at unique points to solve these complex equations with high accuracy. A 
high-precision numerical method generates pole singularities and asymptotic 
regions through a set of master functions, providing a detailed explanation of 
this approach and its potential applications. Specifically, it examines the 
three-loop corrections to electroweak and mixed electroweak-QCD processes, 
propagation integrals, and polygonal boxes to assess the proposed method's 
efficiency and accuracy. The authors also present an example of a four-loop 
correction to a single self-energy diagram, showcasing the method's ability 
to tackle the most complex calculations. The approach can be found in the 
publicly available package EPIC, and the authors estimate it would take around 
twenty years of CRAY-1A processing time to compute a four-loop correction 
using this method. The authors discuss the potential of the semi-numerical 
technique and its implications for the future of particle physics calculations. 
The approach has the potential to efficiently handle the most complex 
two-loop corrections in the near future and is within reach of being 
accurate enough for single-particle calculations at the two-loop level now. 
In the near future, it may also be able to handle two-loop corrections to 
polygonal boxes and even the simple three-loop corrections to certain 
scattering processes. The authors predict that the semi-numerical technique 
will play a crucial role in the future of particle physics calculations. The

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would rather switch to be in a different pairing together. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where large numbers of stable matchings could coexist. Furthermore, we identified a condition under which all stable matchings result in the same total value: instances with symmetric valuations. Additionally, the problem of finding the largest total value stable matching in the worst case scenario was investigated, showing that numbers close to half of the total value could be achieved. Lastly, we looked into finding the most efficient stable matchings in terms of total value when allowing agent rankings to change, which was shown to be an unsolvable problem with no established standard solution. On the other hand, we were able to identify a reliable method for determining the most efficient stable matchings in the most constrained scenario where the rankings of two agents can change. These findings contribute to our understanding of the Stable Roommates problem involving complex valuations and dynamic agent preferences. We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, forming a subclass where distances are naturally established through embeddings in fixed scale. The representability of a cloud in its "natural form" as a subset of a geodesic space, rather than an arbitrarily embedded space, motivates our investigation. Our work focuses on determining the closure of clouds under the Gromov--Hausdorff distance, thereby establishing their geometric nature. The closure is found to be the class of all metric spaces with bounded distances, expressed in equivalent form to the class of spaces with bounded $\varepsilon$-isometries. The study of clouds is a part of broader efforts to classify metric spaces according to their structural properties. The methodical examination of clouds contributes to classification by distinguishing spaces with differing structural properties, such as those with bounded distances versus those with bounded diameters. The closure of clouds is also related to the concept of functorial representations, specifically the closure of the class of spaces with functorial embeddings, where the metric maps between these spaces are distortions of isometric embeddings. The nature of clouds also bears comparison to the concept of "clouds of transformations," specifically the class of all metric spaces formed by combining translations of a geodesic space, where the metric on the space is induced by the translations' diameters. The study of these clouds, where the metric is determined by the distances between the translations' areas of operation, is distinct from the closure of clouds, with an example illustrating their difference. Finally, the closure of clouds is found to be distinct from the class of spaces that can be expressed as subsets of geodesic spaces, where the metric is determined by distances along shortest paths. These investigations into the closure of clouds, a subclass of metric spaces, contribute to the classification of metric spaces, specific and general. The class of spaces with functorial embeddings, where the metric maps between these spaces are distortions of isometric embeddings, is an especially notable candidate for a structurally natural classification system. In pursuit of this goal, it is proposed that the closure of clouds, a subclass of all metric spaces, might serve as a natural and structurally important class of spaces, essential for understanding the nature of metric spaces, specific and general. The study of this class of spaces, where the metric is determined by distances along shortest paths, is distinct from the classification of clouds, an observation contributing to the broader goal

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially rapid correction of single-qubit errors to prevent spreading and the development of 'holes.' In this research, a hybrid approach combining a maximum a posteriori decoding method and a novel low-density parity-check decoder is presented to efficiently decode the surface code in the presence of arbitrary mixed-density matrix states resulting from multiple gate operations gone wrong. Furthermore, the research reveals that the surface code can correct faults from approximately 5-7 years ahead of predictions based on the failure rate of qubits as per the noise-free quantum circuit adjacency matrix. The proposed decoding framework boasts an impressive capability to correct faults at an astonishing rate of of 10^N, where N represents the total number of qubits in the code. The presented work marks a significant advancement in the field of topological error correction, indicating that the surface code may be more resilient to noise than anticipated. The research is expected to open new avenues in the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing. The presented topological error correction approach is versatile and can be adapted for use in various quantum circuits beyond the surface code, thereby finding extensive applications in quantum computing. A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the Rich Feature Construction (RFC) algorithm, also known as Bonsai, which comprises a sequence of iterative training episodes. The algorithm is comprised of discovery episodes where a set of synthetic data points are generated outside the support of the current model, and exploration episodes where the model is trained on these points in an attempt to generalize to the outside region. 

It has been observed that the convergence of the model's performance on the outside region often plateau's before the convergence of the model's performance on the support data. This suggests that the model has achieved rich representations that can be utilized for optimized performance, even when the model is not perfectly accurate. 

Using the robust feature set, we introduce a detection method known as Bonsai Det, which is comprised of two detection metrics. The first detects the synthetic data points and provides hard negative samples for the detection model, while the second uses the rich representations to directly generalize to the unseen data points. 

The Bonsai Det detection method is versatile and can be applied to a variety of deep learning models in two stages. Firstly, the model parameters are frozen, and the rich representation is generated. Secondly, a new detection model is trained on the support data, utilizing the rich representation as a fixed feature set. 

Using Bonsai Det on the MiniImagenet, CUB, and Fashionpedia datasets, we achieve improved results in comparison to the Deep Consistent Learning methods. Furthermore, we observe an improvement in generalization performance when the model is initialized using the robust feature set, in comparison to standard initialization methods. This suggests that the rich representation is beneficial even when the model is not perfectly accurate. 

We hope that the proposed approach and algorithms will serve as a benchmark for deep learning research in handling out-of-distribution scenarios.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may establish a limit comparable to past predictions made for LBNE. We visualize these results for each neutrino type – electron, muon, and tau – indicating that DUNE has a promising capacity to explore previously unexplored areas of sterile neutrino parameter space before the SHiP experiment joins similar research initiatives. Generally, we discover that enhancing the DUNE Far Detector's size could significantly improve their search for sterile neutrinos. Moreover, we identify two significant factors that influence DUNE's ability to discover sterile neutrinos: the accuracy of its neutrino spectrum measurement and the number of neutral hadrons produced within the detector; both requirements must be met to discover these neutrinos effectively. Finally, we determine that improving the precision of the DUNE Far Detector's neutrino spectrum could be accomplished by incorporating an additional 2.5 cm of Water RUC around the detector without substantially increasing its cost. Conversely, intensifying efforts to precisely measure the neutrino spectrum at the Near Detector might be necessary to reach the required level of precision for optimum sterile neutrino discovery. Nevertheless, enhancing the DUNE Far Detector's size remains the primary method to improve its sterile neutrino search capabilities.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively address potential biases stemming from within-study similarities. However, these estimators may produce inflated results, including reduced significance and broader confidence intervals, especially in cases where the number of studies is small.  This paper presents two novel estimators designed to address within-study correlations and provide accurate results, even with limited studies. The first estimator incorporates within-study variance estimations in a weighted manner, while the second builds upon a hierarchical model to quantify between and within-study variances. Both proposals are evaluated in scenarios involving both continuous and binary effect sizes.  The proposed approaches successfully minimized errors in estimations of variance components, effectively addressing issues with biased variance estimators. Additionally, a simulation study revealed that our estimators outperformed existing ones, particularly in small-sample scenarios, by accurately estimating variances and maintaining required asymptotic properties. The method's efficacy is also demonstrated through numerical examples comprising two real-world studies. Investigating the source of radiation energy in the vicinity of the event horizon in black holes is crucial for understanding the Unruh/Hawking evaporation process. To accomplish this, we examine particle creation by a thermal antiparticle in the vicinity of the event horizon. Our findings indicate that this source is initially comprised of particles generated from the negative energy condensate opposite to the horizon, which is then counteracted by a pair produced in succession. We also determine that the energy associated with particle creation is extracted from this condensate. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed solution involves creating memory images, which serve as reference points to determine whether data integrity has been preserved. Researchers have developed a new tool to support this method, testing its efficacy with applications using non-volatile memory and verifying its effectiveness on several critical scientific benchmarks. Our testing has revealed that this method is both accurate and efficient, as demonstrated by its near-linear time complexity and minimal overhead. Our experiments have shown that this method's efficiency is comparable to or better than existing techniques at preserving data integrity. Further details about this research, as well as the method's implementation, can be found at https://github.com/UniversityOfNewMexico/NVMPA. This research introduces a novel set of systematic organizational structures, referred to as information hierarchies, specifically designed to organize intricate real-world data. We contend that such ordered representations are widespread yet often difficult to learn, requiring specialized teaching methods. We have developed a new educational approach, Information Hierarchy Construction (IHC), comprising 15 sequential tasks spanning 20 weeks, tailored for teaching university students. Our IHC curriculum is comprehensive, covering fundamental computer science concepts, data representation, and problem-solving strategies, through the gradual introduction of 10 core concepts, each building on the previous to facilitate seamless learning. Our results from two consecutive offerings of the IHC course to 30 students demonstrate that with proper instruction, students can effectively organize complex data using hierarchical structures, even in the absence of automatic organization tools. Furthermore, course evaluations indicate a strong desire for IHC to be incorporated into the university's curriculum. We have developed an open-source course platform, including teaching materials, available at https://ihc.cs.unm.edu/, to make the course accessible to anyone wishing to teach it. Our research also yields a valuable resource of more than 4000 lines of code, suitable for open-source contributions. A collaborative repository has been established at https://github.com/CSUNM-IHC for this purpose. We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct regions were identified within the non-hierarchical phase space, characterized by distinct statistical properties and patterns, and an extensive analysis on the boundaries between these regions is presented. Moreover, we measured the escape probabilities and obtained clear trends in all four areas. Our research confirms that the phase space structure is independent of mass and a detailed theoretical model can predict escape probabilities with high accuracy. Based on these results, we propose an advanced method to calculate whole phase space escape probabilities. Finally, we compared our findings with observations from the local galaxy and discussed how they relate to the hierarchy problem in cosmology. This research provides substantial statistical information on three-body systems that can be utilized for various applications in the future. We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings. 
Next, we develop a system for representing predicates in continuous logic as subobjects within the category of complete metric spaces and uniform mappings. 
Finally, we demonstrate that the resulting arrangement of predicates satisfies the requirements necessary to formulate a first-order logic whose models can be related through a hyperdoctrine. 
This relationship enables us to explore a range of questions concerning the continuity semantics of first-order logic.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. The proposed method
has been tested using multiple benchmark applications and its effectiveness in
isolating system changes has been confirmed through a comparative analysis. By
introducing an advanced data analysis technique to the field of software testing,
we aim to streamline the process of identifying system modifications and
improve tester productivity. Furthermore, we examine the computational complexity
of the proposed method and explore potential avenues for further optimization. 
Additionally, we provide a fully functional implementation of the proposed technique
to facilitate replication and testing with various types of system modifications. 
Ultimately, we aim to contribute this approach to the SEToolKit collection of
useful software testing methods. 
SEToolKit is an initiative that includes various recognized techniques in
the field and is known for providing reliable tools to streamline software
development and testing. 

Keywords: Shared Memory Parallelism, Software Testing, Regression Testing, SVD,

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the incorporation of Ecological Momentary Assessment records significantly increases the recall of the model in predicting suicidal ideation, from 48.13% using Electronic Health Record data alone to 67.78%. Furthermore, the proposed method offers enhanced interpretability through dimensionality reduction in the latent space and medical feature analysis. The advantage of this method lies in its ability to make predictions ahead of time, yielding a positive Lift value in predicting suicidal ideation up to 7 days in advance. The model's performance in predicting suicidal ideation is evaluated using various performance metrics and is compared to the baseline using Area under the ROC curve with a significant boost in accuracy. All evaluations were conducted using Statistical software R version 3.6.2 and Python 3.7.4 with deep learning libraries Tensorflow and Keras. The code and data used in this study are available for public access at https://github.com/alkhateeb/Deep_Sea.git. Additionally, the data used in this research is available at https://mimhs.cmu.edu/index.php/index/main/project_info/54. As of this paper's submission, the code is still available but the data is subject to change.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present within compact stars like neutron stars and white dwarfs, are investigated.  The study focuses on the behavior of sound velocity in dense matter as density increments, whether due to degeneracy pressure or other causal fluids, and whether pure energy fluids, assuming an equation of state that is independently extracted from first principles.  Computational calculations demonstrate that in dense matter, sound velocity does not exceed the Conformal limit, specifically not exceeding 0.5c at 5 times nuclear saturation density.  The study further examines other physical properties in dense matter, including adiabatic index, compressional wave propagation, and causal propagation speed, all of which align with theoretical constraints.  Consequently, the derived equation of state is suitable for describing compact stars and white dwarfs, yielding consistent mass and radius results for neutron stars as well as appropriate values for the specific energy, surface gravity, gravitational radius, causal speed, and adiabatic index of these objects within theoretical uncertainties.  The study also derives analytical relations for white dwarf stars based on assumed constant Gravitational Constant and Atomic Weight, allowing for the derivation of measurable properties such as mass, radius, lifetime, causal speed, and adiabatic index of white dwarfs as functions of central density, and specifically that for neutron star candidates as 1.25-1.44 solar masses, its radius varies between 10.5 and 12.9 km.  The study further uses observed data on compact stars and white dwarfs to determine the possible range for causality speed in dense matter, specifically between 0.297c and 0.485c at 5 times nuclear saturation density, and specifically that for neutron star candidates as 0.301c to 0.478c.  The study also derives analytical relations for sound speed in compact stars and white dwarfs as functions of mass, radius, and specific energy within specified uncertainties.  The study finally discusses the role of sound speed in dense matter in determining the physical properties of compact stars and white dwarfs within their respective ranges.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters. Additionally, U galaxies are more likely to contain supermassive black holes. The findings of our study paint a more comprehensive picture of U galaxies, shedding light on their origins and connections to other galaxy subtypes. Our data also form the basis for a catalogue of U galaxies, which will serve as a reference for future research. The complete catalogue is accessible at https://uwarpedgalaxies.github.io/. Our binary classification tool is available at https://uwarped-galaxies.github.io/classifier/, along with short videos demonstrating U galaxies at https://uwarpedgalaxies.github.io/videos/. Our data and analysis are open to the public, can be accessed via https://github.com/uwarped-galaxies. Our code is also available at https://uwarped-galaxies.github.io/code/. In this study, we present a novel approach to classifying galaxies based on their morphology and structure, which we hope will stimulate the exploration of U galaxies and their diverse properties through further observations and simulations. Our classification framework is designed to be dynamic, to adapt to any new data that may become available in the future, and to be used in conjunction with existing datasets. Our methodology is tailored to tackle challenges posed by sparse and incomplete data. Our open-source project can be found at https://uwarped-galaxies.github.io/. Our research primarily focused on explaining the presence of U galaxies within groups and clusters, as well as their connection to 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through RPS. Our findings also shed light on the potential relationship between U galaxies and galactic wars, as well as the possibility of U galaxies being a byproduct of galaxy interactions or collisions. Our data are consistent with the notion that RPS could be a significant factor contributing to the number of U galaxies

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Additionally, this work includes a detailed proof of a conjecture initially proposed by Zhong and Miao, involving harmonic functions and their growth on manifolds with negative complex sectional curvature. Furthermore, this work includes an analysis of the growth of one-dimensional Jacobi fields along a geodesic ray within these manifolds. We have derived sharp estimates for harmonic functions on Ricci solitons with a constant scalar curvature, as well as harmonic functions on manifolds with a negative complex sectional curvature. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within molecular fluids. Instead, the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation by Landau and Lifschitz provides a more accurate description. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018). Furthermore, this research builds on previous studies (Messen, 2018; Bezroun et al., 2019) to establish a correspondence between operational probabilistic semantics and denotational views, while improving on their results by achieving a sufficient operational interpretation that facilitates reasoning about while providing a framework for verifying probabilistic code. This research is further extended to consider a higher-level functional programming language with recursive types and abstract data types. The resulting operational and denotational interpretations are parameterised over types and provide a useful tool for proving correctness of code translations between these two views. Utilizing a custom version of Coq, we have formally proved all key properties outlined in this research, ensuring the soundness of our definitions and the adequacy theorem. The full verification can be accessed at https://z-iwata.github.io/stlc/2021/07/28/stlc-verification.html. The underlying code has also been submitted to the Coq official repository at https://coqofficial.repository.uqam.ca/stlc. The operational interpretation is then used to demonstrate the correctness of a probabilistic Curry-Howard correspondence, involving a correspondence between proof normalization and the ability to construct a successful strategy in a probabilistic game. The full details of this investigation can be found in an accompanying paper (Bezroun et al., 2021). Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions on various discussion types and projects. We then introduce and demonstrate two effective techniques - data enrichment and project adaptation - that enhance design mining's reliability and adaptability across different datasets, achieving a satisfactory classification rate of 0.88 within a dataset and 0.80 across different datasets. Additionally, we explore three practical applications of design mining in real-world scenarios. While design mining has been primarily associated with its potential in improving API documentation, this paper highlights its broader contributions to design-based discussions within software development. By providing design mining as an invaluable tool for various software design-related discussions, this paper facilitates the adoption of this technique in a broader range of design-related contexts, promoting its utilization in practical scenarios. Empirical evidence supporting the proposed approaches is provided through the use of two large datasets containing over 41M discussions - the Stack Overflow Q&A platform and the GitHub bug-tracking platform. This research was conducted using a rigorous scientific methodology and is made accessible through an executable technical report. All associated data and models are freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/MDIT-SE/design-mining, providing a reproducible foundation for future design mining research. Nonetheless, this field still necessitates further advancements in both its theoretical foundation and practical applications to fully harness its potential in improving our understanding of software design through discussion mining. This research seeks to bridge the current gap between the existing theory and its practical utilization in real-world contexts, aiming to stimulate future research on design mining to yield more substantial practical outcomes. To this end, this paper is written in accordance with the Instruction for authors at https://mdit-se.github.io/2021/README.html, aiming to convey the design mining research's contributions, limitations, and future prospects to a broad audience within the software engineering community. To achieve this objective, this research is presented as a sequence of discussions involving the exploration of current design mining methods' shortcomings and the introduction of revised approaches - data enrichment and project adaptation - to improve the reliability and adaptability of design mining, while also highlighting its practical applications and future prospects within the software engineering field, ultimately concluding with an enlarged research agenda at https://github.com/MDIT-SE/design

Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid/supersolid state.
Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate" component.
Consequently, it is anticipated that exotic particles that could explain dark matter will not be detected at the LHC. Moreover, it is suggested that the de Sitter horizon associated with holographic dark energy acts as a complete absorber for static detectors, given its infinite redshift effect. As a natural outcome, it is proposed that the universe's acceleration will slow and eventually cease, likely prior to the predicted timing based on the Lambda-CDM model.
Additionally, it is hypothesized that the universe's matter density initially followed a non-thermal distribution, characterized by negative pressure, which would have hindered galaxy formation. Consequently, it is suggested that early universe reionization was facilitated by "beaded" matter structures." These hypotheses are examined in the context of existing observational data, with particular emphasis on the universe's gravitational lensing effects, which is found to support the model's description of dark energy and dark matter. As an alternative to the Lambda-CDM model, this "BEADS" scenario may represent a viable description of the universe's evolution. The model is found to be consistent with a scenario in which the information paradigms "holography" and "maximal entropy" are intertwined. Consequently, it is anticipated that the information content of gravity and dark energy states could be tapped in the future, with dark matter states remaining inaccessible. Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure enables the use of a smoother model. The optimal solution to the original problem is then obtained by applying a smoother optimization method on the new model. In this study, we focus on discovering the proximal gradient method's (PGM) impact on developing a smoother model for nonsmooth loss functions. By analyzing PGM's trajectories, we determine the type of structure that is revealed and provide specific conditions under which a smoother model can be established for various generic nonsmooth loss functions. Moreover, we illustrate that, even when the parameters are kept fixed, PGM's proximal points exhibit a negative semi-definite pattern in their Hessian matrices. The analysis is then narrowed down to nonconvex least squares problems, and we show that PGM's proximal points reveal a sparse pattern in their Hessians, enabling a smoother model based on group lasso. The negative spare of Hessian patterns' accuracy is assessed through numerical experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world data. The study ultimately leads to the development of BSM, an optimization method that applies a smoother model using the Curtis-Hammerle algorithm and yields an optimal solution, while providing a lower bound on the loss function's value. The superiority of BSM over PGM and other methods is evaluated using numerical experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world data. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/krzysztof-rudolf/BSM. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations within the exact same environment in which the imitation policy is to be learned.  However, in many scenarios, the available expertise is restricted to trajectories in a different form (e.g., high-dimensional action spaces, sparse or delayed rewards, or stochastic environments).  We investigate the imitation learning problem under these difficult exploration conditions, focusing on three specific cases.  A key contribution is the introduction of a novel method called Reverse Learning, which seamlessly integrates online learning from expert demonstrations in varying environments.  The approach has been rigorously tested on multiple difficult domains, including those with complex rewards and dynamic system interactions, resulting in highly effective imitation.  The developed framework also facilitates the transfer of expertise across diverse task settings, and its applicability is demonstrated in the domain of robotic learning, specifically through the imitation of complex human joint movements.  The associated source code is available at https://github.com/alexrame/ReverseLearning.  Evaluation experiments indicate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art imitation and reinforcement learning techniques on multiple challenging tasks, including a sophisticated 10DoF robotic joint manipulation task, in which the demonstrated actions are significantly easier to replicate when performed by a neural network trained using Reverse Learning.  The observed success of our method is attributed to its ability to generate informative simulated rewards without the need for optimal reward function design.  The research highlights key challenges in imitation learning from varied task settings and provides insights into the critical conditions under which expertise can be effectively transferred across different exploration conditions.  Furthermore, the integration of our approach with a novel reinforcement learning technique results in improved performance, and the associated source code is available at https://github.com/alexrame/ReverseLearning.  The research highlights the critical importance of domain expertise in achieving successful task completion and illustrates the potential of our approach in facilitating the discovery of novel tasks through alteration of existing task settings. A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in the accretion disk - whether they will merge or remain separate. We concentrate on how the initial mass of these secondary protostars changes in response to an upscaling of the magnetic field in their surroundings. Through the use of high-resolution simulations of magnetohydrodynamics, focused on the inner disk regions, we find that significant increases in the initial mass of these protostars are possible in environments with weak magnetic influences. However, in environments where magnetic forces are strong, the initial mass of the protostars remains low. We attribute these results to the differing effects that the magnetic field has on the accretion of surrounding material in these contexts. In environments with weak magnetic influences, the magnetic field allows for an upscaling of the initial mass of the secondary protostar through the acceleration of nearby material, while in environments with strong magnetic influences, the magnetic field limits this accretion and results in a lower initial mass. However, in both scenarios, the initial mass of the protostar is ultimately determined by a non-ideal process. In environments with weak magnetic influences, this process is the upscaling due to ambipolar diffusion, while in environments with strong magnetic influences, this process is the tidal disruption of the protostar by the binary companion through viscous instability. In the context of our model, increases in the initial mass of the protostar in environments with weak magnetic influences are accompanied by a corresponding decrease in the final mass of the binary companion, suggesting that a minimum mass threshold must exist below which secondary protostars are unable to accrete sufficient material to follow the standard benchmark path of first star formation. In environments with strong magnetic influences, this threshold is determined by the balance between ambipolar diffusion and viscous instability, resulting in a higher initial mass of the protostar in this scenario. In the event that secondary protostars are unable to accrete sufficient material to follow the standard benchmark path of first star formation, we find that a maximum mass cutoff and a rapid decline in the initial mass function should exist at the threshold, potentially resulting in a distinctive 'dip' in the mass function at this point. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  More broadly, the data highlights the potential for court-ordered mental health treatment to reduce recidivism and possibly decrease costs associated with future crime, suggesting judicial systems might boost public safety through strategic deployment of mental health resources.  Further research is needed to confirm these findings and explore specific treatment types that are most effective.  An accompanying online document contains additional analysis not included in this document but is available at http://www.irss.unc.edu/.  The document includes variations of the specified time frame as well as a comparison of our results to those in the national study by Eisenberg, Lotke, and Vogel (1977) who also analyzed the connection between probation, mental health treatment, and future crime.  An analysis of our data across different time frames discloses that the reduction in future crime seen in our study is more pronounced than what was seen in the national study but occurs later.  Additionally, the national study discovered an inverse relationship between the probability of future crime and the probability of receiving mental health treatment as part of their probation, contradicting our findings and highlighting the need for further investigation into this discrepancy. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, as well as demonstrates the creation of an optimization problem to minimize privacy concessions while maintaining data utility for dependent records under a defined threshold. Our results show that OSDP is capable of supporting total privacy breaches up to $e^{-\omega(d^2)}$, where $\omega(d)$ tends to zero as $d$ grows large, even in scenarios with insignificant dependencies. When dependencies are considered insignificant, the framework yields an almost identical recurrence relation to that of fully dependent data with increased efficiency. To facilitate practical use, an open-source implementation has been developed under the name PrivOS. Through experiments with real-world data, we showcase the effectiveness of PrivOS by achieving considerable data utility improvements amounting to $2.5\times$ to $3.5\cdot e$ over the conventional differential privacy approaches. The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where advanced technologies generate vast amounts of data over extended periods of time. This trend is exacerbated by the rapid increase in processing power, resulting in data volumes that surpass the capacity of a single computer processor. In response, researchers have developed high-performance approaches to analyze time-stamped data in parallel environments. This paper introduces a novel parallel algorithm for analyzing time-stamped data using multi-core processors, where each core interprets data on a single data acquisition unit. The algorithm leverages a queue-based method to manage data synchronization and parallel processing. This innovative approach minimizes communication overhead between cores and ensures that data from various units are synchronized. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a practical application in experimental physics, where it achieves significant speedups under realistic conditions. For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 88% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. We publicly release the VICTOR implementation at https://github.com/stevejpapad/Visual-InCompatibility-Transformer. Additionally, an accompanying video can be found at https://youtu.be/6QcMfMvTPgE. The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility of GaN, revealing that aligning GaN under uniaxial compressive strain by matching it to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ inorganic materials flips the order of the heavy and light hole bands, resulting in a reduced hole mass along the compression axis. Consequently, our calculations indicate that matching GaN to ZnGeN$_2$ or MgSiN$_2$ boosts its room temperature hole mobility by 50% and 260%, respectively, when compared to strain-free GaN. Furthermore, our study on the strain-mobility trends discloses a nonlinear correlation. To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods. Our method is then integrated into two new algorithms for online policy updates, and through simulations, we verified that they converge faster than the existing algorithms. We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We show that $P$ can be approximated in Hilbert-Schmidt operations by finite rank operators with accuracy $o(N^{-1/d} \log N^{-1})$. To achieve this, we Resolvent Estimation method utilizes a non-parametric resolvent operator $(I - P^T P)^{-1}$ and exploit the properties of conditional expectation as a smoothing operator. Furthermore, we show that $P$ can be approximated in Hilbert-Schmidt operations with accuracy $o(N^{-1/2} \log N^{-1/2})$ when $X$ and $Y$ are i.i.d. random variables. To compute the approximations, we only need the first two moments of the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$. Our results are illustrated with numerical simulations in the finite dimensional setting. Ultimately, our paper provides a foundation for developing statistical approximation theory for a broad category of integral operators. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. Our method is informed by the techniques of signal processing and past work in graph embeddings. Our findings indicate that SpliMe outperforms existing temporal KGE methods, and in addition, we identify issues with how static model performance on temporal data is typically evaluated, and provide two solutions to address these problems. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/jase-clarkson/SpliMe.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold significant value for people working in operator algebras as well as topological dynamical systems. Moreover, we establish that the first Hochschild cohomology group for the full C*-algebra of a graph is zero when the graph meets two specific criteria, providing a potential approach to determine if it is invariant under Morita equivalence. This new framework provides a new context in which to study Morita equivalence and topological dynamical systems. Finally, we establish a bivariant Kazhdan's property (T) for the complete C*-algebra of a graph, which satisfies two specific conditions, opening up possibilities for further research in the field of topological dynamical systems.
