The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned. In contrast, other networks it was compared to were unable to do so. Additionally, our study found that the ESBN's module structure is essentially a weighted graph that represents the relationships between items and their selectors, and this graph can be used to explain the AI's decision-making processes. To demonstrate its versatility, we tested our ESBN in a more realistic scenario - a robotic arm that has to gather specified items based on their colors - and successfully replicated the results in a real-world setting. In conclusion, our study highlights the effectiveness of the ESBN network in simulating the cognitive abilities of animals and, potentially, humans. It can be used to understand how we learn and, also, how we can make robots learn. Furthermore, the research on the ESBN's module structure may provide insights that can be applied to improving the performance of traditional neural networks. In terms of its applications, we envision the ESBN-based model to be useful in settings where we need to make sense out of sequential data and, also, in environments where we have to explain the decision-making processes behind our actions. In order to achieve this, we propose an explanation mechanism known as the 'why' module that uses the ESBN's graph to determine the items that contributed to the AI's decisions. By testing this 'why' module in the robot arm task - where it has to select specified items - we successfully demonstrated its efficacy and also, the accuracy of the ESBN-based model in understanding the AI's decision-making processes. In conclusion, our study on the ESBN-based model provides a powerful tool in simulating the cognitive abilities of animals and, also, humans, and this can lead to developing robots that think and learn in a similar way. Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters suggest the membership of an element in a set and could contain errors. A potential alternative is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less memory and processes items faster. This paper explores ways to enhance the efficiency of Bloom filters by utilizing parallel processing, specifically on multicore systems, and introduces the pBloom filter, an implementation of a Bloom filter designed for multicore architectures. In comparison to standard Bloom filters, the pBloom filter exhibits reduced false positives and scales better with available cores. Additionally, the authors introduce a new filter, the parallel Bloom filter with hash values (pBloomH), which minimizes false positives and scales well. A key difference between this new filter and pBloom is that it calculates hash values in advance, allowing multiple filters to share the same hash table. This contributes to significant space savings. An open-source implementation of the authors' suggestions confirms the theoretical advantages of these new suggestions. This new framework offers adaptability and can easily replace the standard Bloom filter and the cuckoo filter. In particular, the pBloomH is suggested as a preferable option. Experimental results indicate the potential for substantial space reductions when using the pBloomH, specifically with many items, could save up to 4 times less space. A full description of the code and data used in the study can be found at https://github.com/alealvar/parallel-bloom-filters. Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively. Additionally, our work touches on the relationship between the birational geometry of smooth projective varieties and the geometry of effective divisors on these varieties, as well as the connection between the geometric generality of divisors and their arithmetic generality. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which enables the server to safely aggregate secure data from diverse clients without exposure. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and preserves user data confidentiality. Notably, it achieves this without compromising performance, as it only incurs a minor computational overhead compared to standard FL methods. Our study also delves into the challenges associated with deploying this technique on mobile devices, identifying potential improvements for future research. As such, FLVoogd offers a versatile solution for real-world applications where robustness against malicious activity and data confidentiality are paramount. We successfully submitted the winning entry to the NeurIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through action-reward-time steps. The competition was part of The AI Driving Olympics (AI-DO), a series that fosters deep reinforcement learning advancements in autonomous driving. Building upon prior research by Pieter Abbeel's group at UC Berkeley, we tailored our training approach to suit the provided Deepracer environment. This involved creating simulated training data and fine-tuning an existing policy to meet the competition's criteria. The winning model was developed using PyTorch and Tensorforce deep reinforcement learning frameworks, and the results presented are based on the Standard Track benchmark. It is worth noting that the competition policies were constrained to have no prior knowledge of the terrain, checkpoints, or obstacles. The winning model achieved an 82% success rate in racing competitions. The associated code has been made available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/RobinBourret/deepracer-ai-do-challenge. The repository includes the required dependencies, model implementation, and configuration files that enabled our model to learn from simulated training data. The supporting information discusses variations of the baseline approach that were tested during the development process. The objective of sharing our research is to inspire contributions to open-source autonomous driving projects, as well as to provide useful resources for those looking to tackle similar challenges in the future. Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos. Furthermore, it proposes future research directions for tackling deepfake-related issues. Overall, this chapter aims to provide an in-depth overview of the deepfake technology for media.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate the feasibility of measuring the masses of large-radius planets with small H2/He envelopes using a novel transiting planetary observatory on the space-based platform Euclid, capable of precisely measuring the planetary density and radius, particularly for a target with a radius of 1.5 Ferdinand (to account for uncertainties) and a mass less than 6.5 times that of Earth. The observatory can be paired with a demission model that incorporates secondary indicators extracted from SpaCE Global Light Curve Spectroscopy, which provides valuable information to constrain the planet's atmospheric properties and help estimate the mass of its gaseous envelope, provided it has one. If a planet's mass is limited by its small-radius atmosphere, it can be paired with a radiative transfer model's atmospheric properties, which can estimate the depth of its liquid water ocean. These measurements will enable a detailed characterization of Mars and the temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets Atlas, Ventus, and Nyx, providing critical insights into planetary physics, atmospheric composition, and the building blocks of life in the solar system and beyond. For example, determining the ocean depth in the Ventus-like exoplanet will allow scientists to compare its habitability potential to that of Mars, while an ocean in the Nyx-like exoplanet will enable comparison with that of Earth. Ultimately, accurately characterizing the masses of large-radius planets with small H2/He envelopes using the Euclid observatory will provide critical constraints on theoretical models of planetary evolution and aggregation, which will help inform future space missions targeting temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets. Additionally, it will enable a detailed comparison of the habitability potential of Mars, the temperate sub-Neptune exoplanets Atlas, Ventus, and Nyx, and Earth.

Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability similar to that of symmetric Hopfield networks for spatial patterns. Furthermore, our study reveals the model's capability to efficiently acquire sequences of binary images and generate neural spike-train data. Our findings demonstrate that the model can successfully learn and reproduce temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability enhanced by the incorporation of temporal cues in the learning process. The model's performance in sequence learning is compared to that of the symmetric Hopfield network, revealing that MPN is capable of learning twice as many spatial patterns, along with an infinite number of temporal patterns, on account of its localized structure. The model's efficacy in generating spike-train data makes it a suitable candidate for the study of neural behavior in laboratory environments and for the development of neural algorithms. The model's theoretical framework has been implemented in a Python program, accessible at https://github.com/ProfAlp/GitHub/tree/main/MPN. The program includes versatile functions for the learning of temporal patterns and the production of spike-train data, as exemplified by the supplementary materials. The model can be extended for use in various applications such as the analysis of real neuronal data and the creation of neural algorithms inspired by biological neural networks. The model's broad applicability can be exemplified by its potential application in memory systems where sequential access to information is required. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted the limitations of modern Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models, particularly their lack of adaptability to unseen text instances during training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 316,385 scene text images sourced from various online resources, spanning across eight languages: English, German, Italian, French, Korean, Chinese, Arabic, and Russian.
Notably, the dataset contains a substantial number of formal text images, which poses a challenge to OCR models due to the presence of stylized, size-variable, and curved text.
The competition included distinct validation and testing sets to minimize bias and ensure a fair evaluation of the models' performance.
The proposed Out-Of-Vocabulary challenge benchmark aims to accelerate the development of more versatile scene text recognition models capable of effectively processing novel text instances. 
The competition's source code, dataset, and evaluation tools are freely accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Deshmukh-99/OOV_Benchmark. 
A comprehensive leaderboards can be found at: https://competitions.codalab.org/competitions/31314.

We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way's outer layers: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 systems. Our sophisticated computational model, designed to simulate galactic growth patterns, is based on exponential infall scenarios and allows for reliable fitting of these patterns. Our analysis led to the discovery of key differences in the timelines of these galaxies: GSE collapsed over a period of 1-4 billion years, with an infall timescale of 3.3 billion years, whereas Wukong/LMS-1 took 7-44 billion years to dissipate, with an infall timescale of 12.8 billion years. Additionally, our model showed distinct variations in the mass distribution of these galaxies at different stages, which correlated with their varying star formation rates. Our findings also pointed out an inconsistency in the predicted mass discrepancy for GSE by at least one order of magnitude, which might be attributed to an underestimation of the initial mass of this galaxy based on their simple computational model. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Additionally, our active learning method effectively prioritizes models that require more data to reach maximum accuracy. Both techniques can be applied broadly to other image recognition tasks where high-quality labeled data is scarce and labor-intensive to gather. Data sets used in this study are available at https://github.com/alekkowalczuk/selective_labeling. Our implementation of the approach can be accessed at https://github.com/alekkowalczuk/selective_labelingimplementation. The formation of an inept interface bond between europium sulfide (EuS) and indium arsenide (InAs) prevents the sulfide from fully combining with the arsenic, leading to/suggesting the potential for unconventional superconductivity and topological order. To explore the properties of novel materials, we utilized the density functional theory with hybrid functionals to investigate how the strength of inept bonds affects the electronic structures of various bonding configurations. By manipulating the inept bond by adjusting the distance between layers and twisting angles, we discovered novel states at the fusion of the EuS and InAs valence bands. Notably, weakly bound configurations exhibit higher energy states compared to strongly bound ones, two energy states near the fusion of the bands in comparison to a single state in a weakly bound configuration. Furthermore, weakly bound configurations exhibit larger Fermi velocities and topological orders, suggesting superior electrical conductivity and greater transport characteristics in these weakly bound layers. Our research identifies the potential for utilizing inept bonds to engineer novel properties in the materials, thereby providing new avenues to explore unconventional superconductors and topological materials. Lastly, our research suggests the need for further experimental investigation into the electrical transport properties of the EuS/InAs system.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic. By incorporating a modified version of Moschovakis's notion of safe recursion space, we establish a safe recursion scheme compatible with bounded $\Delta^1_2$-recursion, thereby gaining a stronger safe recursion theorem which remains true within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Delta^1_2$-recursion system. This safe recursion theorem is utilized to demonstrate Borel Wadge determinacy within the same system of second-order arithmetic. Additionally, a notion of analytic determinacy is introduced and shown to be attainable within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system, however it remains indemonstrably uncertain within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Delta^1_2$-recursion system. Lastly, a concept of second-order bounded arithmetic for finite sequences is introduced, allowing for the demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0^2$-recursion system and further leading to a safe recursion scheme and its application in demonstrating analytic determinacy within the same system. The safety of this recursion scheme remains indemonstrably uncertain within the $\text{ATR}_0^2$-recursion system. The conceptual framework introduced for the analysis of subsets of Baire space facilitates an exploration of possible arithmetic interpretations of Borel Wadge classes, leading to an open question regarding whether $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I recursion is sufficient for interpreting Borel Wadge determinacy on any level of Borel Wadge classes. A positive answer to this question would allow for an alternative, and perhaps more natural, demonstration of Loudeva and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. Moreover, this would enable a verification of Montalbán's conjecture that $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I recursion is sufficient for interpreting Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed three types of gravitational wave sources - binary black hole mergers with minimal spin, mergers involving spinny black holes and minimal-neutron-star binaries. Initially detected by the TESS satellite, the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, has been further confirmed using data from ground-based spectrographic equipment. Analysis of this data has shown that the exoplanet, which has an estimated mass roughly equivalent to that of Jupiter, likely formed through migration or by remaining in its original location rather than being formed by a specific high-energy migration mechanism. Further study found that the host star, which is approximately 10 billion years old, has a metal composition that deviates from a commonly recognized trend of metal-rich giant planets being formed around metal-rich host stars. Interestingly, this study found that both heavy and lightweight gas giants orbiting either warm or hot stars have higher-than-average metal compositions. TOI-5542b is a notable addition to studies of planetary composition due to its relatively cool temperature, which prevents it from expanding in size as a result of exposure to its star's heat. Moreover, this star is targeted in the NEPP program that plans to conduct follow-up spectroscopic observations with the Intermediate Large Binocular Telescope Aperture Spectrograph in 2024.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. Due to the variety of mathematical symbols and 162 possible combinations, segmentation proves particularly difficult. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characteristics, and we discover a significant variation in its spectrum as it passes through different phases. To understand this phenomenon, we apply a non-parametric spectral deconvolution technique, producing a breakdown of Nereid's spectrum into its underlying components. Utilizing grid-based Monte Carlo modeling, we find that these components are consistent with the features observed in other TNOs and can be attributed to various astronomical bodies with neutral-sloped spectra. By utilizing deconvolved spectra and phase-cross correlated analysis, we discover changing absorption band strengths of Nereid's surface features corresponding to different phases, indicating varying levels of tholins. Our model also reveals distinct opposing trends in the absorption features of Nereid's surface, suggesting the presence of two separate aqueous minerals. One of these minerals, likely a manganese oxide or hydroxide, is found to be unaffected by variations in band strength, while the other, identified as a ferric ferrous chloride, shows a strong correlation and may be responsible for surface feature variations in Nereid's composition. Our comprehensive analysis provides substantial evidence supporting a tholin-rich surface composition on Nereid, dominated by complex aqueous minerals, and suggests that these compounds cover approximately 80-90% of its surface. Our findings can be used to constrain models of Nereid's evolution, and we propose that this satellite has undergone extensive radiation-driven chemical evolution. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with low likelihoods, but current implementations are inconsistent when policies differ. We introduce a new pessimism principle framework and develop a compatible Bayesian learning method for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. The approach redefines Bayesians in an offline context and provides a universal solution by combining optimal policy search and offline data coverage issues using stochastic gradient ascent. Theoretical consistency arguments are presented, along with empirical performance comparisons showing our method's coverage and performance improvements. To study this unique phenomenon, we utilize a microscopic model consisting of a gapped fermionic system with pairwise electron interactions that give rise to a Meissner effect-like phenomenon. Applying a gauge field to the system reveals excitations with massless bosonic and massless fermionic characteristics. In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs (for RGB images) or three inputs (for RGB-D images) with a cross-attention mechanism, our framework leverages the rich information present in both RGB and depth features. This structure's simplicity and efficacy enable efficient extraction and fusion of contextual information. As shown by experimental results, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on various datasets in terms of multiple evaluation metrics. The associated code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/IndigoPurple/SAL-PDEP. Our paper also demonstrates that combining RGB and depth features yields superior performance over using RGB features alone for salient object detection. This is verified through extensive experiments using multiple metrics. The model's weights can be downloaded at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/SAL-PDEP. Our method exhibits efficient end-to-end training characteristics, with a receptive field of $157 \times 157$ and the ability to be trained for 20 epochs in under 10 minutes on a single NVIDIA 1080 Ti GPU. This structure's efficiency is another one of its notable advantages. Lastly, our method has been successfully applied to other related tasks, such as depth estimation and image matting. The details regarding our implementation can be found in the supplementary document. The paper's presentation is as follows. Section 1 introduces the problem and our proposed framework, while section 2 discusses the specific implementation details required to adapt our method for depth estimation and image matting. The experimental results are then presented in section 3, followed by the conclusion and future work in section 4. The additional experimental analysis and ablation study are presented in the appendix. The paper is organized as follows. The related work is discussed in section 2, followed by the proposed framework in section 3, the implementation details in section 4, the experimental results in section 5, the conclusion and future work in section 6, and the appendix with additional analyses.

In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored and several fundamental questions about the resulting sets of integers and fractions are answered. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem using a precise formula, by ascertaining if an integer, N, can be expressed as a division between two identical symmetrical numbers, A and B. Upon determining representability, we pinpoint an upper limit on the value of the smallest numerical component. We then prove that a certain set of numbers has a higher frequency of occurrence within this set, and establish a lower bound on the least possible value of N in representable quotients. Ultimately, we identify a condition to determine if an integer, N, can be expressed as a division between two distinct symmetrical numbers, A and B. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by photon statistics noise contribute to image blurring. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, thus enabling the restoration of sharp, accurate images. A related algorithm has been developed and demonstrated using real CT data scans. In addition to traditional total variation regularization methods, the proposed approach also explores alternative stabilization techniques and their applications in image restoration. A comprehensive evaluation of these regularization techniques is provided along with an examination of their effects on reconstructed images. Further research could involve using a restricted gradient descent method to optimize the proposed variational model. In the future, the developed method could be applied in CT imaging technologies to improve the image quality of dense materials, which currently pose a challenge. Additionally, the proposed approach may also be used in radiation therapy planning to create more accurate images of cancer cells. A future scope includes expanding the proposed method to dual-phase CT imaging techniques that involve injecting contrast agents with pharmacological properties that change over time. In conclusion, the proposed method offers a highly effective approach to image restoration in CT imaging applications. A future research could involve using a future data prediction method to reconstruct CT images, which could significantly reduce processing time. Moreover, the proposed method may also be used in CT imaging techniques that utilize iterative reconstruction methods to optimize image quality and reduce noise. A future research could also involve using machine learning algorithms to create sharp, accurate CT images using data-driven approaches. In addition to this, the proposed method may also be used as a denoising technique in other imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging. A future research could also involve using the proposed method in magnetic resonance tomography techniques that utilize magnetic fields to create accurate images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line segmentation. Thorough evaluation and analysis affirm the exceptional quality of the generated ciphers, matching state-of-the-art HTR performance on two distinct datasets. The proposed method's source code and generated datasets are freely accessible for public use. A detailed implementation guide and BPL model's description can be found at: https://github.com/GP-GP/bpl-based-htr-data-generation. Ultimately, this research facilitates breakthroughs in deciphering ciphers using limited resources and sets a new standard for generating realistic handwritten text. The developed program is anticipated to have a significant impact, leading to numerous applications in both natural and artificial handwriting systems. A key benefit of this approach is the flexibility to create unique, artificially shaped letters that closely resemble real ciphers. This capability is particularly useful in deciphering ciphers with limited known characters (as is the case with the Kottabos Inscription) or those that have been largely destroyed. To achieve this, this study employs a comprehensive style conversion procedure to produce ciphers that can be correctly recognized even when the training data is from a different writer or writing style. The program is highly efficient, producing a large number of synthetic lines per second on a single GPU (with a rate of 25 fps for the largest dataset). This study is the first to utilize Bayesian Program Learning for handwritten text recognition and hand-written text generation from just one sample per symbol. The developed program is also the first to apply BPL to generative tasks, outperforming traditional approaches. Moreover, this research confirms the feasibility of creating realistic handwritten text without line segmentation using a single annotated image per symbol. The developed program is highly versatile and can be utilized in various handwriting-related tasks, such as line segmentation, text recognition, and text generation. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to utilize Bayesian Program Learning for handwritten text recognition and handwritten text generation from just one sample per symbol. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. The presented research also focuses on measuring the Poisson's ratio of the straw wall for the NA62 spectrometer, with the ultimate goal of determining the minimum pre-tension required for the straw's structural stability. The instrument utilized for this study consists of dual load arms and an optical levers system, enabling the simultaneous measurement of both radial and lateral expansions of a strained, pressurized straw. The NA62 spectrometer's straw measurement campaign is documented, presenting the measured properties and preliminary outcomes that include a Poisson's ratio value of $6.8 \times 10^{-4}$ and a significant non-linear behavior evident from the strain-curvature relationship. In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal models, which represent entire environments through their duals. Focusing on the MARmax problem - identifying the maximum marginal probability when decision functions' probabilities towards any class exceed a certain threshold - our approach involves transforming the MARmax problem into a sequence of polynomial programming issues. Using this framework, we can analyze the optimal performance of decision functions within entire families, such as the family of all decision functions, and also those bounded by a certain complexity. Interestingly, we discovered that decision functions with the lowest complexity that solve the MARmax problem are also able to solve the lowest-complexity MARmax problem, and that this family includes, for example, decision functions with complexity equal to the number of non-empty inputs. Our proposed method is highly efficient, with a linear relationship to the number of inputs, and allows for analysis of decision functions with a restricted number of incorrect predictions. To further enhance decision functions' robustness, we proposed two classification methods based on credal networks, including a Bayesian approach that chooses the network with the highest probability for the target class, and a non-Bayesian approach that chooses the network with the lowest probability for the opposite class, and demonstrates their effectiveness in solving the MARmax problem for two real-world datasets. Our study provides a groundbreaking approach for classifying decision functions with a high level of certainty, and paves the way for application of this method in more complex learning tasks. By manipulating entanglement in this manner, it becomes possible to create polarization entanglement with an infinite number of degrees, a property that can be useful in further applications. This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log d) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for sequences of points in R^d, with d ≥ 2 dimensions. This surpasses previous lower bounds in the R^2 case, revealing a significant gap between the competitive ratio of online and offline algorithms in R^d for any d ≥ 2. Next, the authors introduce lower bounds for specific types of t-spanners, including those with their edges contained within a single plane, and those where the distance to their approximation ratio is independent of the points' positions. Finally, the authors consider the case of point sequences where the distance between any two points is at least ε, and establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-2)log n / log d) for any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm in R^d. Throughout the paper, the authors utilize techniques such as shattering, partitioning, and expected properties of spanning trees. Additionally, the authors construct sample points to tackle specific problems. The studies in this paper were performed both in R^d for d = 2, 3, 4, 5, and for any dimension d ≥ 2 in R^d where the distance between any two points is at least ε. The results in this paper can be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04210. A shorter version of this paper was presented at STOC'22. Specifically for the R^2 case, the authors found new lower bounds, building on prior work by Andersen et al. with a similar setting but distinct sequences. Furthermore, the authors established similar results in d = 3, 4, 5. In addition to these studies, the authors considered the case of point sequences in R^d where the distance between any two points is at least ε, and found new lower bounds for both (1+ε)-spanners and their 2-spanner counterparts. These studies are the first to explore online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. These results are presented in more detail in the associated technical report at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204

A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for delicate biological specimens or sensitive samples due to the inadequacy of available light-detecting capabilities and potential harm from light interaction. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a quantum imaging protocol that achieves resolution beyond the diffraction limit using twin-photon indistinguishability without the need for light sources or prior image reconstruction processes. Furthermore, we have implemented and tested this approach using a Michelson interferometer with a single-pixel detector, utilizing the visibility of quantum correlations to obtain high-resolution images of a sample embedded in a transparent medium. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in obtaining nanoscale-resolution images of a sample, and its applicability to various quantum interferometry techniques makes this protocol a versatile tool for biological and medical imaging. Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by their masses. Our analysis explores the potential for this extra energy to manifest as classical oscillations within inflationary models, and we identify a particular one-body potential model whose symmetry forces the oscillations' frequency to be equal to the inflationary Hubble scale. This unique model can serve as a theoretical foundation for one-sided signals observed in cosmic micromagnetism experiments. This phenomenon could be reproduced in laboratory settings through cosmological colliders, and we estimate a relevant energy scale for this process to be around thousands of GeV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that similar one-body potential models can be developed to generate cosmic dark spots, which are point-like anomalies in cosmic microwave background radiation. This development highlights a broader set of inflationary models whose density spectra exhibit distinct features, and we speculate that these spectra might be characterized by a "tooth-brush" pattern. Finally, we suggest that cosmic colliders offer a unique opportunity to detect dark matter particles through direct detection at their production site, and a future experiment like CReMA (Cosmic Rare MAss) could potentially detect such signals with a planned exposure of 300 kg-years. If completed, this experiment might rule out a substantial portion of the parameter space of the collider physics signals observed in the cosmic microwave background. We estimate that future experiments with comparable sensitivity and exposure may be able to rule out an even larger portion of the collider physics parameter space, and potentially open a window for detecting direct dark matter signals in regions currently excluded by particle physics experiments. Moreover, we anticipate that future cosmic micro-colliders with an order-of-magnitude greater sensitivity and a million-tonne experiment like CReMA may be able to discover dark matter beyond the standard model, and possibly even new particles that could constitute 100% of dark matter in the universe. Lastly, we briefly discuss the potential for future cosmic colliders to discover extra particles in the universe, and how this might be pursued as an active research area in the field. Ultimately, the potential for dark matter detection in cosmic sites presents numerous opportunities for innovative discoveries that could be exploited by future cosmic colliders, and potentially provides a key to understanding the role of new particles in the formation of the universe as we know it.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. Overall, our study's limits on energy scales represent the most stringent constraints on J/ψ decay into invisible matter to date, offering new insights into the properties of light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. Moreover, our analysis's sensitivity to different model parameters can serve as a useful reference for interpreting future experimental data. Lastly, our research's methodology on extracting new physics signals from experimental data can be useful for theoretical and experimental analyses.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing issue of coronal heating. This research aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using datasets from the SOT/Hinode and HiFI/GREGOR telescopes, to gain insights into their characteristics. Employing an automated algorithm to detect magnetic bright points, their movements were tracked, and their statistical properties were analyzed, revealing distinct distributions of area, diameter, and speed. The results indicate that these characteristics exhibit two-component structures, pointing to the presence of two distinct populations of magnetic bright points, associated with different types of magnetic flux elements, and influenced by the varying spatial resolutions of the telescopes used. The findings also show that the size and speed of magnetic bright points are correlated, and that their distributions exhibit a power-law behavior, particularly noticeable at smaller scales, which is consistent with the idea of magnetic bright points representing elementary magnetic flux elements. Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models. Furthermore, humans can improve at recognizing complex actions by focusing on essential spatial features. When human recognition abilities fall short of perfection, they mistakenly identify visible objects and, in difficult cases, resort to rough motion information. These findings reveal that human object, part, and action recognition is not solely based on static or motion cues but rather a combination of both, and this integration can be highly effective. This research aims to inspire the development of deeper network architectures that integrate spatial and temporal information for more robust action recognition. An interesting area of exploration could be designing networks that mimic human integration mechanisms for improved performance. Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of broken $U(1)$ magnetic monopoles in our observable universe as milli-magnetically charged entities confined under electromagnetism. However, the strength of their dark magnetic interactions with ordinary matter is significantly constrained by observations of galaxy halo ellipticities. Furthermore, the ground state of dark monopoles initially stable and chargeless becomes quantum mechanically unstable under an external magnetic field, an instability that can escape galactic potentials and contribute to an excess radiation background. An energy loss mechanism associated with such an instability has the potential to induce a significant dark matter annealing process, effectively reducing the monopole density by several orders of magnitude after galaxy formation. As a result, present-day limits on dark monopole-disk friction can be relaxed, opening up parameter spaces where the dark monopole model becomes more plausible. Nonetheless, the monopole density is prevented from increasing over cosmic time by an instability whose characteristics have yet to be discovered, an occurrence that could occur in the monopole sector through novel magnetic interactions with other dark matter particles that remain undiscovered. Ultimately, the dark monopole model offers an opportunity to study novel magnetic forces by examining the properties of confined entities and their potential impact on phase transitions in massive astrophysical environments. A more in-depth examination of such entities is essential for gaining a deeper understanding of the principles governing their behavior within complex systems. Specifically, in this paper, we investigate the STU model, which incorporates two scalar triplets and a scalar doublet, and demonstrate that its basis of bosons can be described by an SU(3) symmetry, enabling the analysis of potential dark matter candidates within this model. Consequently, we determine the allowed parameter ranges for both sets of dark matter candidates, which also includes the model's physical scalar doublet, charged scalar, and pseudoscalar boson masses. Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0$ to $0.5$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $1/(1-\alpha)$. The verification of this outcome is one of the goals of this article, which also proves that any subset of a given set with a $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ metric has at most two distinct elements. Furthermore, this article provides a characterization of these subsets in terms of equivalence relations connected to the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$. On the other hand, it is shown that the most common equivalence relations associated with $\alpha$ and $\beta$ do not follow specific transitivity principles that would allow them to be identified as normal binary relations. If a subset of a given set has a $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ metric, then its complement must consist of only one element, according to the findings of this research, which are accompanied by the presentation of several illustrative examples. Additionally, this article offers a computer program that can determine whether any given subset is identified as having a $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ metric. This program is primarily built with the use of Python and the help of libraries distlib and typing, which allows it to function efficiently even when dealing with large subsets. Some of the subset identification processes in the program are based on the linear programming method. The conclusions drawn from the research are that the subsets of a given set that use the $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ metric are uniquely characterized as being either an empty set, a set that contains a single element, or a set that contains two elements. The sets that contain an empty set are determined by the parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$, while sets that contain two elements are also determined by these parameters. This information is then combined into a fundamental theorem that provides a set of conditions under which the subsets of a given set use the $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ metric.

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we adopt an unconventional framework incorporating a sequential process of blur removal and subsequent reblurring with the assistance of a module that mimics real-world blur, as well as hand-crafted prior information based on advanced statistical human body models. This module not only enhances the deblurring algorithm's ability to distinguish between human and non-human regions but also improves overall outcomes compared to other recent state-of-the-art methods through adversarial learning. The effectiveness of our suggested approach is demonstrated through comprehensive deblurring benchmark tests on various real-world video datasets, with impressive results surpassing existing benchmarks in terms of pixel-wise accuracy and the quality of the deblurred images. Given its efficiency in generating blurry inputs and the improved outcomes, we propose an open-source implementation of our method in the following link: https://github.com/AlejandroRT/Unblurring-the-Avatar. Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept is further explored in a research paper, which outlines a novel, chemical-based system capable of exhibiting autonomous Hebbian learning through multiple input channels. This artificial neural network model is based on a simple, chemically-reversible reaction system, emulating a biological neuron's behavior, and is demonstrated to identify patterns in the input data it receives. In addition to the fundamental reaction system, the researchers propose more complex variations that incorporate enzymes and compartmentalised reactions to simulate biological systems, as well as a DNA-based system built upon the principle of DNA strand displacement. These innovative models offer promising avenues for exploring autonomous learning and potentially developing biological intelligent systems. The DNA-based system is shown to successfully replicate the behaviour of the original reaction system, and is also used to demonstrate learning in the form of identifying specific patterns within the input data it receives. This work opens up new avenues for exploring autonomous learning, and lays the groundwork for developing intelligent systems inspired by biological chemistry. Furthermore, the research provides an insightful comparison of the complementary roles of enzymes and DNA in autonomous learning systems. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete. Conversely, we found that if the refined version of a set is either open complete or complete, we can derive corresponding conditions on its original set. Additionally, we are unsure about whether the refined version of a set having infinite cardinality always satisfies the diamond property. It has been demonstrated, however, that if the refined version of a set has infinite cardinality and is either open complete or complete, then it does not have the minorating or square properties, respectively. It is worth noting that while the minorating property is not necessarily present in the refined version of a set, we were able to show its presence in specific situations, and even in the refined version of a set when it has a particularly simple structure. This raises questions about whether the minorating property's absence could ever be inferred from purely ordinal properties. Similarly, while the refined version of a set often fails to have the square property, we were able to find instances where the square property is present; thus, we do not know whether the square property's absence automatically implies a set having certain ordinal properties. In an attempt to shed light on this, we investigated and compared various properties present in different refined versions of specific sets, such as the set of natural numbers, the set of integers, the set of real numbers, the set of rational numbers, the set of surreal numbers, the set of integers with an added 'first integer', and the refined version of the set of natural numbers according to ultrafilters. Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, high-performance datasets are often limited to supporting only a small subset of models, hindering further discovery. 

We introduce an innovative approach called Dataset-Model Alignment, which identifies specific models that are perfectly suited to exploit the unique qualities of large scientific datasets, thus unlocking their full potential. This method employs iterative partitioning techniques to break down datasets into smaller subgroups based on varying model responses, ultimately resulting in precise matches between datasets and model families. 

Our study utilizes high-performance datasets from community standards and showcases its effectiveness in pairing datasets with specialized models for text classification, image classification, regression, and synthetic data generation. Notably, we demonstrate that models which previously failed to execute due to resource constraints can now successfully predict on these datasets thanks to the aligned partitions. Moreover, models trained on our partitioned datasets exhibit improved generalization ability and robustness against dataset noise and model regularization. 

The Dataset-Model Alignment code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/learnsvs/dataset-model-alignment. Currently, support is available for Python models and datasets in the Hugging Face dataset library; we intend to expand our scope to encompass additional models and datasets in the future. Additionally, a video summarizing our research can be found at https://youtu.be/6V1zuPvXUXY. We welcome contributions from the community to further develop and apply the Dataset-Model Alignment framework across diverse domains and datasets. We anticipate this approach to complement existing model selection and dataset debugging methods, and ultimately facilitate the development of more efficient AI models through targeted dataset improvement. 

We hope to establish Dataset-Model Alignment as a novel technique that enhances the interoperability of AI models, as well as their ability to process and generate high-performance scientific datasets in various domains such as image analysis, fluid dynamics, and molecular structure prediction. By successfully matching large datasets with specialized models, we can unlock the full potential of these resources, resulting in more accurate and efficient scientific outcomes that were previously unimaginable. 

In the near future, we envision the Dataset-Model Alignment approach to contribute to breakthroughs in scientific research by allowing us to harness the unique qualities of large datasets through precise model alignments. This, in turn, will create opportunities for novel scientific discoveries, improved dataset creation, and targeted dataset improvement. Moreover

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for recovering signals on complex networks, where the structure of the network is also unknown. The algorithm utilizes a data-driven approach, adapting to the characteristics of the network as they are discovered, by selecting the most relevant and influential nodes. The algorithm is based on the Kirchhoff Law, which represents the least aggressive intervention principle, and is developed through the utilization of the Finite Difference Scheme. The effectiveness of the algorithm is tested on various types of networks, with the performance being measured by the L2-norm of the difference between the original and reconstructed signals. The results show that the algorithm achieves optimal recovery on tree-structured networks, and the rate of convergence approaches that of known-network algorithms. The algorithm is also successfully applied to real-world problems in order to reconstruct sparse signals, and the results are compared with existing methods. The effectiveness of the algorithm is further verified through numerical experiments conducted on various types of networks. The author also presents an asymptotic analysis of the algorithm, in which the rate of convergence is determined in relation to the kernel width and the number of iterations. The results indicate that a wider kernel is beneficial in terms of convergence, but may not be desirable due to increased sensitivity to noise. The author discusses this trade-off in the context of the algorithm. The algorithm is implemented in the RPackage IPSG, which can be downloaded from cran.r-project.org/package=IPSG. The package also includes additional functions for signal recovery on known networks, as well as a function for estimating the strength of connections within networks, based on the Lasso principle. The package can be utilized in order to reconstruct signals on known networks, as well as known but noisy networks. The package further includes a function for recovering a sparse vector on an known network, based on the L1-norm minimization principle. The function is implemented through the utilization of the Proximal Gradient Descent Scheme. The strength of connections within networks can be estimated through the utilization of the Inverse Multiplicative Rules, and the results are shown to approach those of the Lasso method as the network size increases. The results are also compared with those of the Zeroth Order Optimal Transport Scheme. The package provides an alternative implementation of the Scaled Inverse Multiplicative Rules, in which the strength of connections is estimated through the utilization of the L2-norm minimization principle, based on the Proximal Gradient Descent Scheme. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Moreover, the concept of backpropagation and learning in GCNNs is presented as an iterative process where the error signal is propagated backwards, triggering a recursive co-adaptation process in neural networks. We hypothesize that this backpropagation effect is an unintended consequence of localised information exchange in neural networks. We further discuss the broader implications of our findings, highlighting the distinct roles of GCNNs' convolutional and non-convolutional layers in feature alignment and learning, respectively. The research sheds new light on the fundamental workings of GCNNs, offering a unified understanding of these networks that can facilitate the design of new GCNN architectures. A related implementation can be found at https://github.com/davidchaoauz/GraphConvolutionalNeuralNetworks. Visual explanations and numerical examples can be found at https://davidchaoauz.github.io/2021/06/23/GraphConvolutionalNeuralNetworks.html.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art strong baselines by significant margins. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that deep contextualization significantly enhances the quality of external sequence models, and this advancement remains unparalleled by other existing methods. An in-depth analysis of our parser's strengths and weaknesses has also been undertaken to inform future research and development. Finally, the source code and pre-trained models for this parser are freely available for public use at the provided link: https://github.com/jaywlee1/DCST_NDP. As an addition to this repository, our results on the WIPT task are also included (see "results_WIPT.txt"). To ensure consistency, we have adhered to the NATLIX standards in terms of dataset and evaluation metrics usage. Specifically, our parser's performance on the WIPT dataset is as follows: SRL: F1 = 69.38, P = 68.19, R = 70.17; DEP: F1 = 79.79, P = 76.35, R = 83.34; S: F1 = 66.35, P = 64.19, R = 68.07. In terms of machine hours, our parser has been implemented to run in approximately 36 hours on 8 GPUs. In contrast, it would require over 700 machine hours to implement the SCD parser on 8 GPUs. We would like to express our gratitude to the following researchers for sharing their code, which significantly facilitated our work: (1) the SCD authors; (2) the DeepContextualization authors; (3) the FlattenedTreeLSTM authors. Additionally, we would like to acknowledge the support provided by the NSF under Grant #1949113. Lastly, we would like to extend our appreciation to the researchers at the UIUC NLP group for their valuable feedback and guidance.

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent challenge lies in resolving the isomorphism problem for unordered Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs, known as the CFI-query, which has remained undefined within CPT despite being classified as a PTIME decision problem. A significant development has been achieved in understanding CPT's expressive power in addressing this issue by formulating a partial characterisation of solvable instances based on symmetric XOR-circuits for these specific graph types: In essence, for the CFI-query to be defined within a given graph class using CPT, either (i) the circuit size must be bounded by $O(\sqrt{n})$, where $n$ represents the number of vertices, or (ii) the graph class can be characterized by a finite set of properties; This finding represents an advancement in understanding CPT's capabilities in addressing the CFI-query by expanding our understanding of solvable instances from just bounded circuit sizes to a more extensive set of properties, while still precluding direct generalisation to the broader class of general unordered CIM graphs. By further examining local properties, defined as those applicable after the removal of any neighbourhood, a prominent discovery has been made: A significant subset of local properties, specifically those defined within low-bandwidth structures, remain inaccessible within CPT. This breakthrough, combined with preceding separate results, now provides separate CPT-vs-PTIME separations for two prominent decision problems: (i) the CFI-query and (ii) the Simon's Circuit Problem on undirected graphs. Furthermore, CPT has been proven inadequate to address any decision problem that, on low-bandwidth structures, admits a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm parameterised by the rank of symmetric XOR-circuits, a problem that includes the CFI-query and extends to other decision problems like general CIM graphs. To explore the properties of the resulting series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 was studied via HAXPES. Interestingly, Bi substitution unexpectedly led to a significant (20 %) reduction in the lattice size at relatively low levels of Bi (3.5 %) doping. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Traditional IBI estimation methods tend to fail in such scenarios, leading us to investigate a deep learning technique that we call the Time-Difference Convolutional Neural Network (TD-CNN). This novel network focuses specifically on inter-beat differences during training, enabling it to accurately identify tachycardia and fibrillation patterns in ECG signals affected by motion noise. Our results show that the TD-CNN outperforms existing approaches, including a leading deep learning method, in a simulated environment that mimics the ECG characteristics of an elite athlete running at high speeds. Furthermore, we successfully tested the TD-CNN on actual signals from wearable devices, demonstrating its ability to effectively handle real-world motion noise and achieve a high level of accuracy. This research provides a foundation for future studies aimed at developing more sophisticated cardiovascular health monitors using deep learning techniques. Such advanced monitors could potentially offer a high degree of accuracy, making them suitable for a variety of applications including wearables, mobile computing, and cloud-based monitoring systems. Currently, we have made our source code and data available to the public through our GitHub repository at https://github.com/jgbaro/TD-CNN. This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture high-definition videos of individuals engaging in various activities and expressions in a vast outdoor environment. Following footage collection, each sequence is annotated with precise 3D joint positions to facilitate efficient and efficient training of computer vision models. The comprehensive dataset comprises approximately 49,000 frames, with a average frame rate of 20 frames per second. The large-scale dataset is made accessible through public download, featuring accompanying annotation files. The planned dataset has the potential to advance state-of-the-art human body expression models via continuous expansion of its collection. The proposed HUMBI dataset focuses on addressing several key challenges and provides valuable resources for developing more sophisticated human body expression models. The utility of this dataset is exemplified through the training of a pose recognition model, which demonstrates the significance of accurately detecting human body postures. The remarkable performance of this model in detecting human body postures underscores the large variety of human body expressions captured within HUMBI, which is anticipated to serve as a valuable resource for the computer vision community. Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development, and maintenance. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant features from the foreign languages it adapts to, as evidenced by the insights gleaned from the model embeddings. The source code, data, and pre-trained models used in this research are freely accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/multi_task_neural_adaptation. The repository includes comprehensive instructions that can aid in replicating the results described in this paper. The language transfer capability is particularly useful for languages that have limited NLP resources but do require advanced models, as seen in our case studies on Czech and Filipino sentiment classification. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Ultimately, our strategy proves to be over 20% more effective than using
a single shared dynamics model in multiple tasks. Our method is also compared
to other established multi-task reinforcement learning techniques for verification. 
Here is a summary of our approach, named TaskIsolation-MBM (Shared Dynamics Model
with Task-isolated Networks): 
1) A single dynamics model is trained to predict observations and actions
from a state in multiple tasks.
2) For each new state, separate sub-networks are used to predict the
next state for each individual task.
3) These sub-networks are used to run policy-optimal samples for each task.
4) Policy-optimal samples are combined to run multi-task policy-optimal samples.
5) Policy-optimal samples and multi-task policy-optimal samples are combined
to run a joint policy.

Our method is distinct from other multi-task reinforcement learning approaches
such as multi-task prior-free model-based reinforcement learning, shared
latent dynamics models, and multi-task state-free model-based reinforcement
learning. Additionally, our method stands out from existing multi-task
reinforcement learning techniques like multi-task reinforcement learning with
shared action-value functions and multi-task reinforcement learning with
shared policies. Our method of shared dynamics models in multiple tasks is
